Asokastami — Incredible India

body:
# Ashoka Astami Brata

Ashoka Astami opens three related but different lines of enquiry: a household vow for children, a prayer involving spring flower buds, and Bhubaneswar’s Rukuna Ratha festival. Their shared name invites comparison. It does not yet establish one story, one deity or one meal across all three.

**Research note: household history and foods remain unresolved; festival legend and textual prescription retain their own scopes.**

## A household vow to Surya

Mahanti describes married women observing a Chaitra bright-eighth vow to Surya for their children’s well-being. His brief entry names no food or household katha. He also says the vow is no longer observed, but gives no survey or locality-level evidence for that conclusion; its present prevalence remains unknown.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed53/PDF69, Ashoka ashtami brata.

## Rama and the festival story

In Mahanti’s separate festival account, Ravana is protected by Durga. Following Vibhishana’s advice, Rama worships her; she withdraws her support on the eighth day. Rama defeats Ravana and celebrates with a chariot procession of Shiva and Durga. This is the author’s attributed legend, not a dated founding event or a recovered story of the household Surya vow.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed107–108/PDF123–124, Ashoka astami puja.

## The public procession as a separate setting

Incredible India places Asokastami at Lingaraja in Bhubaneswar and describes the Rukuna Ratha procession to Rameswara Temple. Its Rama-origin account is presented here as mythology. The page’s general invitation to experience local gastronomy names neither an observance-specific dish nor a verified serving place.

Sources: [Asokastami — Incredible India](https://www.incredibleindia.gov.in/en/odisha/bhubaneswar/asokastami). Historical Roots and Celebratory Myths; The Spectacle of the Rukuna Rath Yatra; Engaging in the Festivities.

## Eight buds in a textual prescription

The opening of chapter CXXXIII in the Garuda Purana translation attributed to Manmatha Nath Dutt prescribes eating eight ashoka flower buds on Chaitra’s bright eighth when joined with Punarvasu. Its prayer addresses ashoka as dear to Hara and seeks release from grief. This is a ritual prescription and promise within the text, not evidence of a health effect.

Sources: [Garuda Purana, Dutt translation: Asokastami Vratas etc., chapter CXXXIII](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-garuda-purana-dutt/d/doc122613.html). Chapter CXXXIII opening paragraph, before Mahanavami.

## What this adds to food history

The bud passage records ritual consumption rather than a complete cooked meal. It does not identify the household Surya vow’s offerings, a fast-breaking dish, an Odisha recipe or a present serving custom. Nothing in the inspected passage supplies curd or a preparation method. The text is recorded for cultural comparison, not as a foraging or eating recommendation.

## History: distinguish witnesses from origins

The digital host labels Dutt’s translation1908; that bibliographic attribution does not date the Sanskrit passage, its arrival in Odisha or the beginning of the household vow. A dated local text, a securely identified edition and situated accounts are needed to connect the three settings historically. Mahanti’s compilation and a tourism retelling cannot establish uninterrupted continuity.

## Significance: care and the wish to lose sorrow

Concern for children, the textual prayer against grief and the festival’s story of recovery offer different ways to explore care and hope. This is an editorial comparison. It leaves room for participants to explain their own meanings rather than fitting every practice into one origin story. In food research, the most useful next question is what each community actually offers, shares and eats.

## For a seasonal visitor

Treat Chaitra as a traditional calendar label requiring a year-specific local check. The public procession and household vow need separate access information. No current date, food seller, tasting arrangement or consenting household host has been established. The named flower in a religious text must not be turned into a visitor menu.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can an original Odia household katha or dated witness identify the Surya vow and its transmission?
- What evidence supports continuity, change or non-observance in named localities?
- Can an identifiable print edition and Sanskrit passage verify the digital Garuda Purana transcription?
- Does an inspected Balarama Dasa Ramayana passage connect Sita and ashoka buds, as a later article suggests?
- What foods are offered, shared and eaten in each household or temple setting, with recipes and local names?
- Can a current authoritative schedule and willing host establish a specific visitor opportunity?

[Samba Dashami](samba-dashami.md). Ashoka Astami’s described Surya vow can be read beside Samba Dashami’s family-care account; shared solar devotion does not transfer a katha, calendar or menu.

[Preparation and variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). A textual item consumed in a rite is not automatically a household recipe or visitor dish; Ashoka Astami keeps those food roles distinct.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No project fieldwork or human cultural review claimed.

body:
# Bada Osha

A fast, a night of Shiva worship and a steamed offering connect Bada Osha to the food year around Dhabaleswar. Its stories deserve to be read alongside the limits of the surviving evidence.

**Early research notes: history and local narrative remain incomplete.** Traditional month: Kartika. No annual visit date is confirmed.

## A story of refuge at Dhabaleswar

Odisha Tourism tells a popular legend in which Shiva turns a black calf white to protect a repentant thief. The story links the shrine’s name to whiteness, mercy and forgiveness. It is a modern institutional retelling of sacred tradition, not a dated historical event or a complete Bada Osha katha.

Sources: [Dhabaleswar Temple](https://odishatourism.gov.in/w/dhabaleswar-temple). Discover the Heritage, opening paragraph.

## Another explanation of the observance

Mahanti relates Indra bathing in the Mahanadi and worshipping Shiva at Dhabaleswar to escape Brahma’s curse. He attributes this to the Padma Purana but supplies no edition or verse here. We have inspected his account, not the cited Puranic passage. The Indra story and the calf legend answer different questions and should not be joined into one origin narrative.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed pp.58–59 / PDF74–75.

## Fasting, worship and the offering

Mahanti describes the fast ending towards midnight after the deity’s bada singhara adornment, a large lamp and offerings of gaja bhoga and atakali. This is his ritual sequence, not a verified timetable for an upcoming festival.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.59 / PDF75.

## Two descriptions of steamed gaja

Mahanti describes rice-dough balls with a sweet coconut filling, cooked by steaming. The Jagatsinghpur gazetteer instead emphasizes linga and snake shapes. Both describe steamed offerings; they do not establish one universal form. Neither description identifies this food with fried chhena gaja or the wheat-and-sugar gaja in our separate food-name study.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Odisha District Gazetteers: Jagatsinghpur](https://jagatsinghpur.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2023-05/2018051050.pdf). Mahanti printed p.59 / PDF75; Jagatsinghpur printed p.52.

## Atakali has a separate place

Mahanti names atakali alongside gaja and describes it as a wheat-flour preparation resembling kheeri. Quantities, cooking times, local variants and a current temple recipe remain unverified.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.59 / PDF75.

## Why the calendar remains unresolved

Mahanti gives Kartika’s bright thirteenth or fourteenth day, while the Jagatsinghpur gazetteer names Kartika Purnima. We retain those statements separately. A difference between fast, offering and fast-breaking dates is a question for an annual temple notice, not a reconciliation established by these texts.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Odisha District Gazetteers: Jagatsinghpur](https://jagatsinghpur.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2023-05/2018051050.pdf). Mahanti printed p.58 / PDF74; Jagatsinghpur printed p.52.

## Reading the meaning through food

The sequence makes food more than an ingredient list: preparation and waiting lead to an offering, then eating. This is an editorial reading of the documented sequence. Shaping, filling and steaming are practical culinary skills; these accounts provide no measured thermal study, nutrient analysis or demonstrated health benefit.

## A source disagreement we will not hide

Incredible India’s text says the thief becomes a white cow, whereas Odisha Tourism says the calf changes colour. We record the discrepancy without declaring it a distinct local tradition or silently correcting either publisher. Their temple-history assertions also lack the original records needed here to establish a founding date.

Sources: [Dhabaleswar Temple](https://odishatourism.gov.in/w/dhabaleswar-temple), [Visit the divine Dhabaleswar Temple in Cuttack](https://www.incredibleindia.gov.in/en/odisha/cuttack/dhabaleswar-temple). Odisha Tourism opening paragraph; Incredible India: A tale of divine intervention and The magnificence of Dhabaleswar Temple.

## Reading before a visit

The food association can guide cultural curiosity in Kartika, but it does not promise a meal or permission to join worship. Confirm the festival notice, access arrangements and offering distribution separately. This study establishes no annual date, serving venue, opening hours or present bridge conditions.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Which dated Bada Osha katha and exact Padma Purana passage can be inspected?
- How do temple cooks distinguish gaja shapes, filling and atakali across occasions?
- What does a temple-issued annual schedule say about fasting, offering and distribution?
- What original record can reconcile the two tourism retellings and the shrine’s construction chronology?

[Gaja and Kanti evidence](../../food/gaja-kanti-evidence.md). Compare names and preparation methods without treating different foods as aliases.

body:
# Baisakha Brata

Baisakha Brata joins a month of devotion to a repeated evening meal. The food matters through its place in a daily sequence of worship, reading and restraint. Broader Vaishakha stories also give food another role: hospitality to people travelling in the heat.

**Research note: published Odisha practice and a comparative devotional story; local text, origin and recipe remain unresolved.**

## A month of Vishnu devotion

Mahanti describes Baisakha Brata throughout the lunar month, observed by married women and widows. Worship of Vishnu or a temple visit, together with reading the Vishnu Purana, precedes the meal. He says no formal brata is worn. Dash also lists Baisakha, but supplies no further description. These accounts do not establish a universal household rule or current participation rate.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed 45 / PDF61; Dash printed 16 / PDF2.

## The meal: havishanna or kechudi

Mahanti names havishanna or kechudi as the single meal taken towards evening. He supplies no proportions, grain or pulse variety, vegetables, seasoning or cooking method. The two names are retained without turning them into a fixed recipe or assuming they denote exactly the same preparation. A local account should explain how the meal is made and who shares it.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed 45 / PDF61.

## A comparative story of hospitality

In V. D. N. Rao’s condensed Skanda Purana telling, King Kirtiman encounters Vasishtha’s disciples offering shade, fruit and drinks to travellers. After learning about Vaishakha, he extends such service across his kingdom. Vishnu protects his devotion when Yama objects to its extraordinary results. This is a religious narrative from a broader tradition, not a documented Odisha king or an identified local Baisakha katha.

Sources: [Essence of Skanda Purana: Vaisakha Month’s Significance](https://www.kamakoti.org/kamakoti/details/skandapurana28.html). Web chapter 28, King Kirtiman paragraphs.

## Food given and food eaten

Rao’s account commends supplying water, meals and shelter in Vaishakha. These gifts belong to its account of charity. They do not establish the ingredients of an Odisha observer’s evening meal. Mahanti’s reference to reading the Vishnu Purana likewise does not identify this Skanda Purana story as the text read locally.

Sources: [Essence of Skanda Purana: Vaisakha Month’s Significance](https://www.kamakoti.org/kamakoti/details/skandapurana28.html), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Rao web chapter 28, water-charity paragraphs; Mahanti printed 45 / PDF61.

## History still needs its own evidence

No dated origin for the Odisha vow or complete identified Odia telling has been established here. Search-index results point to museum catalogue entries titled Baisakha Mahatmya, but the catalogue originals could not be retrieved in this run. A title match cannot identify the work recited by a household, date the custom or prove separate textual variants. Manuscript contents remain unread.

## Significance and the questions food opens

An editorial interpretation can follow two kinds of work: sustaining one’s own observance and offering refreshment to others. The comparison invites questions about kitchens, ingredients, water provision and learning across generations. It does not prove that a particular Odisha practice descended from the comparative story. Pana Sankranti, Akshaya Tritiya and the month-long vow require their own evidence; sharing a seasonal setting is not enough to merge their foods or histories.

## For seasonal visitors

Baisakha is a cultural browsing cue, not a verified annual appointment. A solar month label, a lunar observance and a specific festival day should be checked against the relevant local calendar before travel. No current-year dates, serving venue, household invitation, host consent or special menu have been verified.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can an identified Odia Baisakha text, cover, imprint and relevant narrative/food pages be recovered?
- What are the museum catalogue’s exact identifiers, script, language, copy dates and contents for Baisakha Mahatmya?
- Which work and passages do named local observers read, and how do these relate to the Vishnu Purana reference?
- What is the earliest dated Odisha evidence for the month-long vow?
- How do local households distinguish havishanna and kechudi, and prepare and share them?
- What local start/end rule and consenting public food offer can support a visitor listing?

[Preparation And Variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). Baisakha names havishanna and kechudi but supplies no recipe; preparation research should document an attributed local version.

[Magha Brata](../../culture/osha/magha-brata.md). Mahanti describes both Baisakha and Magha as month-long vows, but their named meals and local calendar rules need separate evidence.

[Rai Damodara Brata](../../culture/osha/rai-damodara-brata.md). The three-month comparison in Mahanti connects Baisakha with Kartika devotion; it does not transfer a Kartika food recipe or story into Baisakha.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No local interviews or human review claimed.

sources.title: Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha
Bajra Mahakali Brata O Phuleri Osha Katha — Project Pothi scan

body:
# Bajra Mahakali Brata

In the Bajra Mahakali story, a household prepares an offering while a young daughter-in-law makes a small, consequential mistake: she tastes two grains of rice. Food becomes the thread connecting fear, a difficult promise, separation and a return home. The recovered Odia text also remembers work around the kitchen and the sharing of prasad beyond the family.

**Narrative checkpoint: one Odia scan read; dating, local practice and recipes remain unresolved.**

## The observance in a published Odisha account

Mahanti places Bajra Mahakali Brata on Aswina amabasya. He describes married women fasting, preparing the household space, offering varieties of pitha to Kali and listening to the brata-katha. Hopes for children are part of his account of devotion, not evidence of a fertility effect. His statement that few people now observe the vow has no stated survey denominator and is not adopted as a current prevalence measure.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed49/PDF65.

## A promise made beside the rice

The inspected story opens in a prosperous sadhaba, or merchant, household with seven sons and seven daughters-in-law. As the women prepare for the goddess’s worship, the youngest daughter-in-law tastes two grains of soaked rice. Bajra Mahakali confronts her for tasting the unoffered food. Afraid her mother-in-law will hear, she promises the goddess her future sons. The narrative’s accusation and punishment belong to its ritual world; they are not a judgment on women today.

Sources: [Bajra Mahakali Brata O Phuleri Osha Katha — Project Pothi scan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Bajra_Mahakali_Brata_O_Phuleri_Osha_Katha.pdf). PDF2–3.

## The loss and the return

The goddess takes six sons in succession. During the seventh pregnancy, the mother-in-law drives the young woman out on the observance day. In the rain and darkness, the goddess meets her as an old woman, hears her suffering and shelters her. After the seventh birth, she returns the six earlier sons too. The mother comes home with all seven children and explains what happened. The ending presents continued observance as the outcome of the goddess’s test and mercy. These are events within the katha, not verified historical events.

Sources: [Bajra Mahakali Brata O Phuleri Osha Katha — Project Pothi scan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Bajra_Mahakali_Brata_O_Phuleri_Osha_Katha.pdf). PDF6–11.

## What the kitchen passages actually say

The women soak rice and biri, and the rice is to be pounded into flour. A preparation called aradra in the transcription is cooked in a handi; at first it fails to cook, then succeeds after the daughter-in-law appeals to the goddess. The text does not provide ingredient proportions, the complete method or enough detail to identify this preparation with a familiar modern pitha. That identification remains an open food-history question.

Sources: [Bajra Mahakali Brata O Phuleri Osha Katha — Project Pothi scan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Bajra_Mahakali_Brata_O_Phuleri_Osha_Katha.pdf). PDF3–4; aradra spelling compared with Wikisource transcription.

## Offerings and food shared with neighbours

The worship scene places aradra on seven pumpkin leaves. It names banana, coconut and a preparation of seven kinds of greens, without naming the greens individually. It also uses the categories nishankhudi and shankhudi; their precise contents here require local explanation. After the worship and story, the prasad is shared among those present and given to neighbours. Plants and branches arranged for worship are recorded separately from edible dishes; their presence does not make every plant an ingredient.

Sources: [Bajra Mahakali Brata O Phuleri Osha Katha — Project Pothi scan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Bajra_Mahakali_Brata_O_Phuleri_Osha_Katha.pdf). PDF5.

## Names and dates need their own evidence

The title pairs Bajra Mahakali Brata with Phuleri Osha, while the body uses Polari/Polori forms and names Aswina amabasya. This supports an association within this particular text, not a universal equivalence with every similarly named Pithori observance elsewhere. No Gregorian date or named locality’s present calendar has been verified.

Sources: [Bajra Mahakali Brata O Phuleri Osha Katha — Project Pothi scan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Bajra_Mahakali_Brata_O_Phuleri_Osha_Katha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). PDF1–2,7,10–11; Mahanti printed49/PDF65.

## History: a recovered witness with an undated imprint

Project Pothi’s repository credits Prateek Pattanaik with providing and scanning the booklet and records its upload in2017. Its description gives a1934 date and claims a sixteenth-century or sixteenth-to-seventeenth-century author, but the supplied pages show no original imprint establishing these claims. The anonymous scan is a recoverable textual witness; neither the composition date nor the beginning of the observance is established. Its merchant-family setting alone is not evidence of an overseas-trade origin.

Sources: [Bajra Mahakali Brata O Phuleri Osha Katha — Project Pothi scan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Bajra_Mahakali_Brata_O_Phuleri_Osha_Katha.pdf). Commons description/date/author and file-history fields; all11 PDF pages inspected for imprint.

## Significance: household labour and belonging

Read as a story, the katha brings a young woman’s vulnerability into the same space as ritual discipline, cooking and family authority. The reunion changes the course of blame and exclusion. The food scene adds a social dimension: offerings become something the family and neighbours share. This is an editorial interpretation of one narrative, not a claim that all participants explain the vow this way. A future account from willing local practitioners should be allowed to differ.

## For a seasonal food journey

The text provides questions for a guide or food researcher: what is aradra called locally, which greens are used, who prepares the offering, and how is it shared? It does not verify a tasting venue, public invitation, purchasable meal or current household practice. Keep the food association visible, and confirm a willing host and local date before planning an encounter.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can an original dated edition, publisher record or manuscript establish the composition and print history?
- How do named local participants distinguish Phuleri, Polari/Polori and other Pithori names and calendars?
- What preparation does aradra denote here, and what are its ingredients, method and local variants?
- Which seven greens and which nishankhudi/shankhudi foods are meant in a named household?
- What food breaks the fast, as distinct from the story’s offered and shared prasad?
- How do participants interpret the daughter-in-law’s vulnerability, the goddess’s test and the family reunion?
- Can a willing host verify an annual date, access and an actual food arrangement?

[Sathi](sathi.md). Bajra Mahakali and Sathi both bring children and household care into ritual stories; compare their separately sourced narratives without merging deities, foods or calendars.

[Preparation and variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). Bajra Mahakali’s text names aradra and seven greens, but a textual food name is not a complete recipe or verified current preparation.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No field interviews or human language review claimed.

Socio-Cultural Context and Aesthetic Values of 'Jhoti'

body:
# Bali Trutiya

Bali Trutiya brings together a vow, a story of choosing a husband, and food withheld, offered and eventually eaten.

**Narrative checkpoint; origin date, local variation and public availability remain open.**

## Sand gives the observance a tangible form

Mahanti describes married women worshipping Shiva and Parvati through sand images on Bhadraba’s bright-fortnight third day. He explains the name through bali, meaning sand. Dash lists Bali Trutiya or Tija Brata Katha among bratas. These descriptions establish a named tradition in modern accounts, not its starting date.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed57 / PDF73; Dash printed16 / PDF2.

## The story in the recovered Odia text

Parvati asks Shiva how she came to marry him. He recalls her father’s promise to Vishnu, her distress, and a friend who takes her into the forest. Beside a river she fasts and worships Shiva; he grants her wish. Her father later accepts her chosen marriage. This is the booklet’s ritual narrative, not a historical event.

Sources: [Bali Trutiya ba Tija Brata Katha — scanned Odia text](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/33/Bali_Trutiya_Brata.pdf). PDF pp.3–10; narrative decision pp.6–7, river and vow pp.8–9, resolution p.10.

## Fruit offered, fruit eaten

In the story, Parvati breaks her fast with forest fruit after the immersion. Later instructions separately list fruit among offerings and prohibit eating on Tritiya. These are different food roles within one text. The passage supplies neither fruit species nor a cooked-dish recipe.

Sources: [Bali Trutiya ba Tija Brata Katha — scanned Odia text](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/33/Bali_Trutiya_Brata.pdf). PDF p.9, banajata phala and parana; p.10, phala nibedana; p.11, fasting injunction.

## Reading its significance

The friend’s intervention makes this story useful for discussing companionship and a woman’s expressed choice, alongside family authority. That is an editorial reading, not evidence of how every practitioner understands the vow. The text’s threats of misfortune for women who eat are devotional rhetoric; the encyclopedia does not attribute bereavement or suffering to someone’s food choices.

## A season, not a confirmed travel date

The booklet names Bhadraba shukla Tritiya with Hasta nakshatra. This is a traditional calendar rule; converting it into a date for a particular year requires a separately checked local calendar.

Sources: [Bali Trutiya ba Tija Brata Katha — scanned Odia text](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/33/Bali_Trutiya_Brata.pdf). PDF p.4 and pp.8–9.

## What can be said about its history?

The archive’s approximate eighteenth-century attribution, its metadata date of 8 February 1934, and the newsletter’s 2005 label do not agree. The supplied scan contains an excerpt and a digital cover, with no verified publication imprint. Edition and composition dates therefore remain unknown. Mahanti also relates a Rama-before-Lanka legend and attributes a Parvati account to the Padma Purana; neither an original Purana chapter nor the relationship between these versions has been established here.

## A maritime interpretation remains unresolved

Biswal and Dash’s jhoti article associates a celebration named Bali Trutiya with boat drawings and trade with Bali. That account has not been reconciled with the sand-image Shiva–Parvati descriptions. It is retained as a source conflict requiring locality and textual verification, not adopted as maritime history or an explanation of this name.

Sources: [Socio-Cultural Context and Aesthetic Values of 'Jhoti'](https://utkaluniversity.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Man-in-Society-Anthropology.pdf). Printed116 / PDF117 item7.

## Practical knowledge and visitor use

A useful next inquiry would document sand selection and shaping, preparation of offerings, the order of immersion and eating, and who performs that work in a named locality. The present evidence does not establish recipes, preservation techniques or health benefits. Visitors can use Bhadraba as a cultural reading window; there is no confirmed event date, serving venue or host invitation in this record.

History comparison: [scan catalogue](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bali_Trutiya_Brata.pdf), [2021 newsletter](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Indic_Wikisource_Community/Newsletter/January-March_2021), and [Mahanti](../../sources/osha-mahanti.md), printed57 / PDF73. These dates are held, not adopted.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Recover the parent Bratabali volume and its imprint; resolve the archive’s conflicting dates and author identity.
- Compare the original Odia wording with a second dated witness and an identified Purana passage.
- Document local food preparation, offering, sharing and fast-breaking without treating the story as a universal household menu.
- Identify the locality and source behind the boat-jhoti interpretation; establish whether it concerns the same observance.
- Verify annual dates and any consented public food offers separately.

[Sabitri Brata](sabitri.md). Compare women’s expressed choices in two ritual narratives without treating their plots or food rules as interchangeable.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No interviews, human cultural review or image permissions claimed.

[Gouri Brata](gouri-brata.md). Some discovery accounts associate Gouri Brata with Bali Trutiya; compare the saved Bali narrative before accepting an alias or transferring its calendar and foods.

body:
# Bata Osha

A village path becomes a place of prayer. Accounts of Bata Osha bring sweeping, family welfare and food offerings into the same ritual space, while disagreeing on its calendar and related names.

**Early research notes: history, local identities and calendar remain incomplete.** No annual visit date is confirmed.

## A story of protection

Sarangi relates a tradition that Kunti performed this worship during the Pandavas’ exile and entrusted her sons’ protection to Yama. This is her retelling; an exact epic passage or dated katha witness has not been inspected. It cannot establish when the observance began.

Sources: [ଓଡିଆ ଘରେ ‘ଶୀତ ଋତୁ’](https://samadhwani.com/1311). Margasira road-sweeping/Bata paragraph before Prathamastami.

## The work of tending a path

Sarangi describes girls sweeping together with bajramuli brooms during Margasira, accompanied by a song. Her account culminates at the full moon with a decorated panthei pit and images of the Pandavas and Yama. She interprets cleared paths as helping families carrying harvested rice. That practical explanation is an author’s interpretation, not demonstrated proof of the ritual’s origin.

Sources: [ଓଡିଆ ଘରେ ‘ଶୀତ ଋତୁ’](https://samadhwani.com/1311). Margasira opening, song and following paragraph.

## Worship outside the house

Mahanti describes women worshipping Yama at crossroads for husbands and children, with the offering covered by a bajramuli branch. He treats the outdoor location as meaningful in relation to Yama. This describes a source-specific practice; it does not identify a present public ceremony or permission for visitors to join.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.60 / PDF76.

## Manda, chakuli and the covered offering

Sarangi names fruit, manda and chakuli pitha as offerings. Dash and Mahanti describe covered bhoga without specifying that same menu. We therefore keep the named foods attributed to Sarangi. Her passage does not specify dough, filling or cooking method; it cannot identify the manda as the particular sijha preparation in our food entry.

Sources: [ଓଡିଆ ଘରେ ‘ଶୀତ ଋତୁ’](https://samadhwani.com/1311), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Sarangi Bata paragraph; Dash printed15 / PDF1; Mahanti printed60 / PDF76.

## Names that should not yet be merged

Dash lists Bata with Yama and separately lists Danda Panhara with Shiva in Pausa. Mahanti calls the observance Bata or Danda pahara and describes Yama worship. We preserve both records without declaring the names universally interchangeable or claiming two independently established traditions. Local naming and textual comparison remain necessary.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed15 / PDF1; Mahanti printed60 / PDF76.

## Why there is no single date here

Mahanti specifies Pausa’s dark-fortnight second day. Sarangi’s sequence culminates at the Margasira full moon. We do not reconcile these descriptions by guessing at local calendars or ritual stages. The traditional timing stays source-specific, and no annual Gregorian date is supplied.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [ଓଡିଆ ଘରେ ‘ଶୀତ ଋତୁ’](https://samadhwani.com/1311). Mahanti printed60 / PDF76; Sarangi Margasira/Bata sequence.

## What the practice makes visible

An editorial reading connects care for relatives with work in shared village space. Sweeping and food preparation are practical skills, but these accounts provide no measured health outcome, sanitation trial or botanical identification of bajramuli. Nor do an author’s statements about decline establish that the practice has disappeared across Odisha today.

## A book lead, not a recovered history

OdiaPortal advertises a Bata Osha–Danda Pahanra text and directs readers to an Android app. Its claim of a 1970s book has not been checked against an imprint. The landing page was readable; the book’s contents, authorship and date remain unverified. No complete katha or earliest historical witness is claimed.

Sources: [Download Bata Osha – Danda Pahanra Bahi Gita](https://www.odiaportal.in/2015/12/Bata-Osha-Danda-Pahanra-Brata-Katha-Odia-PDF.html). About Book and app-only download notice.

## For a visitor following the food year

Use this entry to understand a cultural association and ask about local practice. No venue, public food distribution, annual event date, host consent or current serving availability has been established. Manda and chakuli can be explored as foods without treating a private vow as a bookable experience.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Which dated Bata or Danda Panhara text can be inspected with its imprint?
- How do local observers distinguish Bata, Danda Panhara and similarly named Panthei practices?
- Do the different calendar statements describe local variants, stages or an error?
- Which manda and chakuli preparations are offered in a named household or locality?

[Manda pitha](../../food/manda-pitha.md). Connects a sourced offering name to separately documented preparations; no single ritual recipe implied.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md). Individual observance narrative, food context and source boundaries.

[Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No interviews, human cultural review or image permissions are claimed.

## 2026-10-07 · Pandu comparison

[Pandu Osha](pandu.md). Compare related road-sweeping accounts without merging their identities or resolving the disputed sequence.

## 2026-10-07 · Shani/Tota comparison

[Shani / Tota Osha](shani-tota.md). Compare how sources describe outdoor ritual settings without treating the observances as the same tradition.

Rice culture and sacred siblingship: Nua Khai and Bhai Jiuntia celebrations in Western Odisha, India

body:
# Bhai Jiuntia

Food and a returning sister’s place in the family are central questions for reading this western Odisha vow.

**Research note.** Practice and food accounts are documented; full ritual stories and earliest histories remain open.

## Sisters, brothers and the autumn calendar

Mahanti describes sisters invoking Durga on Ashwina’s bright-fortnight eighth day, returning to parental homes and exchanging gifts. He names jugara and tikhiri as offerings shared by sisters and brothers.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed pp.49–51 / PDF65–67.

## A recent ethnographic window

Indhubala Kesavan reports eleven months of fieldwork during May2022–December2023 in Bargarh district. The village name is a pseudonym. Her account connects married sisters’ homecoming, gifts and ritual duties with rice cultivation.

Sources: [Rice culture and sacred siblingship: Nua Khai and Bhai Jiuntia celebrations in Western Odisha, India](https://journals.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/paideuma/index.php/paideuma/article/download/2046/2237/4542). Printed pp.15,31–35 / PDF1,17–21.

## Malathi and Mathana Kumar: a story in recitation

Kesavan records an elderly participant’s story of Malathi, whose prayers to Durga save her brother Mathana Kumar from death. The participant associates it with a Bhai Jiuntia osa-katha booklet; the researcher also observed married sisters gathering to recite the story on the festival evening. This is an attributed narrative synopsis and witnessed recitation, not a complete recovered text or historical event.

Source: [Rice culture and sacred siblingship: Nua Khai and Bhai Jiuntia celebrations in Western Odisha, India](https://journals.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/paideuma/index.php/paideuma/article/download/2046/2237/4542). Printed22/PDF8, second story paragraph.

## From paddy to lia jugar

Kesavan describes an older woman collecting household paddy, roasting and redistributing it. Stored parched rice is mixed with melted jaggery into conical lia jugar for worship, then shared. This documents collective processing and skilled labour; temperatures and proportions are not supplied.

Sources: [Rice culture and sacred siblingship: Nua Khai and Bhai Jiuntia celebrations in Western Odisha, India](https://journals.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/paideuma/index.php/paideuma/article/download/2046/2237/4542). Printed p.33 / PDF19; preparation and distribution paragraphs.

## Honour alongside unequal treatment

The study also records caste-separated worship and discusses women’s ritual importance alongside structural inequality. These findings belong to the study’s setting, not a statewide measurement. Food sharing does not by itself establish social inclusion.

Sources: [Rice culture and sacred siblingship: Nua Khai and Bhai Jiuntia celebrations in Western Odisha, India](https://journals.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/paideuma/index.php/paideuma/article/download/2046/2237/4542). Printed pp.19,33,35 / PDF5,19,21; abstract p.15.

## What kind of history is this?

The ethnographic account documents a narrated story and contemporary practice; it does not establish an ancient founding date. A complete Bhai Jiuntia booklet and its edition history remain unrecovered. The Malathi synopsis must not be expanded into invented episodes or treated as every community’s version.

## Related traditions without collapsing identities

Thread tying provides a useful comparison with other observances, but it cannot establish one origin or a single statewide ritual. Pua Jiuntia remains a separate profile. Dalkhai offers another contextual reading route; an association with this occasion is not proof of a scheduled performance.

## Seasonal reading for visitors

The lunar date is a cultural label, not a confirmed event listing. Serving availability and public access remain unknown. The ethnographer’s anonymized village must not be converted into a destination or host recommendation.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can the indexed Susil Kumar Panigrahi article be recovered with its issue and pages?
- Which local kathas and dated historical witnesses explain the vow?
- How do food preparation and invitation customs vary across western Odisha communities?

title: Binayaka Brata
description: Binayaka Brata — attributed narrative, food roles and historical evidence.

sources.title: The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview
ବିନାୟକ ବ୍ରତକଥା · Binayaka Brata Katha
The Orissa Gazette, 29 October 1937: catalogue entry 172, Binayaka Brata Katha
Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha

body:
# Binayaka Brata

Twenty-one sweets become a small map of giving: one for Ganesha, ten for a Brahmin and ten for the person observing the vow. A recovered Binayaka booklet makes this division explicit. It offers a way to explore devotion through food, while a separate government record takes the printed history of a same-titled work back to 1936.

**Narrative checkpoint: an Odia booklet and a separate historical catalogue record inspected; origin, edition dating and local preparation remain open.**

## The annual vow and its neighbours

Dash lists Binayaka Brata in Bhadrab as Ganesh worship. Mahanti places annual Ganesh Puja on Bhadrava’s bright fourth and distinguishes it from recurring bright-fortnight Binayak and dark-fortnight Sankati vows. Their similar names do not establish identical menus or fasting rules.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed16/PDF2; Mahanti printed43–44/PDF59–60 and79/PDF95.

## A booklet with more than one calendar passage

The recovered booklet opens with Bhadraba bright-fortnight Chaturthi and a rule involving midday. Its later katha also names other months, including Srabana and Margasira. These passages need fuller textual comparison before their calendar relationships can be explained. No annual Gregorian date is calculated here.

Sources: [ବିନାୟକ ବ୍ରତକଥା · Binayaka Brata Katha](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=12JXOi753dG0dGBS9HU-R0oLX_dLhwqPs). PDF3/printed1 opening directions; PDF7–8/printed5–6 Sanskrit verses and Odia explanation.

## Yudhishthira asks how to recover what was lost

The katha frames its teaching through Suta’s narration to sages. Yudhishthira asks Krishna which deity he should worship to overcome his troubles and regain his kingdom. Krishna directs him to Ganapati and explains the vow. The text draws on a wider sacred world of exemplary devotees, then says Yudhishthira followed the teaching and recovered his kingdom. This is a devotional account of the vow’s power, not evidence that these events occurred historically or that the practice began in Odisha at that time.

Sources: [ବିନାୟକ ବ୍ରତକଥା · Binayaka Brata Katha](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=12JXOi753dG0dGBS9HU-R0oLX_dLhwqPs). PDF6–8/printed4–6 opening dialogue; PDF11–14/printed9–12 examples and conclusion.

## A birth story is a different narrative layer

Mahanti recounts another story: Parvati gives life to a boy made from sandalwood paste and asks him to guard her bath. A confrontation with Shiva leads to his beheading; he is revived with an elephant’s head. This attributed birth story explains Ganesha’s form. It is kept separate from the booklet’s dialogue about performing the vow.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed80–81/PDF96–97; short synopsis of this author’s version.

## Twenty-one modaka and their distribution

The booklet instructs the observer to prepare 21 modaka: ten go to a Brahmin, ten are eaten by the observer and one is offered to the deity. The later Odia directions describe the sweets as cooked with ghee. Flowers and fruit also appear in groups of 21. This is a prescription in one printed witness; it does not establish a universal household practice.

Sources: [ବିନାୟକ ବ୍ରତକଥା · Binayaka Brata Katha](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=12JXOi753dG0dGBS9HU-R0oLX_dLhwqPs). PDF6/printed4 directions; PDF9–10/printed7–8 Odia explanation, continuing over the page.

## The recipe is still missing

The inspected directions name modaka and ghee but do not give a complete ingredient list, measurements, shape or cooking sequence. A familiar modern modak recipe cannot simply fill these gaps. Neither the booklet’s name nor its allocation of sweets proves that every Odisha household makes the same preparation.

## From a household vow to a shared school meal

Mahanti describes students decorating clay images, fasting before midday worship and breaking coconuts. Teachers and students later share an evening feast after arati. He also describes household pujas and women observing Vinayaka Brata. The feast’s dishes are unnamed; it cannot be treated as the booklet’s modaka distribution or a verified public meal today.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed79–80/PDF95–96; school and household settings.

## What a 1937 record tells us

A government catalogue published on 29 October 1937 lists Binayaka Brata Katha as an 8-page work published by Gobind Sahu of Ganjam in 1936. Entry 172 describes Sanskrit worship directions and an Odia vow story. It identifies Pharmacy Press, Berhampur, names Keshab Narayan Patnaik and records 1,000 copies. This documents a printed witness by 1936; it does not date the tradition’s beginning or measure readership.

Sources: [The Orissa Gazette, 29 October 1937: catalogue entry 172, Binayaka Brata Katha](https://law.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2021-01/Appendix%20to%20the%20Odisha%20Gazette%201937%20No.1%20of%20October%2029,1937.pdf). Printed17/PDF17, entry 172; catalogue covers registrations in the quarter ending 31 March 1937.

## Two book identities, not one dated scan

The Gazette entry and the recovered Dharmagrantha Store booklet have not been matched as editions. The scan has two cover images, 12 printed text pages and an advertisement; no publication year or named author has been verified. Its cover says new impression. The 1936 date belongs to the separately catalogued work and must not be assigned to this scan.

Sources: [ବିନାୟକ ବ୍ରତକଥା · Binayaka Brata Katha](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=12JXOi753dG0dGBS9HU-R0oLX_dLhwqPs), [The Orissa Gazette, 29 October 1937: catalogue entry 172, Binayaka Brata Katha](https://law.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2021-01/Appendix%20to%20the%20Odisha%20Gazette%201937%20No.1%20of%20October%2029,1937.pdf). Scan PDF1–2 cover, PDF14/printed12 ending and PDF15 advertisement; Gazette printed17/PDF17 entry 172.

## Reading the significance through food

The division of sweets makes food both an offering and a relationship between deity, ritual specialist and observer. The school feast presents a different setting of shared eating. Together they suggest questions about how devotion moves between household and institution, without assuming that one setting grew historically from the other. This is an editorial reading of the evidence.

## For the seasonal food guide

Use Bhadrava Ganesh Chaturthi as a cultural browsing lead. Ask a willing maker what their household calls modaka, how it is prepared and how it is shared. Confirm the local date and any public food offer separately. School and household observances do not by themselves establish visitor admission. No serving venue or current availability is verified.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can a physical copy of the 1936 Gobind Sahu edition be located and compared with the undated Dharmagrantha Store scan?
- Can the recovered booklet’s impression date, printer and named author or compiler be verified?
- How should the opening Bhadraba rule and later month alternatives be read together in this edition?
- Can ORPR-231 and ORPR-214 catalogue leads be inspected in their original record and then as manuscripts?
- Which local modaka ingredients, shape and cooking method correspond to these textual directions?
- How do named households and institutions describe offerings, fast-breaking food and shared meals separately?
- Which local annual date and consented public serving offer can be verified?

[Preparation and variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). Binayaka’s modaka prescription connects to preparation research; its food name and ghee reference do not establish a complete local recipe.

body:
# Bipattarini Brata

Bipattarini Brata brings the hope of protection into a household’s ritual life. To understand its food culture in Odisha, the first task is to identify which story and practice a family follows. The name appears in an Odisha inventory; the fuller accounts recovered here come from Bengali settings and remain comparisons.

**Research note: Bengali narrative and temple food comparisons; Odisha story, calendar and menu remain unresolved.**

## What the Odisha record establishes

Dash’s2006 inventory names Bipattarini Brata but supplies no dedicated story, date or menu. Mahanti describes a Tarini Brata on Ashadha’s bright fourth, with a fast, red thread and the Ghatagaon Tarini shrine as context. Similar names and protective themes do not establish that these are one observance. Tarini’s calendar is therefore not assigned to Bipattarini.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed16 / PDF2; Mahanti printed46 / PDF62.

## A riverbank story of protection: Bengali comparison

In Amrita Bhattacharyya’s2011 account of Bengali brata stories, Narada meets women worshipping Durga beside the Kartoya river. He recalls Shiva invoking Durga while drinking the poison from the churning of the ocean, and Yashoda tying a protective armlet on Krishna. Krishna also remembers Durga in danger. This is the article’s attributed sacred narrative, not verified events or an inspected Odia household text.

Sources: [River as a metaphor and actual presence in rites and rituals of Meyeder Bratakatha](https://indiantribalheritage.org/wp-content/uploads/Folklore-and-Folkloristics-Vol.-4-No.-1-2010-National-Folklore-Support-1046-4304-1-PB.pdf). PDF16–17, Bipattarini paragraph.

## Historical evidence and its limits

The2011 article places this Bengali observance in Ashar. Its bibliography cites Rama Devi’s Meyeder Bratakatha, edited by Gopalchandra Bhattacharya, without a known year; that edition was not recovered. These modern records establish published descriptions, not the vow’s founding date, earliest textual witness or route of transmission into Odisha.

Sources: [River as a metaphor and actual presence in rites and rituals of Meyeder Bratakatha](https://indiantribalheritage.org/wp-content/uploads/Folklore-and-Folkloristics-Vol.-4-No.-1-2010-National-Folklore-Support-1046-4304-1-PB.pdf). PDF16 and PDF19 note1.

## Fruit, sweets and the number thirteen: Rajpur comparison

Rajpur’s Bipattarini Chandibari in West Bengal describes vegetarian food on the preceding day, then fruit and sweets when breaking the fast. Thirteen kinds of fruit are offered: the temple explains twelve as the year’s months and one as the worshipper. It also describes a red thread with thirteen knots. No fruit varieties, sweet names, recipe or quantities are given. This is the temple’s own account, not an established Odisha menu.

Sources: [About Bipattarini Chandibari](https://www.bipadtarinichandibari.org/about-us.php). About section: previous-day, fast-breaking, thirteen-fruit and thread paragraphs; address footer.

## Keep the calendar attached to its place

The Rajpur page’s general rule is a Tuesday between Rath Yatra and Ulto Rath in Bengali Ashar. Its dated banner calls21July2026 the fourth of Shravan1433. The different calendar labels have not been reconciled here; neither becomes an Odisha annual date. A dated temple announcement also does not verify present service or food availability.

Sources: [About Bipattarini Chandibari](https://www.bipadtarinichandibari.org/about-us.php). About section annual festival paragraphs and announcement banner; research limitation appended.

## How food can carry meaning

The Rajpur account distinguishes food withheld, food offered and food eaten after a fast. That sequence offers a way to ask about household memory and care: who chooses the fruit, prepares food, tells the story and shares the meal? These are research questions for Odisha participants, rather than conclusions that the same rules apply everywhere. The number thirteen in this account does not establish a historical link with the saying Bara Masa, Tera Parba.

## What is still missing locally

An identifiable Odia brata-katha or a situated account from Odisha is still needed. The queen-and-friend story found in a modern translated devotional page is another transmission lead, not a verified local version or independent proof of origin. No specific Odisha dish, cooking method, household variation, historical start date or human review is established.

## For seasonal visitors

Use this page to learn what to ask about, rather than as a food booking or festival-date guide. There is no verified Odisha serving venue, public meal, host invitation or current date attached to this entry. If a consenting local host shares a practice, record its name, place and distinction between offering and meal before recommending it to visitors.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Which named Odisha localities observe Bipattarini Brata, and how do participants distinguish it from Tarini Brata?
- Can an identifiable Odia katha edition be recovered with title page, story pages and publication metadata?
- Which narrative versions are read locally, and in which languages?
- What is offered, what ends the fast, and which dishes are actually prepared in each locality?
- Which local calendar rule is followed, and how is an annual date confirmed?
- How are food preparation, storytelling and sharing divided among participants?

[Preparation And Variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). Bipattarini research distinguishes offerings from fast-breaking foods and keeps a Rajpur, West Bengal account separate from unverified Odisha recipes.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No local interviews or human review claimed.

## 2026-10-10 · Related Tarini reading

[Tarini Brata](tarini-brata.md). Tarini and Bipattarini share protective themes, but name similarity does not establish identical vows, calendars, narratives or foods.

body:
# Budhei Osha

Budhei brings a kitchen’s grinding stones into worship. Across successive Wednesdays, a coconut is kept for the final offering and chapters are read aloud. This creates a food story about waiting and return: familiar objects and ingredients acquire a new role within the household. Published accounts name different deities and different calendar boundaries; those differences belong in the story.

**Research note: full katha, historical origins and local practice remain incomplete.** No annual visit date confirmed.

## The kitchen stone becomes a ritual figure

Mahanti describes women worshipping sila and silapua, bathed with turmeric or aonla water, marked with vermilion and collyrium and wrapped in a red sari. He glosses the pair as mortar and pestle; the local report uses the Odia names. We retain sila and silapua rather than silently turn the objects into a single standardized kitchen implement. Their everyday food work invites an editorial connection to preparation, but does not establish the observance’s historical origin.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed56–57/PDF72–73.

## Names do not settle one deity

Dash names Bimala or Tarini; Mahanti gives Mangala with Bamana as Jagannatha and also records a feminine Budha-graha identification. These are attributed explanations, not proof that all communities mean the same deity or that Budhei, Sudhei and Budhibaman are universally interchangeable. Mahanti distinguishes this Bhadraba observance from year-round Wednesday Budha worship.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed15/PDF1; Mahanti printed56–57/PDF72–73.

## The coconut carries the month

Mahanti says the first Wednesday’s coconut is broken and offered on the last; fruit and unspecified pitha accompany worship, and one katha chapter is read each Wednesday. That gives a sequence rather than a one-day menu. The object kept from one week to another ties preparation to anticipation. The latter is our editorial reading, not a measured social effect.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed57/PDF73.

## A Bolagarh report names the foods

Pradhan’s27September2023 report lists coconut, banana, fruits, muan, ukhuda, khai and kakara as offerings. It describes the retained coconut being used in pitha on the final Wednesday and at least five pitha/pana types for the closing observance. It does not identify all five preparations or quantities. Kakara is a named association here; its general preparation versions do not establish this household’s recipe.

Sources: [ଉତ୍କଳୀୟ ସଂସ୍କୃତିର ପାରମ୍ପରିକ ପର୍ବ ବୁଧେଇ ଓଷା ବା ବୁଧିବାମନ ଓଷା।](https://upantaodisha.com/27/09/2023/15263/). Report food paragraphs, web29,31.

## A published summary points toward several stories

Puriwaves summarizes a wine dealer’s wife and a pregnant Brahmin woman receiving divine help. It also names a Magadha merchant couple, a Sundhi couple of Jajatinagara and Bandhu Mohanti of Jajpur as story strands. These are this website’s attributed myth summaries, including healing beliefs; they are neither historical events nor medical claims. The complete episodes and their relationship to successive readings remain unverified.

Sources: [Budhei Sudhei Osha – Budhi Bamana Osha](https://puriwaves.nirmalya.in/feature-article/budhei-sudhei-osha). Myth-summary paragraph, web19.

## Where a history must begin

Institutional records list OL-2022, OL-2443 and palm-leaf OL/2636. Their catalogued extents differ, but that does not establish independent variants, composition dates or an earliest observance. Banamalli’s book route returned403. The recovered OdiaPortal page offers an app link rather than an inspected text. A locked Pratilipi series is another lead; no author attribution is transferred to the older katha.

Sources: [Orissa State Museum manuscript catalogue](https://www.namami.gov.in/sites/default/files/Orissa_State_Museum_Bhubaneswar_Odisha.pdf), [Oriya Literature manuscript catalogue](https://www.odishamuseum.nic.in/?field_abstraction_tid=All&field_author_value=&field_category_tid=All&field_subject_value=&page=4&q=palm-leaf-ol), [Budhibaman Osha (Budhei Osha) Odia Bahi Gita — download listing](https://www.odiaportal.in/2016/08/Download-Budhei-Osha-Budhibaman-Osha-Bahi-Katha-Free-eBook.pdf.html). NMM PDF13,45; museum OL/2636; portal app link.

## Significance in repetition and care

The repeated reading and first-to-last coconut make time visible through household actions. The saved accounts frame worship around hopes for children and their wellbeing. We can narrate those hopes respectfully while keeping reported beliefs distinct from effects. A fuller story needs a particular reader, locality, text and preparation; no interviews or local review have yet supplied them.

## Use the season as an enquiry

Mahanti gives Bhadraba Wednesdays. Pradhan reports four or five observances and differing Gamha-Purnima or sankranti boundaries. No universal count or Gregorian date follows. The report’s fasting account is descriptive, not a visitor instruction. Confirm the local calendar and a publicly offered preparation separately; household worship and a named food do not establish a serving venue or invitation.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [ଉତ୍କଳୀୟ ସଂସ୍କୃତିର ପାରମ୍ପରିକ ପର୍ବ ବୁଧେଇ ଓଷା ବା ବୁଧିବାମନ ଓଷା।](https://upantaodisha.com/27/09/2023/15263/). Mahanti printed56–57; report web30–31.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Collate original OL-2022, OL-2443 and OL/2636 episodes, copying dates and author/edition evidence; retry accessible text routes17October.
- Distinguish local Budhei/Sudhei/Budhibaman deity names and the relation of merchant, Sundhi, Brahmin and Bandhu Mohanti episodes.
- Document a named final-Wednesday menu and Kakara/coconut-pitha preparation without assuming a universal set of five.
- Confirm local lunar or solar boundaries and consent for any visitor encounter; no annual date or venue established.

[Text witness register](../osha-text-witnesses.md). Archival references, inspected passages and remaining comparisons.

[Back to the collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md). Cultural association does not establish a serving venue or access to private worship. No local interviews or human editorial review are claimed.

[Related reading](../../food/kakara-pitha.md) — A dated local report names Kakara as a Budhei offering; general preparation versions do not establish the ritual recipe or a serving venue.

body:
# Chaitra Mangala Osha

A Tuesday gathering, a seasonal drink and a story about a woman confronting royal power offer three ways into Mangala’s spring observance.

**Partial narrative and food checkpoint.** The Odia katha remains unread; no earliest observance date is established.

## The seasonal gathering

Dash places Mangala worship on Tuesdays in Chaitra. Mahanti describes mostly married women gathering under a tree, shaping an image on sand or earth and decorating it with cloth and flowers. At midday they offer seasonal fruits and pana, accompanied by conches, bells and women’s ululation. This is an attributed description; its geographical distribution and present-day prevalence are not measured.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed p.15; Mahanti printed p.62 / PDF p.78.

## Shriya and the king: a partially recovered story

The English introduction to an odia.org booklet tells of Shriya, a woman subjected to caste exclusion, whose devotion includes wine, meat and eggs. After she calls the king’s appearance inauspicious, he has her sons killed beneath a husking lever. Mangala restores them; the king learns a lesson, and the queen’s worship is rewarded with children. This is the booklet’s synopsis, not a verified event or a complete reading of its Odia verses.

Sources: [Chaitra Mangalabara Osha — Festivals of Odisha #101](https://ewb.seedsnet.in/modules/od-odia.org/books/Literary%20Works%201/Chaitramangalabar.pdf). PDF p.3 / printed p.1 English synopsis, web extraction only.

## Reading power, dignity and devotion

The synopsis can be read as a reversal of power: royal punishment fails to silence a socially excluded devotee, and the ruler’s household comes to recognise her goddess. That is an editorial interpretation. Shriya’s name alone does not establish that this is the same character or text as the Shreeya story associated with Manabasa; the narratives need comparison. Neither miracles nor a moral reversal establish a historical biography.

## Pana, ingredients and the act of offering

In a 2023 Mint interview, Alka Jena explains pouring pana into a small well outside the home as an offering to Mother Earth, shared with other creatures. Swetak Abhisek Mohapatra names raw-mango pieces and a small variety of gram in the offering. These are named informants’ accounts; their description of required ingredients is not a rule verified across Odisha.

Sources: [Pana, the drink of gods in Odisha](https://www.livemint.com/mint-lounge/food/pana-the-drink-of-gods-in-odisha-111681396901209.html). 14 April 2023, domestic religious practices paragraphs.

## The story does not supply a universal menu

Mahanti’s fruit-and-pana description and the booklet’s wine, meat and eggs occupy different kinds of evidence: a practice account and a story synopsis. They should not be harmonised into one menu or used to declare all Mangala worship vegetarian or non-vegetarian. The term pana also does not identify every offering as bela pana. A recipe needs its own locality, ingredients and preparation evidence.

## A literary trail, not an established beginning

A 2009 essay by Satyabrata Das and Lalit Kumar Lenka cites Chaitra Mangala Osha at Madhya Parva, 885, in Sarala Mahabharata. The article is inspected, but its cited edition and the epic passage are not. This is a useful route toward historical evidence, not a verified founding date, proof of unchanged practice since the fifteenth century, or proof that the booklet synopsis occurs in that passage.

Sources: [Folk Elements in Sarala Mahabharata](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/orissareview/2009/April-May/engpdf/or-april-2009.pdf). Printed p.58, first paragraph.

## What a visitor can learn now

The traditional month and named foods provide a reading route. No year-specific Tuesday, serving venue, public invitation or host permission is established. Chaitra Mangala is kept distinct from Pana Sankranti and from the autumn observance Nisha Mangalabara until source-specific relationships are demonstrated.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Which edition supplies Madhya Parva page 885, and what does the passage say?
- Can the complete Odia booklet be recovered, read and compared with other katha witnesses?
- Which households or localities document the raw-mango and gram preparation, quantities and handling?
- How do local observers explain the miniature well, collective worship and sharing?

[Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). Separates cultural food associations from verified visitor availability.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md). Individual observance narrative, food context and source boundaries.

No interviews, human Odia review or current serving arrangements were completed by this project.

## 2026-10-10 · Related Gouri reading

[Gouri and Srabani research](gouri-brata.md). Compare the separately sourced calendars and food roles before treating Mangala Gauri and Chaitra Mangala as related observances; a shared deity name does not establish a common vow.

body:
# Dutiya Osha

Dutiya’s food story begins before the curry is cooked. Produce is gathered for an offering, then becomes ghanta for a meal and exchange. Reading the occasion through that movement reveals women’s ritual work and relationships between households. Its stories and names need equally careful handling: a published Jimutavahana retelling, a coastal description and western Pua Jiuntia accounts are related reading, not one interchangeable history.

**Research note: full local katha, history and situated practice remain incomplete.** Ashwina association; no annual visit date confirmed.

## Produce changes its role

Pratap Kumar Dash’s2006 essay describes fruits and vegetables arranged as bhoga and used for ghanta the next day. Mahanti’s coastal account names twenty-one seasonal vegetables under an aparamanga leaf, later cooked and exchanged as ghanta tarkari. Dash names an Apamaranga branch elsewhere. A branch and a covering leaf are different descriptions; neither source here establishes the plant’s botanical identity. These accounts support a sequence of offering, cooking and sharing, rather than a compulsory ingredient list.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed15/PDF1 and17/PDF3; Mahanti printed58/PDF74.

## A maternal vow and its figures

Mahanti presents Dwitibabana as Surya’s son through a Brahmin widow and describes women praying for children’s long lives or hoping for a child. This is a belief account, not biological or historical evidence. He names sand figures of a fox and kite; Dash says fox and eagle. We retain those source words rather than assign one bird species. The complete local story explaining the figures has not been recovered.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed58/PDF74; Dash printed15/PDF1.

## A published story of choosing to protect another

Rajalakshmi Tripathy’s2023 essay retells Jimutavahana discovering the remains of snakes sacrificed to Garuda. He offers himself in a snake’s place; the arriving snake intervenes, and Jimutavahana persuades Garuda to renounce violence. The retelling ends with his marriage to Malayavati and her introduction of the vow. Tripathy calls it an Odia Ramayana story without identifying an edition or passage. We present her retelling, not an established founding event or the recovered fox-and-bird katha.

Sources: [ଆମ ଓଷା ସାହିତ୍ୟରେ ଜିମୂତ-ବାହନ ପୂଜା ବା ଦୁତିୟା ଓଷା](https://odishasambad.in/jimut-bahan-puja-or-dutiya-usha-in-our-literature-an-article-by-rajalakshmi-tripaty/). Published6October2023; narrative paragraphs, web27–28.

## An offering list is not a recipe

Dash’s food paragraph prints jambila, naranga, kerandakoli and padma puskar among Dutiya’s required fruits/items. These source forms remain unresolved here; we do not identify species or treat them as the complete curry. The adjacent list of Dudha gainthala, mula kanji, muga manda and muga paiti belongs to his discussion of Danda Panhara and must not be copied into Dutiya’s menu. A named household preparation, quantities and substitutions are still needed.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Printed17/PDF3, right column, Dutiya passage followed by Danda Panhara.

## Compare western Odisha without erasing it

The saved Pua Jiuntia study records Mahanti’s jugara and tikhiri offerings, followed by a vegetable curry, suji manda and kheeri. E Kiran Mohan’s Barpali account differs in vegetable count, wrapping leaf and thread placement. Those details remain on that regional page. Shared Dutibahana naming and a maternal vow invite comparison but do not establish that every coastal Dutiya household follows the same sequence, dishes or story.

## Where history still needs a text

Saved institutional catalogue records identify Duti Bahana Osha at ORPR-106 and Dwitia Osha at OL-2452, and museum palm-leaf entries OL/2673 and OL/2674. Their contents and copying dates remain uninspected. The existing portal lead advertises a22-chapter Bruhat Dwitibahan Osha credited to Purusottam Das but offers an app-only route. Neither listing verifies authorship, edition date or earliest observance. Tripathy’s early-panji and Dhauli claims stay quarantined because no identified original passage has been recovered.

Sources: [Orissa State Museum manuscript catalogue](https://www.namami.gov.in/sites/default/files/Orissa_State_Museum_Bhubaneswar_Odisha.pdf), [Oriya Literature manuscript catalogue](https://www.odishamuseum.nic.in/?field_abstraction_tid=All&field_author_value=&field_category_tid=All&field_subject_value=&page=4&q=palm-leaf-ol), [ଆମ ଓଷା ସାହିତ୍ୟରେ ଜିମୂତ-ବାହନ ପୂଜା ବା ଦୁତିୟା ଓଷା](https://odishasambad.in/jimut-bahan-puja-or-dutiya-usha-in-our-literature-an-article-by-rajalakshmi-tripaty/). NMM PDF21,45; museum OL/2673,2674; Tripathy web26; existing text-witness portal lead.

## Reading significance through food and care

The offering-to-meal sequence gives this page its organising idea: ritual food becomes food exchanged between people. Mothers’ preparation and fasting make care visible in the published accounts; exchange makes the occasion larger than an individual plate. This is an editorial reading of documented actions, not a measured social, nutritional or economic effect. The wish for children’s protection stays within the observers’ belief.

## A seasonal enquiry, not a promised meal

Mahanti gives Ashwina’s dark eighth, while the saved register retains Tripathy’s seventh-day statement as a conflict. No annual date is generated. Odisha Tourism also describes ghanta in a general Jajpur food listing; that does not establish a Dutiya meal or an operating venue. A visitor enquiry should identify the preparation, confirmed date, provider and welcome separately. Private worship and shared household food do not themselves establish visitor access.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Odisha Tourism: Jajpur — Local Food & Cuisine](https://odishatourism.gov.in/en/destinations/jajpur). Mahanti printed58/PDF74; retained text-witness calendar conflict; Tourism gastronomy heading.

## Further reading and questions

[Pua Jiuntia](pua-jiuntia.md) · [Ghanta](../../food/ghanta-tarkari.md) · [Text witness register](../osha-text-witnesses.md) · [Identity guide](../osha-identity-guide.md).

- Recover an identified local fox-and-bird katha and collate ORPR-106, OL-2452, OL/2673 and OL/2674 before claiming story identity or chronology.
- Identify Tripathy’s cited Odia Ramayana and early panji editions; retain Dhauli claim quarantine until an exact inscription supports it.
- Identify the named plant and offering items from a sourced botanical/local account; separate leaves, branches, fruits and curry ingredients.
- Document an attributed household ghanta, sharing recipients and regional sequence; confirm local panji before annual-date advice.

[Seasonal guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md) · [Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md). No fieldwork, human review or serving availability claimed.

[Related reading](pua-jiuntia.md) — Source-linked comparison retains regional names, food roles and thread/leaf differences; related reading does not establish identical practices or stories.
