body:
# Nagala Chaturthi

A serpent image, an offering and a story about stopping revenge open this Kartika vow to study. Similar names and shared stories need careful separation.

**Research note: identity, literary comparison and attributed offerings; local katha and earliest history remain open.**

## Two observances, two calendar rules

Mahanti distinguishes Nagala Chaturthi on Kartika shukla Chaturthi from Naga Panchami on Sravana shukla Panchami. His joint entry describes serpent worship, fasting and women’s prayers for children. Dash places Nagala in Kartika, naming Shiva in the inventory and serpent worship later. Shared devotion does not make the two dates interchangeable.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed55 / PDF71; Dash printed15–17 / PDF1–3.

## Offerings are not yet a household menu

Mahanti’s joint account names milk and rice as offerings. OdiaPortal’s Nagala landing page instead names milk and dry fruits. Neither establishes a named household’s preparation, what worshippers eat afterwards, or a cooked dish. Dash’s nearby bundi reference belongs to Sankata Chaturthi and must not be transferred here.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Download Naga Chaturthi Brata Puja eBook in Odia Script](https://www.odiaportal.in/2015/11/Naga-Chaturthi-Osa-Bahi-Odia-PDF.html), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed55 / PDF71; OdiaPortal The Legend; Dash printed17 / PDF3.

## Astika asks the king to stop

In Ganguli’s translation, Jaratkaru sends her son Astika to help her serpent kin. He wins an audience with Janamejaya and asks him to end the snake sacrifice, refusing wealth in its place. The king finally grants that request. The story makes an appeal for relatives more valuable than a material reward. This is literary narrative, not a verified historical event.

Sources: [Mahabharata, Volume I, Adi Parva — Astika Parva, sections LIV–LVIII](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15474). Adi Parva, Astika Parva, sections LIV, LVI and LVIII.

## The calendar ending changes between accounts

Mahanti attaches the rescue story to Sravana Panchami. Samal’s 2019 retelling attaches its ending to Kartika Chaturthi. Their overlapping wording cannot serve as independent confirmation of either association. The inspected Ganguli sections contain no corresponding month-and-tithi statement. They also name Astika’s mother Jaratkaru; the later accounts name Manasa. These differences require textual comparison, not a silently harmonised story.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Nagala Chaturthi Brata and its associated Rituals, Believes with some stories:](https://thesrinibash.wordpress.com/2019/10/29/nagala-chaturthi-brata-and-its-associated-rituals-believes-with-some-stories/), [Mahabharata, Volume I, Adi Parva — Astika Parva, sections LIV–LVIII](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15474). Mahanti printed55–56 / PDF71–72; Samal Story2; Ganguli LIV–LVIII.

## The local katha has identifiable leads

The National Mission for Manuscripts catalogue lists Nagala Chaturthi titles at Odisha State Museum under CY-666, ORPR-66, ORPR-209 and CY-2106, plus a composite record containing that title. These are five catalogue records, not five inspected or independently established versions. Copy dates, authorship and textual relationships remain unknown. OdiaPortal advertises a Raghunath Das book, but its full text is app-only.

Sources: [Orissa State Museum manuscript catalogue](https://www.namami.gov.in/sites/default/files/Orissa_State_Museum_Bhubaneswar_Odisha.pdf), [Download Naga Chaturthi Brata Puja eBook in Odia Script](https://www.odiaportal.in/2015/11/Naga-Chaturthi-Osa-Bahi-Odia-PDF.html). NMM PDF19,21,36,61; OdiaPortal2017 book-list entry and linked availability note.

## Significance and practical knowledge

Read together, the offerings, family prayers and interruption of violence suggest questions about care and coexistence. This is an editorial reading. To study practical knowledge, we need named local accounts of image-making, grain preparation, storage, fasting and sharing. The sources do not establish conservation outcomes, nutritional benefits or protection from snakebite. Reported live-snake customs are descriptions, not visitor activities recommended by this guide.

## History and a seasonal visit remain open

The complete Odia Nagala katha and its imprint have not yet been inspected. The epic episode cannot date the Odisha observance, and the modern publication dates establish only those publications. Kartika is a reading window here: no annual date, public host, serving place or food availability has been verified.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can the five museum catalogue records be obtained and collated, including their colophons and copy dates?
- Which Raghunath Das is credited in the advertised book, and what does its imprint establish?
- How do named Odisha practitioners distinguish Nagala Chaturthi from Naga Panchami?
- Which local text attaches Astika’s story to each calendar date, and how are Jaratkaru and Manasa represented?
- What is offered, eaten, shared or avoided, and which preparation techniques are documented in a named locality?
- Can a dated public observance and independent serving information be verified?

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Text witnesses](../osha-text-witnesses.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No local interviews, human review or media rights claimed.

Text witnesses provide research leads for a local katha; a catalogue record alone does not establish its contents, date or an independently verified variant.

## 2026-10-08 · Related Naga Panchami study

[Naga Panchami](naga-panchami.md) adds an attributed Deogaon sculptural witness. Shared serpent narratives invite comparison, while the sources distinguish Sravana Panchami from Kartika Chaturthi; neither image dates nor shared ingredients erase that distinction.

## 2026-10-09 · Sankata comparison now documented

[Sankata Chaturthi](sankata-chaturthi.md) now has a dedicated food-and-identity note. The rice-cake association remains attached to that source heading and is not transferred to Nagala.

body:
# Nisha Mangalabara Osha

Night worship gives this Ashwina observance its distinctive setting. Its food, stories and local forms still need to be read source by source.

**Research note.** The textual lead is identified, but no full katha or historical origin is established.

## An autumn night of worship

Mahanti describes married women observing the osha at night in Ashwina: some on every Tuesday, others on the last Tuesday. He explains the name through its night-time observance. These are recorded alternatives, not one fixed statewide rule.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.58 / PDF p.74, Nisa Mangalbara osha paragraph.

## Whom do the sources name?

Dash’s April 2006 survey names Mangala. Mahanti’s description instead names Durga and mentions drawing her image with rice powder. Both labels are retained with their sources; the passages do not establish whether they describe the same local form or explain the difference.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed p.15; Mahanti printed p.58 / PDF p.74.

## What can we say about the food?

Mahanti records a cooked offering without naming a dish. He also reports a cock sacrifice, but does not say how the bird was used afterward. Rice powder belongs to the image-making passage. None of this supplies a recipe or a serving menu.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.58 / PDF p.74, image, offering and sacrifice sentences.

## Significance without a claim of ritual effect

Mahanti presents the worship as an appeal for protection from calamities. An editorial reading places women’s preparation and hopes for household security at the centre. The source does not measure whether the ritual changes outcomes, and its brief account cannot establish present-day prevalence.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.58 / PDF p.74, closing invocation.

## A book identity, not yet a recovered story

WorldCat records Brhat Khulana sundari, ba, Nisa Mangalabara osha, OCLC 22766659, an Odia book from Dharmagrantha Shtora in Kataka. Its date is displayed as [197-], and the cover title is Khulana sundari. This is a useful textual lead. The contents have not been inspected: the catalogue does not establish a plot, food passage, author or origin date.

Sources: [Brhat Khulana sundari, ba, Nisa Mangalabara osha — OCLC 22766659](https://search.worldcat.org/title/Brhat-Khulana-sundari-ba-Nisa-Magalabara-osha/oclc/22766659). Title, edition-date, publisher, physical-description and cover-title fields.

## A modern link with maritime remembrance

Kalinga History describes a two-day gathering at Sambhav Farm in Nayagarh, invited by Sabarmatee, with maritime discussions and a midnight visit to a temple holding Nisha Mangalabara worship. The entry was added on 24 October 2025; that is not a confirmed event date. Its framing connects the observance with concern for merchants at sea. This documents modern heritage interpretation, not the historical founding of the osha.

Sources: [Nisha Mangalabara: maritime remembrance at Sambhav Farm](https://kalingahistory.org/kalinga-history.php). Named Nisha Mangalabara entry, date and event-description paragraphs.

## History and practical knowledge still to recover

The book identity and short modern descriptions give research a firmer starting point, but a historical narrative needs inspected editions, dated local testimony and comparison of variants. Cooking, drawing and arranging an offering involve skills; the present passages do not document their techniques or scientific explanations. A generic account of fasting or vegetarian food should not replace this observance’s specific evidence.

## How this belongs in a seasonal guide

Ashwina is a useful cultural browsing label, with the Tuesday variants visible. No named food, current serving venue, annual date or invitation to private worship is verified. Food served at a modern heritage gathering cannot automatically become the ritual’s prescribed offering.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can OCLC 22766659 be inspected, including its title page, edition statement and food passages?
- How do practitioners explain the Mangala and Durga names in particular places?
- Which cooked dishes are offered and shared, and how do local preparations differ?
- What dated evidence supports the maritime association beyond modern heritage interpretation?

[Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). Separates cultural food associations from verified visitor availability.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md). Individual observance narrative, food context and source boundaries.

No new local interviews, human Odia review or media permissions are claimed.

Nuakhai: Festival of Social Harmony

body:
# Nuakhai

The first taste of new rice opens a celebration of food, household work and renewed relationships. Nuakhai belongs here as an agrarian parba, alongside the collection’s osha and brata.

**Research note.** Food and practice accounts are documented; earliest chronology and regional coverage remain incomplete.

## The first rice and its season

Mahanti describes Nuakhai, also called Nabanna, on Bhadraba’s bright-fortnight fifth day. The name joins newness with eating. His account centres the newly harvested crop; this is not evidence that every field’s harvest is complete.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.121 / PDF137.

## What the historical account can establish

P. K. Singh’s September2012 essay says the exact origin is unknown. It presents Ramai Dev’s adoption of the festival as oral tradition, and reports a 1991 order for a common observance day. Neither a contemporary medieval witness nor that order has been inspected here. These are research leads, not a settled founding date.

Sources: [Nuakhai: Festival of Social Harmony](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2012/sep/engpdf/24-26.pdf). Printed pp.23–24 / PDF1–2; origin and calendar paragraphs.

## A family’s first offering

In Kesavan’s Bargarh fieldwork, the village priest distributes new grain. Ground new-season grain mixed with jaggery is offered to deities and ancestors, then shared with family members from a leaf bowl. This is one ethnographic account; its anonymized village is not a visitor location.

Sources: [Rice culture and sacred siblingship: Nua Khai and Bhai Jiuntia celebrations in Western Odisha, India](https://journals.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/paideuma/index.php/paideuma/article/download/2046/2237/4542). Printed pp.28–29 / PDF14–15; saved original visually inspected.

## The meal has several documented forms

Mahanti names jau or kheeri and arisa made with the new grain. Singh names manda pitha and khiri among offerings, then lists rice, dal, vegetables, hendua karadi khata and saga bhaja in the communal meal. These descriptions should not be merged into a compulsory menu.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Nuakhai: Festival of Social Harmony](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2012/sep/engpdf/24-26.pdf). Mahanti p.122 / PDF138; Singh p.25 / PDF3.

## Skills and preparation

Singh describes rice grinding with pestles, collecting leaves and women’s advance preparation. These details identify practical work. They do not establish measured temperatures, ratios, storage life or health benefits. Preparation names require further locality-specific evidence before becoming recipes.

Sources: [Nuakhai: Festival of Social Harmony](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2012/sep/engpdf/24-26.pdf). Printed p.24 / PDF2, household preparations.

## Greetings, kinship and their limits

Kesavan describes unmarried sisters performing rites for brothers and receiving gifts, followed by greetings among neighbours. She interprets new rice and family relationships together. Her analysis also retains unequal gender roles; ritual honour cannot be treated as proof of equality.

Sources: [Rice culture and sacred siblingship: Nua Khai and Bhai Jiuntia celebrations in Western Odisha, India](https://journals.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/paideuma/index.php/paideuma/article/download/2046/2237/4542). Printed pp.28–31 / PDF14–17; broader gender discussion pp.27–28.

## An origin comparison is not a chronology

Mahanti suggests a connection with Vedic crop offerings. This comparative interpretation does not establish an unbroken lineage or the age of today’s Nuakhai. A stronger history needs dated texts, local records and careful comparison of changes. No single katha has been established as a universal foundation for this agrarian festival.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.121 / PDF137, proposed Vedic connection.

## How visitors can use this record

Bhadraba provides a browsing season, while individual event dates and serving offers need separate confirmation. The recorded dishes are leads for asking about local food. No restaurant, household invitation, public feast, annual date or booking is verified. A diaspora gathering or temple rite must be identified on its own terms.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can the original 1991 calendar/holiday order and its exact scope be recovered?
- What dated evidence supports the Ramai Dev tradition, beyond later retellings?
- How do offerings and calendars differ across western Odisha communities and temples?
- Which named cooks can document grain processing and regional recipes, with consent?

No project fieldwork, human cultural review or image permissions are claimed.

body:
# Pandu Osha

Pandu Osha connects a full-moon observance with family welfare, offerings and girls’ ritual work. Its name points towards epic figures, but the surviving descriptions do not tell one settled history.

**Early research notes: complete katha, historical chronology and local variation remain open.** Traditional month: Margasira. No annual visit date is confirmed.

## Pandu or Yudhisthira?

Dash’s 2006 inventory associates Pandu Osha Brata with Yudhisthira. Mahanti records both Yudhisthira and Pandu, father of the Pandavas, as reported dedications. We keep those alternatives visible. The appearance of epic names in these accounts does not date the observance to the epic period.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Dash printed15 / PDF1; Mahanti printed60 / PDF76.

## Brief stories, not a recovered katha

Puriwaves gives two brief traditions: an unnamed Kalinga royal couple whose fortune changes after observing the vow, and Kandu receiving an appearance of Pandu Nrusingh at Puri. Neither is a dated historical event, and the page supplies no inspected original text for either account. We do not combine them into one origin story.

Sources: [Pandu Purnima Osha](https://puriwaves.nirmalya.in/festivals/pandu-osha-in-odisha). Two narrative paragraphs preceding food description.

## A shaped offering under the full moon

Puriwaves describes chanda as a moon-shaped preparation of puffed rice, milk and sugar, offered with fruit, khechudi and white manda. Its photograph caption uses Chanda Chakata and credits odiafoods.in. This is an attributed food description, not a verified recipe or universal menu. The rice-processing term and the relationship between caption and preparation need confirmation.

Sources: [Pandu Purnima Osha](https://puriwaves.nirmalya.in/festivals/pandu-osha-in-odisha). Food paragraph and Chanda Chakata caption.

## The work of girls and the unsettled sequence

Mahanti connects the observance with girls praying for brothers and says road sweeping begins on the full moon and continues into the next month. Puriwaves instead says the sweeping cycle concludes then. Our Bata study records another related sequence. These differences remain unresolved; the observances are linked for comparison, not treated as interchangeable names.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Pandu Purnima Osha](https://puriwaves.nirmalya.in/festivals/pandu-osha-in-odisha). Mahanti printed60 / PDF76; Puriwaves sweeping paragraph.

## Rice also appears as a drawing material

Biswal and Dash’s 2020 journal article names Pandu among observances associated with jhoti. Their general technique section describes rice paste applied with fingers, cloth or a simple cloth-tipped stick. It does not identify a Pandu-specific design. That distinction lets us connect food and material skill without inventing an offering or ritual pattern.

Sources: [Socio-Cultural Context and Aesthetic Values of 'Jhoti'](https://utkaluniversity.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Man-in-Society-Anthropology.pdf). Printed117 / PDF118, item9 and Raw materials and Techniques.

## What can be said about its significance

An editorial reading places family care beside collective work and shaped offerings. The full moon may help a reader understand the food’s reported form, but this study has not demonstrated the historical origin of that symbolism. Preparing paste, shaping food and organising shared activity are practical knowledge; no measured health effect or food-science experiment follows from these descriptions.

## History and calendar boundaries

Mahanti places Pandu Osha on Margasira Purnima. No annual Gregorian date has been verified here. Puriwaves’ worship-time wording is unclear and is not used to prescribe a schedule. Mahanti’s statement about the practice no longer being observed has no supplied survey or observation date, so we do not treat it as proof of statewide disappearance today.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Pandu Purnima Osha](https://puriwaves.nirmalya.in/festivals/pandu-osha-in-odisha). Mahanti printed60 / PDF76; Puriwaves food/timing paragraph.

## An author name is a research lead

OdiaPortal’s post of 20 December 2018 labels its advertised Pandu Osha book as written by Ananta Das. The scan is app-only in this pass. We have not inspected an imprint, matched that name to a particular historical author or read the text. The post therefore supplies a lead, not a composition date or verified authorship.

Sources: [Download Pandu Osha Bahi Gita – Odia eBook](https://www.odiaportal.in/2018/12/Download-Pandu-Osha-Odia-eBook.pdf.html). About Book, displayed post date and app-only notice.

## For a visitor following seasonal foods

The reported manda name does not identify the specific sijha manda preparation in our food entry. Nor does a temple photograph or festival-food caption establish a serving venue. Current availability, access to worship, annual dates and host consent remain unknown.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can the advertised Pandu Osha text be recovered with title page, imprint and readable passages?
- How do local observers explain Pandu, Yudhisthira and Kandu/Nrusingh associations?
- Does the sweeping cycle begin or conclude at Pandu Purnima in each named locality?
- Which rice preparation is used in chanda, and how do cooks distinguish it from other moon-shaped offerings?

[Manda pitha](../../food/manda-pitha.md). Compare a reported offering name with separately documented preparations; no single Pandu recipe implied.

[Bata Osha](bata.md). Compare related road-sweeping accounts without merging their identities or resolving the disputed sequence.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No interviews, human cultural review or image permissions claimed.

## 2026-10-09 · Identifying a full-moon observance

[Which Osha?](../osha-identity-guide.md) A specifically named Margasira observance; not automatically an alias of every Purnima Osha.

body:
# Prathamastami

Prathamastami brings the eldest child into the centre of family attention. New clothes arrive from the maternal household, an older woman offers blessings, and enduri parcels carry a recognisable food tradition into the celebration. Looking closely at those parcels also reveals variation: an offering menu, a published recipe and a gift between friends are different kinds of evidence.

**Narrative checkpoint; history and local review remain incomplete.** Traditional month: Margasira. No annual visit date is confirmed.

## The child, the mother and the maternal uncle

Mahanti describes the eldest child, a girl or boy, wearing new clothes and sitting on a wooden pidha before a kalasha. A mother or older woman performs bandapana and prays to Sasthi for the child’s long life. The maternal uncle sends clothing and worship materials. Enduri and kheeri are offered as bhoga. This account describes a family relationship through gifts, blessing and food; it is not a survey of every household.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed59 / PDF75, Prathamastami osha.

## An Odia account names a fuller offering

In her 8 January 2018 essay, Namita Sarangi describes bathing and dressing the eldest child in clothes from the maternal home, then offering turmeric-leaf enduri, radish dalma, kheeri and fish to Sasthi before bandapana. Her locality and household sample are not specified. The fish reference belongs to her Prathamastami description; dried fish in the following Kanji Anla passage has a separate role. Neither a universal vegetarian menu nor a requirement to include fish follows from this account.

Sources: [ଓଡିଆ ଘରେ ‘ଶୀତ ଋତୁ’](https://samadhwani.com/1311). Prathamastami paragraph, web line172; preceding sentences before the Kanji Anla transition.

## What happens inside the leaf

Lipi Das’s 2015 ICAR-CRRI compilation documents a rice–black-gram batter and a filling containing coconut and paneer, with jaggery or sugar, cardamom and pepper. The filled turmeric leaves are folded and steamed. The book describes both a steamer and parcels placed on cloth tied across a pot’s mouth under a lid. Odisha Tourism’s shorter description names coconut and jaggery. These are attributed descriptions, not one compulsory recipe; the dairy ingredient in the book’s version should remain visible. No recipe testing or health benefit is claimed here.

Sources: [Traditional Rice Foods: The Rich Heritage of India — Lipi Das](https://icar-crri.in/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/final_book_ldas.pdf), [The Taste of Odisha](https://odishatourism.gov.in/content/tourism/en/the-taste-of-odisha.html). Das printed19 / PDF30, Enduri Pitha or Haldi Patra Pitha; Tourism Enduri Pitha heading.

## Food also travels between people

Soumya’s Svanir blog recalls receiving enduri from Sunanda aunty, a friend of the writer’s mother-in-law, and learning about the occasion through family conversation. This is one published personal account of gifting and learning, not a household survey or an interview conducted for Utkal. The operator-hosted story supplies no dated public menu or confirmed visitor serving arrangement.

Sources: [Prathamastami - Celebrating the First Born](https://svanir.com/blog/prathamastami-celebrating-the-first-born). Opening first-person paragraphs, web lines14–16; Article metadata.

## Kinship in a temple setting

IGNCA’s Bharati Matha inventory records Prathamastami among the site’s rituals and describes Lingaraja visiting his uncle at the matha. Mahanti separately mentions the representative image Chandrashekara going to Papanasini tank. These records make a comparison with household kinship possible, but do not establish a complete procession route, shared origin or current timetable. The matha inventory’s building-age field cannot date the festival.

Sources: [Bharati Matha heritage documentation, OR/KDA/BSR-16](https://ignca.gov.in/asi_reports/orkhurda019.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). IGNCA PDF2, section7 Association; Mahanti printed59 / PDF75 final paragraph.

## A historical lead, with its missing link visible

An unproofread OCR page in the 1991 volume Studies in the Cult of Jagannatha points to a Prathamastami reference in Smrtisarasangraha and cites a Cuttack edition edited by Pandit Govinda Rath in 1915. The original page image and the cited edition remain uninspected. This is a lead for textual research, not an accepted first mention or a date for the beginning of the household observance.

Sources: [Studies in the Cult of Jagannatha: Prathamastami textual lead](https://www.wisdomlib.org/history/book/studies-in-the-cult-of-jagannatha/ocr/1883728/78). Printed65 / digital78, footnote30; OCR title/imprint2–3; original recovery incomplete.

## A season to enquire about, not a fixed itinerary

Mahanti and Sarangi both describe Margasira’s dark eighth. The saved register also retains a conflicting indexed temple description; no current annual date is generated. Sarangi lists enduri again in her Manabasa paragraph, so Prathamastami association must not become an only-day-of-the-year claim. For a visitor, the useful question is who is actually preparing which version on a confirmed date, and whether they welcome an enquiry. Food availability and household access remain unknown.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [ଓଡିଆ ଘରେ ‘ଶୀତ ଋତୁ’](https://samadhwani.com/1311). Mahanti printed59 / PDF75; Sarangi web172–173; preserved calendar-conflict register.

## Further reading and questions

[Enduri preparation](../../food/enduri-pitha.md) explains the documented method. [Kanji Anla](kanji-anla.md) retains its separate food roles and calendar disagreement. [Seasonal guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md) separates cultural association from visitor offers.

- Recover the 1991 chapter image and its named chapter author, then the cited1915 Smrtisarasangraha passage; distinguish temple mention from household origin.
- Which family and locality does each food account describe, and who prepares or sends the enduri?
- Which fillings, leaf substitutions and steaming vessels are used in an attributed household demonstration? No alternative leaf is established here.
- Confirm a dated local panji and the temple-fortnight discrepancy before any annual-date or procession advice.

[Back to the collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md). No local interviews, human review or current serving availability claimed.

[Related reading](../../food/enduri-pitha.md) — Preparation and festival context explain different parts of the same food association; neither establishes a universal recipe.

[Related reading](kanji-anla.md) — Adjacent seasonal accounts retain distinct offering roles and conflicting next-day/evening timing; related reading is not an identity merge.

PUA JIUNTIA [ପୁଅ ଜୀଉନ୍ତିଆ]

body:
# Pua Jiuntia

A mother’s vow, a thread and a shared meal provide an entry into this western Odisha observance.

**Research note.** Practice and food accounts are documented; full ritual stories and earliest histories remain open.

## A different vow from Bhai Jiuntia

Mahanti places mothers’ worship of Dutibahana on Ashwina’s dark-fortnight eighth day. Bhai Jiuntia follows on the bright-fortnight eighth, with sisters praying to Durga for brothers. Similar names do not make the observances interchangeable.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.49 / PDF65.

## Offerings and the following meal

Mahanti names puffed-rice jugara and moong-dal tikhiri as offerings. His following-day account adds a twenty-one-vegetable curry, suji manda and kheeri, shared with relatives and friends. This records a sequence, not a verified standardized recipe.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed p.50 / PDF66.

## A dated Barpali account

E Kiran Mohan’s 2011 account describes mothers assembling with plates of thread, grass, juggar and twenty vegetables. Its opening caption identifies a gathering at Tehsil Chowk, Barpali, on 1 October 2010. This is a dated local witness; it does not date the beginning of the custom.

Sources: [PUA JIUNTIA [ପୁଅ ଜୀଉନ୍ତିଆ]](https://barpalidays.blogspot.com/2011/08/pua-juintia.html). Published13August2011; opening caption and ritual-plate paragraph.

## Keep the differences visible

Mohan describes Rengal-pattar wrapping and an eight-knotted thread worn at the child’s neck. Mahanti describes sal-leaf wrapping and wrist tying. The accounts also differ between twenty and twenty-one vegetables. Geography, household custom or description may explain these differences, but the evidence does not settle which.

Sources: [PUA JIUNTIA [ପୁଅ ଜୀଉନ୍ତିଆ]](https://barpalidays.blogspot.com/2011/08/pua-juintia.html), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Mohan following-day paragraph and plate paragraph; Mahanti pp.49–50 / PDF65–66.

## Significance and the history still missing

An editorial reading sees preparation, care and sharing made visible through household work. A fuller history still requires dated ritual texts and accounts from particular communities. We have not recovered a complete Pua Jiuntia katha in this batch. The relationship with Dutiya deserves comparison without erasing either regional identity.

## Food knowledge to investigate

The named preparations raise useful questions about grain processing, pulse preparation, wrapping leaves and changing seasonal vegetables. Names alone cannot establish quantities, temperatures, nutritional effects or when a technique began. Record those details with a named source before writing a recipe or scientific explanation.

## Seasonal reading for visitors

Ashwina and the lunar rule support cultural browsing. No annual date, public host, serving venue or access permission is verified. A household offering is not automatically a food visitors can buy.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Which dated local katha witnesses can be inspected?
- How do communities explain the vegetable, wrapping-leaf and thread variants?
- Which preparation details and consensual public food offers can be independently documented?

[Dutiya](dutiya.md) now retains an attributed Jimutavahana retelling alongside distinct coastal food/animal descriptions. Its full local fox-and-bird katha is still missing; shared names do not erase this western page’s differences.

Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha

body:
# Pusa Rabibara Brata

A wedding procession is still on the road and daylight is slipping away. In the Pusha Rabibara story, a bride asks the sun to wait. The request begins a tale that brings a royal household to the tulsi courtyard, where flowers, food and a Sunday vow become part of making amends.

**Narrative checkpoint: one Odia text inspected; historical dating and local food preparation remain open.**

## A seasonal Sunday vow

Dash lists Pusa Rabibara Brata in Pausa as worship of the sun. The Odia text’s directions specify Sundays in Pusha. Dash separately lists Rabinarayan in Margasira; a shared solar dedication does not make these entries interchangeable.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [ପୁଷ ରବିବାର ବ୍ରତ କଥା · Pusha Rabibara Brata Katha](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pusha_Rabibara_Brata_Katha.pdf). Dash printed16/PDF2; scan PDF7, directions beginning after the account of the curse.

## The prince and the merchant’s daughter

The scanned katha opens with a king, queen and their son, who wants to marry after his companions have done so. A Brahmin intermediary finds a merchant’s daughter in Karnataka, and a wedding is arranged. These places and characters belong to the story; the text supplies no verified historical itinerary.

Sources: [ପୁଷ ରବିବାର ବ୍ରତ କଥା · Pusha Rabibara Brata Katha](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pusha_Rabibara_Brata_Katha.pdf). PDF2–5, opening royal household through marriage and return procession.

## The sun is asked to pause

On the return journey, the bride fears darkness will fall before the gifts and procession reach home. She asks Aditya to pause until they enter the palace. He grants the request. His mother, waiting for him, angrily curses whoever delayed his journey. When she learns why he is late, she tells him that the bride can seek relief through the Pusha Sunday vow.

Sources: [ପୁଷ ରବିବାର ବ୍ରତ କଥା · Pusha Rabibara Brata Katha](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pusha_Rabibara_Brata_Katha.pdf). PDF5–7, request to Aditya, delayed return and the mother’s response.

## The story reaches the courtyard

The bride becomes afflicted; the royal household seeks guidance from its religious advisers. She undertakes the vow and, in the story’s ending, recovers and prospers. The narrative presents devotion as the remedy. It is a sacred healing story, not medical evidence or advice to replace treatment.

Sources: [ପୁଷ ରବିବାର ବ୍ରତ କଥା · Pusha Rabibara Brata Katha](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pusha_Rabibara_Brata_Katha.pdf). PDF7–8, affliction, advice and concluding observance.

## Preparing a place before sunrise

The directions call for rising before sunrise on Pusha Sundays, bathing, preparing the area at the tulsi plant with cow dung, establishing a sun mandala, decorating with flowers and inviting a Brahmin for worship. These are directions in this textual witness; present-day household adaptations have not been documented here.

Sources: [ପୁଷ ରବିବାର ବ୍ରତ କଥା · Pusha Rabibara Brata Katha](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pusha_Rabibara_Brata_Katha.pdf). PDF7, ritual directions.

## What the text offers

The clearly legible offering terms on PDF7 include sugar, pitha, ripe fruit, bananas and coconut. The passage gives no named pitha variety, quantities or cooking method. Its list describes offerings for worship, not a verified fasting diet or public meal.

Sources: [ପୁଷ ରବିବାର ବ୍ରତ କଥା · Pusha Rabibara Brata Katha](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pusha_Rabibara_Brata_Katha.pdf). PDF7, offering lines after the instruction to invite a Brahmin; selected terms only, not full transcription.

## A food name carried into the market

In her essay Muan, Dr Jayashree Nanda reports that seasonal sweets are sold under names including Pusha Rabibara muan, Dhanu muan and Makara muan. This is an attributed cultural account. The shared naming context does not prove identical ingredients, and the essay does not identify a current seller for this observance.

Sources: [ମୁଆଁ · Muan](https://antarangakalinga.org/muan-2/). Opening market-name paragraph, after visible author credit.

## A wider Sunday practice, kept separate

Mahanti’s weekly Rabibara entry describes sun worship, fasting with one meal towards evening and almsgiving. It does not explicitly identify those rules as Pusa Rabibara Brata. The Pausa profile therefore leaves the actual fast-breaking time and meal open.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed63/PDF79, separate weekly Rabibara entry.

## History: a recovered text, an unresolved date

Project Pothi’s scan gives us a readable textual witness. The Commons page credits Prateek Pattanaik with providing and scanning it, calls the author unknown and labels it part of Bratabali. Its eighteenth-century description and 8 February 1917 publication field have not been confirmed from an original imprint. They cannot establish when this vow began in Odisha.

Sources: [ପୁଷ ରବିବାର ବ୍ରତ କଥା · Pusha Rabibara Brata Katha](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pusha_Rabibara_Brata_Katha.pdf). Commons Summary and file history; PDF1–8 inspected without a verified original imprint.

## How to read its significance

The story places a bride’s journey within the sun’s daily movement, then brings the consequences into household worship. Food is part of the act of devotion, alongside a prepared courtyard, flowers and spoken guidance. The seasonal market name adds a different kind of memory: how an observance may help people name a sweet. This is an editorial interpretation, not a universal account of belief.

## For a seasonal visitor

Ask about Pusha Rabibara muan during the locally observed Pausa season, and ask the maker what that name means in their practice. Confirm ingredients, preparation and current availability before planning a visit. Household worship requires an invitation; the textual offering list is not a restaurant menu. No seller, annual date or public serving arrangement is verified here.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can the parent Bratabali volume, imprint and author attribution be recovered for this seven-page textual fragment?
- What is the basis for the Commons eighteenth-century and 8 February 1917 metadata?
- Can manuscript CY-1907, Pausa Rabibara o Anyanya, be inspected and compared with this printed witness?
- Which pitha varieties are used by a named household, and what is eaten when the fast ends?
- How does a maker define Pusha Rabibara muan relative to Dhanu and Makara muan?
- Which locality-specific calendar and consented public food offer can be verified?

[Preparation and variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). Pusa Rabibara’s textual pitha offering and reported muan market name connect to preparation research; neither establishes a universal recipe or current serving place.

body:
# Rabinarayana Brata

Rabinarayana Brata brings the sun, the lunar calendar and everyday materials into one act of devotion. Its offerings show why food culture includes more than a list of dishes: fruit, grain and prepared sweets can have different ritual roles.

**Research note: calendar descriptions, food roles and manuscript leads; full story and local history remain unresolved.**

## A weekday meets a lunar day

Mahanti describes the observance when Ekadashi falls on Sunday and identifies the deity as Surya. His passage does not specify the fortnight or restrict the month. Dash instead lists Rabinarayan in Margasira and separately lists Pusa Rabibara in Pausa. Those entries should not be merged into one Sunday festival. The calendar descriptions remain unresolved; we have not assigned a Gregorian date.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed 44–45 / PDF 60–61; Dash printed 16 / PDF 2.

## Materials counted in sevens

Mahanti describes women wearing a ritual thread containing seven blades of duba grass, seven barakoli leaves and seven raw rice grains, tied with seven folds of thread. After bathing they offer water to Surya and worship with seven kinds of flowers and seven kinds of fruit. The rice here is part of the thread assembly, not a documented cooked offering or meal. The fruit species, sharing practice and food eaten afterwards are unspecified.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed 45 / PDF 61, Rabinarayana entry.

## Mua and manda in an Odia account

Bishnumohan Adhikari’s 2020 account on Antaranga Kalinga specifies bright-fortnight Ekadashi on Sunday. It names seven mua and seven manda among the offerings, alongside flowers and durba, and describes a seven-knotted thread and water offering. This is an attributed cultural description; it gives no recipe, filling, grain variety or preparation method. We therefore keep its prepared-food names beside Mahanti’s fruit account without combining them into a mandatory menu.

Sources: [Rabinarayana Ekadashi — ରବିନାରାୟଣ ଏକାଦଶୀ](https://antarangakalinga.org/ରବିନାରାୟଣ-ଏକାଦଶୀ/). Calendar paragraph and final offering paragraph.

## The story has identifiable textual leads

Mahanti says the Rabinarayana brata katha is read but does not recount it. The National Mission for Manuscripts’ Odisha State Museum catalogue lists Rabinarayana Brata under ORPR-218 and ORPR-236, and a combined Rabi Narayana Brata Katha, Kanchi Kaberi record under CY-1847,1848. These are three catalogue records, not three established versions of the story. The listed extents cannot supply a date of composition, author or plot, and the combined record’s extent is not the length of the brata alone.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Orissa State Museum manuscript catalogue](https://www.namami.gov.in/sites/default/files/Orissa_State_Museum_Bhubaneswar_Odisha.pdf). Mahanti printed 45 / PDF 61; catalogue PDF 21 and 55.

## Hope, memory and the work of observance

Mahanti associates the vow with women’s hopes for children. That describes a devotional intention, not evidence of fertility treatment. As an editorial reading, repeated counting and assembling plant materials may offer a useful way to explore how practice is remembered and taught. The calendar rule also invites research into who consults an almanac and how dates are settled locally. Neither detail establishes a particular astronomical calculation, an ancient scientific theory or an explanation for the number seven.

## Keeping related solar observances distinct

The separate Rabibara paragraph in Mahanti describes Sunday fasting, an evening meal and almsgiving. Those details are not explicitly attached to Rabinarayana in its own entry. Likewise, Samba Dashami’s story and named dishes belong to that observance’s sources. Sharing a solar dedication does not establish an identical narrative, date or menu.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed 63 / PDF 79, separate Rabibara entry; Dash printed 16 / PDF 2.

## For seasonal food exploration

Manda and mua are useful names to ask about, with the source limitations kept visible. No current serving venue, consenting household host, annual event or visit date is verified. The full identified Odia text and accounts from named localities are needed before a complete narrative or practical food itinerary can be offered.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can ORPR-218, ORPR-236 and the brata component of CY-1847,1848 be inspected and compared?
- Can an identified printed Odia edition supply the complete story, colophon and publication history?
- How do practitioners reconcile the Sunday–Ekadashi rule with the Margasira inventory entry?
- Which fruits, mua ingredients and manda preparation are used in named households, and what is shared or eaten afterwards?
- Who makes the thread, reads the katha and consults the calendar?
- Can a dated public programme or consenting host and actual food availability be verified?

[Manda preparations](../../food/manda-pitha.md). Connects an attributed Rabinarayana offering name with separately documented manda preparations; no ritual recipe or filling is established.

[Samba Dashami](samba-dashami.md). Both observances involve solar devotion, but their sources describe distinct calendar rules and food roles; a shared deity does not establish a shared menu or origin.

[Pusa Rabibara Brata](pusa-rabibara-brata.md) now has a separate Odia narrative and offering checkpoint. Dash distinguishes the seasonal entries; solar dedication alone does not establish identical vows or menus.

body:
# Radhastami Brata

Radhastami brings the celebration of Radha’s appearance into songs, worship and the rhythm of fasting and eating. Its food culture is not yet a reliable list of special dishes: the evidence takes us through a meal inside a sacred story, offerings in a text, and prasada shared after a fast.

**Research note: attributed narrative and food roles; original edition, local dishes and historical origin remain open.**

## The observance and its season

Dash’s Odisha inventory identifies Radhastami with Radha worship. Mahanti places it on Bhadrava’s bright eighth lunar day and describes flower-decorated Radha–Krishna images, fasting and devotional song. Tripathy’s 2003 Jagannath festival list gives the same lunar-day rule. These are source descriptions, not evidence that every household follows an identical practice.

Sources: [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Festivals of Lord Jagannath](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/july2003/englishchpter/The%20Festivals%20of%20Lord%20Jagannath.pdf). Dash printed16/PDF2; Mahanti printed48/PDF64; Tripathy printed39/PDF3.

## An Odia story told through questions

In Shubhapallaba’s verse text, Rukmini asks Krishna about Radha; Satyabhama asks how the eternal Radha relates to her earthly life. Radha accompanies Krishna’s descent and appears as a child on a lotus in Kalindi. Vrishabhanu brings her home to Queen Chanchala. When Narada assures her that Krishna has come to earth, she asks for food, and her mother hurries to her. This is an attributed sacred narrative, not a verified historical birth.

Sources: [ରାଧାଷ୍ଟମୀ ବ୍ରତ - ସମ୍ପୂର୍ଣ୍ଣ ପୂଜା ବହି](https://collection.shubhapallaba.com/2020/08/radhastami-osha-full-book.html). Opening dialogue; Krishna’s answer; lotus-child episode; Narada and Chanchala meal episode.

## Another textual account

The Padma Purana translation tells of Lilavati joining a Radhastami observance and later being rescued by Vishnu’s messengers. In its Radha appearance passage, Vrishabhanu finds her on sacrificial ground. This differs from the lotus setting in the Odia text. The accounts remain distinct; their relationship and transmission into particular Odisha households have not been established.

Sources: [The Greatness of Rādhāṣṭamī: Padma Purana, Brahma-khanda chapter7](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-padma-purana/d/doc365291.html), [ରାଧାଷ୍ଟମୀ ବ୍ରତ - ସମ୍ପୂର୍ଣ୍ଣ ପୂଜା ବହି](https://collection.shubhapallaba.com/2020/08/radhastami-osha-full-book.html). Padma Brahma-khanda chapter7, verses13–24 and25–42; Odia lotus-child episode.

## Food inside the story is not a festival recipe

The Odia episode describes Chanchala bringing food of six tastes, without naming dishes. Its ritual directions include fasting, flowers, akshata, shriphala and tambula. These are textual categories, not a recovered cooked menu. The story’s meal cannot be promoted to a household recipe or claim about current offerings.

Sources: [ରାଧାଷ୍ଟମୀ ବ୍ରତ - ସମ୍ପୂର୍ଣ୍ଣ ପୂଜା ବହି](https://collection.shubhapallaba.com/2020/08/radhastami-osha-full-book.html). Narada/meal episode; Brata Bidhana ending.

## Offerings and the meal after fasting

Mahanti describes devotees ending the fast towards midday with temple prasada, explained as cooked food offered to the deities. The passage names no dishes, quantities or kitchen. The Padma chapter describes fruit among the offerings, but supplies no fruit varieties or Odisha preparation. Prasada names a ritual relationship to food; it does not by itself identify a sweet, pitha or complete menu.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Greatness of Rādhāṣṭamī: Padma Purana, Brahma-khanda chapter7](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-padma-purana/d/doc365291.html). Mahanti printed48/PDF64; Padma Brahma-khanda7, verses13–20.

## Puri and Sakhigopal need their own context

Behera’s 2019 Puri account describes taking Sudarsan to four ashrams on Radhastami. It does not specify a household menu. Mahanti separately places Radha-pada darshana at Sakhigopal on Kartika’s Aonla Navami. That foot-viewing occasion should not be moved into a Bhadrava itinerary simply because both observances concern Radha. Current routes and visitor access remain unverified.

Sources: [Fairs and Festivals of Lord Jagannath](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2019/Jun-July/engpdf/Fairs-and-Festivals-of-Lord-Jagannath-100-106.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Behera printed103/PDF4; Mahanti printed48/PDF64.

## What is known about textual history

The Odia post is dated 25 August 2020 and carries differing verse signatures: Kshetramohan, Kshetra and Kshetrabasi. The printed exemplar and author identity remain unverified. Modern publication dates do not date the beginning of the vow. Manuscript-catalogue search leads were found, but the original catalogue could not be recovered for this pass; they remain unverified leads in the research record.

## A recent Konark announcement, kept in its scope

Radha Govind Dham Konark advertised Radhashtami sankirtan for 19 September 2026, 9:30 AM–2:00 PM. On 9 October its page still labelled this upcoming. The announcement establishes an advertised programme at a named Odisha institution; it does not show that the programme occurred, identify a meal, or confirm current visitor access.

Sources: [Radha Govind Dham Konark: Radhashtami programme announcement](https://www.rgdkonark.co.in/). Home-page Upcoming Event banner and address footer, read9October2026.

## Why the distinctions matter

Read together, these accounts invite attention to several ways food enters devotion: a parent’s care in a story, something offered to a deity, and a meal received after abstaining. This is an editorial reading of the records, not a claim that one caused the others. A useful local account would explain who cooks, who offers, who shares and which names the household uses.

## For seasonal visitors

Use Bhadrava’s bright eighth as a cultural research window. Confirm the year’s local date and ask the host what, if anything, is open to visitors. No particular Radhastami dish, serving venue or invitation is verified here. General prasada descriptions and a past programme notice are not food-booking information.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Which printed edition underlies the Odia transcription, and how should its differing verse signatures be attributed?
- Can OL-1457, OL-3117 and ORPR-199 catalogue leads be verified against original pages and manuscript colophons?
- Which narrative is used in a named Odisha household or temple, and in which language?
- Which dishes are offered and eaten after the fast, with what local names and preparation?
- How do household observance, Puri ritual and Sakhigopal practice differ?
- Can an annual local date, consented visitor access and any public meal be verified separately?

[Preparation and variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). Radhastami research separates a narrative meal, textual offerings and fast-breaking prasada before seeking locally named dishes and preparation.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No interviews or human review claimed.

# Rai Damodara Brata

Rai Damodara Brata connects the ritual year with the everyday work of eating: choosing ingredients, preparing a restrained meal and receiving temple food. Its story also brings the household world into Jagannath devotion.

**Research note: attributed legend, food descriptions and textual context; origin history and local variation remain open.**

## A name within the Kartika cycle

Mahanti groups Kartika and Rai Damodara under one heading. He describes month-long observance, especially by widows, and a five-day panchuka option. Dash places Rai Damodara in Kartika. This supports a shared research entry, not the claim that every Kartika practice is identical.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed51–52 / PDF67–68; Dash printed16 / PDF2.

## Rai and Lakshmi: the remembered story

Mahanti recounts a legend in which Rai, a Puri servitor’s daughter, marries Jagannath. Lakshmi grants that Rai will be worshipped alongside her. This explains the name within that telling; it is neither a dated marriage record nor evidence of the observance’s historical beginning.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed51 / PDF67.

## Food during the vow

Mahanti describes habishanna or Mahaprasad eaten once daily. These are reported alternatives; he supplies no recipe. The distinction matters: a meal associated with a vow and food received after temple offering have different ritual roles.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed52 / PDF68.

## A described Habisha Dalma

Visit Bhubaneswar describes unroasted moong cooked without turmeric, with restricted vegetables including elephant apple and raw banana, and pepper in place of chilli. This is one attributed preparation. The previously saved 2019 chef-menu account is a separate contemporary context, not proof of household or temple uniformity.

Sources: [Odia Cuisine: Dalma and Habisha Dalma](https://visit.bhubaneswar.me/taste/eat-exclusive/odia-cuisine). Dalma section, Habisha paragraphs; chef context linked through Dalma page.

## History and the limits of textual prescriptions

Patra and Punit’s 2018 study interprets Kartika devotion through Puranic texts and widowhood. Its panchaka discussion describes arua rice and vegetables, with milk and curd on specified days. The underlying passages remain uninspected here. Prescriptive texts illuminate religious ideals but cannot establish what every participant ate or an uninterrupted Odisha chronology.

Sources: [Seeking Refuge in the Lord: Antiquity and Continuity of the Puranic Tradition of the Kartik Brata by Widows at Jagannath Puri](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2018/Nov/engpdf/33-38.pdf). Printed34,36,38 / PDF2,4,6; note30 cites Skanda2.4.32.47,50–51.

## Two calendar questions remain open

Mahanti’s printed25 says the month-long vow starts on Kartika purnima, whereas printed51–52 describes the whole month and its final five days. The discrepancy is retained. Patra and Punit distinguish a month-long vow from a separate five-day vow on textual grounds. A local account must clarify which observance is meant before an annual date is assigned.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [Seeking Refuge in the Lord: Antiquity and Continuity of the Puranic Tradition of the Kartik Brata by Widows at Jagannath Puri](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2018/Nov/engpdf/33-38.pdf). Mahanti printed25,51–52; Patra and Punit printed36 and38 note28.

## Significance: a season made through daily work

An editorial reading can examine devotion through repetition: planning a meal, learning restrictions and sustaining daily observance. It should also make room for participants’ own motives and the labour of cooks and carers. Historical restrictions surrounding widowhood deserve study without treating them as desirable rules or speaking for present-day women. The useful next step is an attributed account of how one household or community kitchen adapts its food, rather than a universal recipe.

## For seasonal visitors

Kartika is a cultural browsing cue; the calendar has no confirmed current-year date. Habisha Dalma is a food to ask about, but a named venue must confirm its menu and serving day before it becomes a recommendation. No household invitation, public meal, host consent or temple access has been established by this research.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can an identified Odia Rai Damodara katha and its imprint be recovered and compared with Mahanti’s synopsis?
- What is the earliest dated Odisha witness, rather than a general Puranic precedent?
- How do named local practitioners distinguish month-long Kartika, Rai Damodara and the five-day vow?
- Which calendar rule resolves the conflicting start statement in Mahanti?
- How do households and community kitchens define habishanna and vary dalma ingredients, methods and serving practices?
- Can a consenting public host, current date and actual Habisha menu be verified?

[Dalma](../../food/dalma.md). Rai Damodara’s Kartika context connects to an attributed Habisha Dalma preparation; the association does not establish a universal recipe or current menu.

[Mahaprasad](../../food/mahaprasad.md). Mahanti names Mahaprasad as food received during the vow; that ritual role does not establish a special seasonal dish or visitor access.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No local interviews or human review claimed.

## 2026-10-08 · Baisakha: related vows and meal research

[Baisakha Brata](baisakha-brata.md). The three-month comparison in Mahanti connects Baisakha with Kartika devotion; it does not transfer a Kartika food recipe or story into Baisakha.

## 2026-10-09 · Identifying a full-moon observance

[Which Osha?](../osha-identity-guide.md) Month-long vow and five-day option are distinguished from a single full-moon day; existing calendar conflict remains unresolved.

body:
# Raja Parba

Raja can be read through a household kitchen as well as a swing. Food made ahead, time away from everyday work, visits to relatives and portions of pitha sent between homes bring the season into social life. The festival connects the coming rains with a belief in the Earth’s menstrual rest; its foods help tell how that rest is imagined and organised.

**Narrative checkpoint: origins, local variation and present visitor offers remain under research.**

## The Earth at rest

In Mahanti’s account, Basumati or Bhu-devi is believed to menstruate for three days as the rainy season approaches. Cultivation pauses, and a fourth-day Basumati snana marks renewal. This is the festival’s sacred explanation, not a literal account of the soil or a dated event in its origin. The author places particular emphasis on Cuttack and surrounding districts; the account does not establish a uniform custom across Odisha.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed116–117 / PDF132–133, Raja parba.

## A calendar organised around Sankranti

Mohapatra’s June 2006 article describes Pahili Raja at the end of Jyestha, Raja or Mithuna Sankranti at the start of Ashadha, and Bhuin Dahana on the following day. It notes a fourth-day Basumata Puja in some places. These are traditional calendar descriptions, not a fixed Gregorian itinerary. Mahanti uses Basi Raja for the third day and gives a solar Mithuna/lunar Jyestha description. Preserve the calendar systems and names rather than silently treating every month label as interchangeable.

Sources: [Raja Sankranti: The Festival of Swings](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/june2006/engpdf/122-123.pdf), [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Mohapatra printed122 / PDF1; Mahanti printed116–117 / PDF132–133.

## Preparing food before the pause

Mahanti connects the suspension of cutting, grinding and cooking with food prepared in advance, naming podo pitha, arisha and muan. He also describes pitha exchanged between relatives and neighbours. Read together, these passages make the kitchen central to the festival: a period of rest relies on work already done, and a cake can become a gift between households. That connection is an editorial reading of his description, not a measured account of who performs the preparatory labour today. His claim that these foods remain unspoilt for several days is not adopted as storage advice.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed117–119 / PDF133–135.

## Poda pitha, arisa and the wider festive meal

The saved Odisha Tourism description presents poda pitha as slowly cooked fermented rice batter, using sal leaves and an earthen pot. The saved ICAR-CRRI compilation describes arisa made from rice flour with jaggery or sugar syrup, shaped and fried. These are separately attributed institutional preparation summaries, not standardised household recipes. Mohapatra lists rice powder, molasses, coconut and ghee among poda-pitha ingredients and describes cakes being shared; he gives no reproducible recipe. The saved June 2026 Akashvani report also names poda and arisa in Raja celebrations. Together these records support the association while leaving proportions, cooking vessels, fillings and household versions open.

Sources: [The Taste of Odisha](https://odishatourism.gov.in/content/tourism/en/the-taste-of-odisha.html), [Raja Sankranti: The Festival of Swings](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/june2006/engpdf/122-123.pdf), [Raja Festival begins across Odisha — Akashvani News, 15 June 2026](https://newsonair.gov.in/raja-festival-begins-across-odisha/). [Traditional Rice Foods: The Rich Heritage of India — Lipi Das](https://icar-crri.in/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/final_book_ldas.pdf). Tourism Poda Pitha heading; ICAR-CRRI printed9 / PDF20, Arisa; Mohapatra printed123 / PDF2; Akashvani15June2026 third body paragraph.

## Swings, songs and visiting

Mahanti describes swings hung from mango or banyan trees, groups singing Raja ballads, puchi games and visits among friends and relations. Food sharing belongs to this setting of sociability. His recollection of improvised footwear made from areca-palm material is a remembered detail, not a date for the festival’s beginning. The account’s general claim that Raja is fading has no supporting survey here; the later food-service and news records likewise cannot measure whether participation is growing or declining.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed117–119 / PDF133–135; footnote53.

## Rest, pleasure and restrictions

Raja’s imagery offers a way to discuss the value attached to the Earth, girls’ social lives and respite from routine labour. The same descriptions record limits on movement, washing and household work and frame girlhood through future marriage. A careful narrative can acknowledge pleasure and restrictions together. It should not claim that every participant experiences empowerment, stigma or rest in the same way. Situated accounts from women of different ages and communities are still needed.

## A documented change in food distribution

An official July 2021 tourism newsletter reports OTDC’s Pitha-on-Wheels during pandemic restrictions, with takeaway sales scheduled for 14–16 June 2021. The programme named poda pitha, manda, kakara, arisa, chakuli and chandrakala and six pickup areas in Bhubaneswar. It offers a dated example of public provision of festival food alongside household preparation. It does not establish when commercial Raja cooking began, that every outlet stocked every dish, or what is available now.

Sources: [Pitha Hits the Road Amid Raja Restrictions — Odisha Unravelled, July 2021, issue 8](https://odishatourism.gov.in/documents/35730/41982/ODISHA%2BUNRAVELLED%2B%2BJULY%2B2021.pdf/f4b34a83-0523-98e2-9019-f5d1faac9bc1?t=1776688897355). Odisha Unravelled July2021 issue8, printed8 / PDF8.

## What the historical record establishes

The 2006 article is a dated witness to a published description of Raja. The undated Mahanti compilation adds remembered and narrated practices; the 2021 programme and 2026 report provide later dated records. This sequence is a history of the evidence inspected, not a continuous history of the festival. No securely dated first observance, founding dynasty or earliest literary passage has been established. Similar descriptions in two publications do not prove independent testimony.

## Looking for Raja food as a visitor

Use the June seasonal association to begin an enquiry, then check the intended year and place. Poda pitha and arisa are useful foods to ask about; a historical programme’s wider menu is not a current offer. Before recommending a visit, establish the serving date, named operator, menu, price and access. Household cooking is a private setting unless a host has agreed to receive visitors. No current seller or household invitation has been verified for this profile.

## Continue reading

[Poda pitha](../../food/poda-pitha.md) · [Arisa pitha](../../food/arisa-pitha.md). The Raja account connects preparation ahead and shared pitha with a pause in everyday work; dish-level pages retain their own preparation evidence.

[Dated serving evidence](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-offer-evidence.md). A festival-food association and a dated public sale answer different questions; the serving-evidence study preserves that distinction for Raja.

## Open research questions

- Can dated Odia literature, gazetteers or archival descriptions establish earlier Raja witnesses without mistaking a literary reference for an origin date?
- Can the museum-hosted Rajo, The Swing Festival of Kalinga (India) be recovered with its issue, byline, references and historical claims checked?
- How do names, cooking schedules and foods vary by locality, community and household?
- Who does the work before and during the festival, and how do participants describe rest and restrictions in their own terms?
- Which dated public offers actually name foods, prices and visitor access for the intended year?

[Osha, brata and parba collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No fieldwork or human cultural review claimed.

body:
# Rambha Trutiya

A pair of bangles, a prayer for harmony and a name that also belongs to a longer cycle of vows: Rambha Trutiya asks us to read household description and ritual literature together, with their differences intact.

**Research note: Odisha description and a complete printed textual passage compared; local katha and foods remain unresolved.**

## The Odisha description

Mahanti places the osha on Jyestha shukla Tritiya, observed by married women seeking harmony in marriage. He describes worship of a pair of bangles representing Rambha and Lakshmi. Dash’s earlier inventory also places Ramba trutiya in Jyestha, without describing this rite. Neither passage identifies a particular household, observed event or participant sample.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf), [The Perishing Tradition of Osha, Brata and Mela in Orissa: An Overview](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/April2006/engpdf/The_perishing_tradition_of_osha.pdf). Mahanti printed54 / PDF70; Dash printed16 / PDF2.

## The story we have, and the story still missing

Mahanti connects Rambha with the apsara emerging during the churning of the ocean of milk. He also says that, according to unspecified Puranas, Parvati observed the vow to obtain Shiva as her husband. These are attributed religious accounts. His brief paragraph is not a complete Odia katha, and it supplies no named chapter for the Parvati claim.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed54 / PDF70, Rambha trutiya osha.

## An older printed witness describes a different scope

Chapter CXX of Dutt’s1908 English Garuda Puranam begins a similarly named vow on the bright third lunar day of Margashira and continues through a year of goddess worship. Sanskrit Wikisource’s displayed chapter1.120 likewise opens in Margashirsha. This is a comparison of textual prescriptions with the Odisha descriptions. It does not move the Odisha osha to another month or prove that both accounts describe the same local practice.

Sources: [The Garuda Puranam — Chapter CXX, Rambha Tritiya Vratam](https://archive.org/details/garudapuranam00duttgoog), [Garuda Purana, Acharakanda120 — Sanskrit digital transcription](https://sa.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=गरुडपुराणम्/आचारकाण्डः/अध्यायः_१२०&oldid=307780). Dutt printed359–360 / PDF380–381; Sanskrit1.120.1–11.

## Food has more than one ritual role

In the printed translation, the Magha passage separates a butter regimen from Mandas offered to Subhadra. The Phalguna passage distinguishes barley gruel after worship from S’askulis offered to Gomati. Its Jaishtha passage offers khanda, translated as treacle, while separately naming cloves for the observer. The closing rite includes a meal for a Brahmana pair and distribution of ghee confections. These are features of Dutt’s textual translation, not a verified menu for an Odisha household.

Sources: [The Garuda Puranam — Chapter CXX, Rambha Tritiya Vratam](https://archive.org/details/garudapuranam00duttgoog). Printed359–360 / PDF380–381, monthly passages and closing paragraph.

## Read food names and translations carefully

The Sanskrit transcription has mandaka at1.120.3 and ghritodana at1.120.10. Dutt prints Mandas and describes ghee confections in the closing passage. Their meanings and recipes require edition comparison; similarity to the name manda pitha does not establish the same preparation. We therefore retain source wording and ritual role instead of mapping these terms to modern Odisha dishes. The text is evidence for studying prescriptions, not a tested recipe or a fasting recommendation.

Sources: [The Garuda Puranam — Chapter CXX, Rambha Tritiya Vratam](https://archive.org/details/garudapuranam00duttgoog), [Garuda Purana, Acharakanda120 — Sanskrit digital transcription](https://sa.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=गरुडपुराणम्/आचारकाण्डः/अध्यायः_१२०&oldid=307780). Dutt printed359–360; Sanskrit1.120.3 and1.120.10.

## What its significance allows us to ask

The bangles in Mahanti’s account make a familiar household object part of a prayer about relationships. The longer text organises devotion through changing months, materials, gifts and shared food. Comparing them opens questions about how families select, adapt and transmit a vow. It does not establish a line of transmission, a scientific benefit from fasting, or a recipe preserved unchanged over centuries.

## History, food and seasonal visits remain open

The1908 imprint dates the inspected translation only. The first Odisha observance, a complete local story and specific local foods remain unestablished. Mahanti’s suggestion of declining practice has no measured participation series here. The guide therefore retains Jyestha as an attributed calendar rule, no converted annual date, and no promised dish or serving venue. A named local account and a dated public offer are needed before this becomes a food stop for visitors.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Which Odia katha, manuscript, panji or named-locality account documents Rambha Trutiya and its bangles?
- What is the exact Puranic passage behind Mahanti’s Parvati account?
- How do practitioners distinguish the Jyestha observance from the Margashira-starting annual textual cycle?
- What foods are offered, consumed, shared or avoided in a documented Odisha observance?
- Which Sanskrit edition underlies the transcription, and how should mandaka, ghritodana and other food terms be translated?
- Is there a consented public observance with dated serving information?

[Bali Trutiya](bali-trutiya.md). Both profiles mention Parvati and Shiva, but their inspected texts, calendar rules and food evidence differ; related reading does not establish identical vows.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No interviews, human cultural review or media permissions claimed.
