body:
# Tarini Brata

Tarini Brata brings a hope of protection into the ritual year. Its food story needs several separate strands: fasting in the vow, coconut offerings at Ghatagaon, cooked temple offerings and a coconut sweet associated with the surrounding area. Evidence for one strand does not automatically establish the others.

**Research note: shrine narrative and historical food evidence inspected; household katha, chronology and menu remain open.**

## The vow named in an Odisha account

Mahanti places Tarini Brata on Ashadha’s bright fourth lunar day. He describes women fasting and worshipping the goddess, with some tying a red thread on the arm, in the hope of relief from difficulties. He locates the observance around Tarini shrines and names Ghatagaon in Keonjhar as the principal shrine. This description gives neither a complete katha nor a food or fast-breaking menu.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed46/PDF62.

## Keep three identities distinct

The Tarini vow named here is not automatically an alias for Bipattarini. Nor is it the Tara-Tarini yatra that Mahanti separately describes on Chaitra Tuesdays at the hill shrine near the Rushikulya in Ganjam. Names, deities, locality and calendar must be matched before stories or food rules are joined.

Sources: [Fading Festivals of Odisha: A peep into the religious practices in Odisha](https://www.esamskriti.com/essays/pdf/17%20FINAL%20Fading%20Festivals%20of%20Odisha%20%281%29.pdf). Printed46/PDF62 and printed158/PDF174; Bipattarini comparison retained in its existing profile.

## The story of the backward glance

Mallebrein records a shrine legend in which Tarini agrees to follow Gobinda Bhanja from Puri provided he never looks back. When her bells fall silent at Ghatagaon, he turns; she becomes stone and stays there. This is an attributed shrine narrative, not a recovered household brata-katha.

Sources: [Creating a kshetra: Goddess Tarini of Ghatgaon and her Development from a Forest Goddess to Pan-Orissan Deity](https://krepublishers.com/02-Journals/JSS/JSS-08-0-000-000-2004-Web/JSS-08-2-085-178-2004-Abst-PDF/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-150-Mallebrein/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-Mallebrein_Tx.pdf). Printed158–159, Kanchi-war narrative; author-copy text. [Inspected author copy](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228768760_Creating_a_kshetra_Goddess_Tarini_of_Ghatgaon_and_her_Development_from_a_Forest_Goddess_to_Pan-Orissan_Deity).

## Dating the shrine is not dating the vow

The paper questions the royal chronology behind the familiar 1480 story, citing a tentative seventeenth-century alternative in Senapati’s district history. Neither date establishes the beginning of Tarini Brata. The cited historical work was not independently inspected here.

Sources: [Creating a kshetra: Goddess Tarini of Ghatgaon and her Development from a Forest Goddess to Pan-Orissan Deity](https://krepublishers.com/02-Journals/JSS/JSS-08-0-000-000-2004-Web/JSS-08-2-085-178-2004-Abst-PDF/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-150-Mallebrein/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-Mallebrein_Tx.pdf). Printed162–164, historical discussion and note23; claim limited to author’s reported comparison. [Inspected author copy](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228768760_Creating_a_kshetra_Goddess_Tarini_of_Ghatgaon_and_her_Development_from_a_Forest_Goddess_to_Pan-Orissan_Deity).

## Coconut as an offering

Kendujhar’s official district page describes devotees offering coconuts to Tarini at Ghatagaon. That supports a shrine-offering association. It does not identify the food of Ashadha’s household vow or show what visitors can obtain today.

Sources: [Maa Tarini Pitha Ghatagaon](https://kendujhar.odisha.gov.in/en/tourism/tourist-places/maa-tarini-pitha-ghatagaon). Culture & Heritage introduction, coconut sentence.

## A historical food change with two starting years

Mallebrein’s 2004 paper, based on 2002 fieldwork, reports the introduction of cooked anna bhoga and prasad distribution after an earlier fruit-and-coconut practice. It gives 1978 on printed 157 but 1975 on printed 158. Both readings remain unresolved; no single starting year is adopted.

Sources: [Creating a kshetra: Goddess Tarini of Ghatgaon and her Development from a Forest Goddess to Pan-Orissan Deity](https://krepublishers.com/02-Journals/JSS/JSS-08-0-000-000-2004-Web/JSS-08-2-085-178-2004-Abst-PDF/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-150-Mallebrein/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-Mallebrein_Tx.pdf). Printed157–158; fieldwork year in printed164 note1. [Inspected author copy](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228768760_Creating_a_kshetra_Goddess_Tarini_of_Ghatgaon_and_her_Development_from_a_Forest_Goddess_to_Pan-Orissan_Deity).

## Nadia kora belongs to the place evidence

The same study associates Ghatagaon with nadia kora, a coconut sweet. This is historical place-food evidence, not a verified Tarini Brata dish, complete recipe or present shop recommendation.

Sources: [Creating a kshetra: Goddess Tarini of Ghatgaon and her Development from a Forest Goddess to Pan-Orissan Deity](https://krepublishers.com/02-Journals/JSS/JSS-08-0-000-000-2004-Web/JSS-08-2-085-178-2004-Abst-PDF/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-150-Mallebrein/JSS-08-2-155-165-2004-Mallebrein_Tx.pdf). Printed158, coconut distribution and local sweet paragraph. [Inspected author copy](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228768760_Creating_a_kshetra_Goddess_Tarini_of_Ghatgaon_and_her_Development_from_a_Forest_Goddess_to_Pan-Orissan_Deity).

## Why these distinctions matter

Food can be withheld during a vow, offered to a deity, distributed as prasad or sold as a local sweet. Those roles tell different stories about care, devotion and livelihoods. Joining them too quickly would manufacture a festival menu. Here the household vow and shrine food practices remain connected questions, with each source’s setting visible.

## What remains to be recovered

A dated Odia Tarini brata-katha, its edition or manuscript witness, a named locality’s ritual calendar and household preparation remain missing. An online page titled Maa Tarini Brata Katha repeats the saved Mahanti description, mixes in Tara-Tarini material and states that the PDF is unavailable; its title and ten-page label do not establish a recovered text. The original study’s page images and the underlying temple records are also needed to resolve its conflicting food dates.

## For visitors exploring food and faith

Treat Ghatagaon as a place to investigate the relationship between offerings, prasad and local sweets, with a willing local guide or host. Confirm dates, access and any food arrangement directly before travel. No shop, meal service, household invitation or annual Brata date has been verified for visitors. Coconut offerings do not by themselves create a seasonal tasting itinerary.

## Questions for the next research pass

- Can an original Odia Tarini Brata text be recovered with author, edition or manuscript identity?
- What local evidence distinguishes Tarini, Bipattarini and Tara-Tarini practices?
- Which temple records resolve1975 versus1978 for the introduction of anna bhoga?
- Can Senapati’s cited chronology and the original shrine pamphlets be inspected without treating legend as dated events?
- What is offered and eaten during Ashadha Tarini Brata in a named, consenting household?
- What are the ingredients and preparation of locally made nadia kora, and is any specific Brata association documented?
- Can a willing custodian verify dates, visitor access and actual food service?

[Bipattarini Brata](bipattarini-brata.md). Tarini and Bipattarini share protective themes, but name similarity does not establish identical vows, calendars, narratives or foods.

[Preparation and variation](../../food/preparation-and-variation.md). Tarini research separates household fasting, shrine offerings, cooked prasad and a local sweet; each food role needs its own preparation and locality evidence.

[Osha collection](../osha-brata-seasonal-food.md) · [Seasonal food guide](../../visitor-index/seasonal-food-guide.md). No field interviews or human language review claimed.

body:
# Pala and its culture

Pala belongs at the meeting point of performed poetry, musical storytelling and community life. A 2012 festival account connects these ballad traditions with literature, rhythm, humour and epic narratives. [Pala and Daskathia Utsav](https://www.narthaki.com/info/rev12/rev1245.html).

## How to begin listening

Listen for the story, the explanation of a verse and the exchange between the lead voice and accompanying performers. The official 2025 Sammilan account explicitly credits singers and Bayaks for communicating Odia poetry. [48th annual state-level Pala Sammilan at Parklane, Kendujhar](https://cm.odisha.gov.in/en/latest-news/participated-48th-annual-state-level-pala-sammilan-organized-parklane-kendujhar). Detailed roles, instruments and local terminology need an attributed demonstration before becoming a performance manual.

## Forms and history: preserve the source’s vocabulary

Dash’s January 2011 article distinguishes **Pothi Pala** performed seated, **Thia Pala** performed standing, and **Badi Pala**, where singers take turns on a stage. These notes come from the indexed passage at printed page 73; direct PDF access failed. [The Socio-Cultural Value of Odia Folkdance: Pala](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2011/Jan/engpdf/72-74.pdf).

A full history needs separately examined evidence for Satyanarayana/Satyapir associations, manuscript dates, teacher lineages and later stage practice. Those are research questions here. A devotional origin account cannot supply a verified founding date; older claims of decline do not measure the present condition.

## Performers and repertoire

The 2009 Sangeet Natak Akademi citation recognises **Jagannath Behera** for Pala theatre and names his teachers. The indexed citation is retained with its full-PDF access gap; its historical age and offices must not become present-day claims. [Jagannath Behera — Akademi Award: Pala (Orissa)](https://sangeetnatak.gov.in/public/uploads/awardees/docs/Jagannath_Behera.pdf).

A contemporary report of the 19–21 July 2012 festival at Rabindra Mandap provides these credited examples:

| Performer | Presentation as reported |
|---|---|
| Santilata Sahu | Hanuman’s meditation in Dwapara Yuga |
| Manorama Panda | Naga Jyoti |
| Kumudini Patel | Sasirekha Parinaya |
| Madanamohana Jena and troupe | Papamochan Yajna |
| Laxman Charan Rout and troupe | Mahadani Ajigarta |

[Pala and Daskathia Utsav](https://www.narthaki.com/info/rev12/rev1245.html). These are dated performance credits, not a complete artist directory. The women performers deserve their own researched biographies. Keep Pala and Daskathia distinct even when a festival presents both.

## A living archive and a dated gathering

The [Shree Jagannath Pala Research Foundation](https://www.sjprf.in/) offers routes to performer material and documentary notices. Its [Pala Kabita catalogue](https://sjprf.in/index.php/pala-kabita) records author attributions, including Bhagabata Bandana by Sarat Chandra Dash. These are useful discovery routes; recordings, editions, translations and rights need item-level checks.

The Chief Minister’s office dates its report of the **48th annual state-level Pala Sammilan in Kendujhar to 28 December 2025**. [48th annual state-level Pala Sammilan at Parklane, Kendujhar](https://cm.odisha.gov.in/en/latest-news/participated-48th-annual-state-level-pala-sammilan-organized-parklane-kendujhar). This establishes a reported gathering and edition number; attendance, artist totals, payments and current booking availability remain unknown.

## Story opportunity

**An evening where poetry becomes performance.** Follow a named artist from choosing a text to explaining it to an audience; credit accompanying artists and the community that hosts the performance. This is an editorial proposal, not a filmed or interviewed story.

## Next research

Recover the two government PDFs; verify performer biographies and women’s participation through independent records; catalogue named texts and legally viewable recordings; document instruments, apprenticeship and community settings. Add dated troupe, funding or earnings statistics only when units and coverage are clear. No local interview, Odia review, verified event calendar or media licence is claimed.

[odissi](odissi.md) — Related reading on Odisha’s performance traditions; no claim that the two forms are identical.

[people and creations](../people/people-and-creations.md) — Connects named performers with the existing people-and-works research framework; performance credit is not a completed biography.

## Source recovery follow-up · 1 October 2026

The Behera award citation has now been retrieved and its one-page text checked. The earlier indexed-only limitation is resolved for that citation alone; see its [updated source record](../sources/pala-sna-behera2009.md). Dash’s 2011 paper remains a full-text gap: direct retrieval encountered an expired TLS certificate, and the search service could not fetch the full issue. No certificate check was disabled. A [feature draft](pala-feature-draft.json) is prepared for editorial development; it is not included in the public website edition.

# Pipili appliqué

## Sourced knowledge

The tourism profile links Pipili appliqué with Jagannath chariot traditions and decorative objects.[^pipili]

## Story opportunity

Use colour, cutting and stitching to make a craft process film.

*Editorial proposal; audience response has not been measured.*

## Next research

Identify the maker and object; confirm ritual context and workshop access.

## Connections

[Related knowledge](raghurajpur-pattachitra.md) · [Research standards](../about/research-method.md)

[^pipili]: [Pipili](https://odishatourism.gov.in/content/tourism/en/discover/attractions/arts-crafts/pipili.html)

## Place and visitor evidence · 30 September 2026

The [tourism profile](https://odishatourism.gov.in/content/tourism/en/discover/attractions/arts-crafts/pipili.html) connects Pipili appliqué with chariot decoration and several decorative and household objects. Its general visitor listing gives 08:00–20:00, free entry and parking. This does not establish every shop's hours, workshop permission or demonstration prices.

The same page's bank and hotel guidance names Bhubaneswar; those amenities must not become onsite Pipili facilities. body:
# Tantric traditions: sites, texts and interpretations

**Odisha’s Yogini temples tell a story through circles, sculpture and the relationship between goddesses and Shiva.** Start with two distinct places: [Hirapur](../places/hirapur-yogini.md) in Khordha and [Ranipur-Jharial](../places/ranipur-jharial-yogini.md) in Balangir. Their open-air architecture gives this heritage collection a strong visual identity without needing claims of national uniqueness.

## Two places, different evidence

| What to notice | Hirapur | Ranipur-Jharial |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Form | Circular sanctuary, eastern projection and central mandapa | Circular sanctuary and central pillared mandapa |
| Divine figures | Yoginis, Bhairavas and exterior Katyayini figures | Yoginis surrounding a central eight-armed dancing Shiva |
| Material or scale recorded | Sandstone structure; black-chlorite interior images | 16.60 m external and 13.60 m internal diameter |
| Dating in the IGNCA inventory | Early tenth century, argued from style; Bhaumakara attribution | Ninth–tenth centuries with early tenth specified; Somavamsi attribution |

Sources: IGNCA’s [Hirapur inventory, pp.1–3](https://ignca.gov.in/asi_reports/orkhurda040.pdf) and [Ranipur-Jharial inventory, pp.1–3](https://ignca.gov.in/asi_reports/orbolangir001.pdf). These are institutional heritage inventories, not original foundation inscriptions. Neither carries a survey/publication date. Their named listers and reviewers are credited in the source records; Utkal has not obtained human review.

## Three contexts to distinguish

**Yogini** names a category of divine figures and associated traditions; it does not identify one uniform religion or modern yoga practice. **Shakta** describes a goddess-centred emphasis, while **Shaiva** refers to Shiva-related traditions. At these sites, Yogini and Bhairava/Nataraja imagery should be read together, without requiring the two emphases to be mutually exclusive.

**Buddhist Vajrayana** has its own Yogini-tantra traditions. Shaman Hatley’s openly available scholarly introduction discusses both Shaiva Bhairava traditions and Buddhist Yogini texts. Shared terminology creates a subject for comparison; it does not establish that either Odisha temple was a Buddhist monastery or that all these traditions followed one lineage. [Hatley, 2020, Introduction](https://academic.oup.com/reference/62357/reference-article-abstract/554513529).

## A textual connection worth investigating

Sabbi Lall’s SOAS report of Hatley’s 2020 lecture describes possible parallels between Hirapur’s images and goddesses in the Devīpurāṇa. The reported argument stops short of asserting that the text inspired the temple. Keep this as an **attributed iconographic hypothesis**, with the text’s date, edition and relevant passages still to examine. The lecture recording and original Sanskrit passages have not been reviewed here. [SOAS report, 14 January 2021](https://blogs.soas.ac.uk/yoga-studies/2021/01/14/in-search-of-yoginis/). The report and Hatley’s Oxford entry share a scholar; they are not independent confirmation.

## What stays open

- **Hirapur’s date and patronage:** Odisha Tourism’s saved account gives the ninth century and Hiradevi; IGNCA argues early tenth century and names the Bhaumakaras generally. Preserve both attributions pending inscription-level or specialist review.
- **Ranipur-Jharial’s image count:** the inventory states 65 niches, but its categories total 66 (48 + 11 + 7). No corrected count is invented, and no current surviving-image total is published.
- **Ritual and access:** IGNCA labels Hirapur living and Ranipur-Jharial non-living, without a survey date. These labels cannot establish present practice, availability or an unbroken ritual tradition. Its brief Kapalika attribution is not enough to reconstruct historical rites.
- **Text and transmission:** direct passage-level links with Buddhist or Jagannath traditions remain unestablished. No secrecy-based promotional claims, supernatural claims as fact, or undocumented origin chain is adopted.

## Editorial story seed

**A circle of goddesses, a sky above.** Explore Odisha’s Yogini heritage through two places whose architecture invites a closer look at sculpture, belief and preservation. This is draft campaign language grounded in form; photographs, visitor details and publication still need their own checks.

[Structured evidence](../references/data/culture-learning.json) retains individual claims, locators and conflict flags. [Related reading](../history/buddhist-learning.md) — Points to questions about Buddhist Vajrayana while keeping Buddhist and Yogini/Shakta histories distinct.

body:
# Odisha’s universities: institutions and evidence

**Compare institutions by their role, legal category and dated evidence.** The [Higher Education Department directory](https://dhe.odisha.gov.in/en/universities/list-of-univerisities-in-odisha) supplies the following starting selection, not a best-university league table or a complete statewide census.

| Directory category | Selected institutions to profile |
| --- | --- |
| State public | Utkal, Ravenshaw, Sambalpur, Berhampur, OUAT, Utkal University of Culture, Odisha State Open University, National Law University Odisha |
| Central | Central University of Odisha |
| State private | Centurion, Sri Sri, Birla Global, ASBM, GIET, Silicon |
| Deemed to be university | KIIT, Siksha ‘O’ Anusandhan, KISS |

Deemed status is a legal category; it does not itself establish government ownership. Directory inclusion does not verify current programme approval, admissions, accreditation or every institutional name change. IIT, NIT, NISER, IISER and AIIMS coverage needs a separate institution-type check.

**One dated finding:** NIRF’s **2025 University category** places **Siksha ‘O’ Anusandhan 15th** (63.14) and **KIIT 17th** (62.87). These are India ranks in that category, not ranks among all institutions or subject-specific outcomes. [Original ranking table](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2025/UniversityRanking.html).

The attempted 2026 table could not be retrieved. These numbers are explicitly 2025; no latest-ranking claim is made.

The initial research agenda covered UGC identities, establishment dates and comparative performance. The checkpoint below completes selected identity and outcome checks; discipline-specific strengths and broader outcome coverage remain to be expanded. Keep score, rank, category and year together; do not infer growth from rank movements alone.

## Identity check: eighteen existing entries verified

On 2 October 2026 UTC, the UGC public register was checked against all 18 institutions already selected above. The source’s institution IDs, names, state, type and status are retained in the [structured record](../references/data/culture-learning.json). This is our selected directory, not Odisha’s total institution count. [UGC register](https://www.ugc.gov.in/universitydetails/university?type=MuOh4z0uqRaY2k8Ag10I0g==).

### Establishment has several dates

| Institution | What the original record establishes |
| --- | --- |
| Utkal University | State category in UGC; section 3(1)(i) of the 1989 Act continues the identity under the 1966 Act. These dates do not replace its earlier foundation history. |
| Central University of Odisha | Central category; the 2009 Act’s First Schedule names Central University of Orissa. The Act’s commencement 15 January 2009 and assent 20 March 2009 are separate events. |
| Centurion, Odisha | Private category; the 2010 Act describes a self-financed private university. Establishment notification effective 23 December 2010 follows the Act’s August assent/publication. |
| KIIT | UGC deemed-category register date 16 February 2004 |
| SOA | UGC deemed-category register date 17 July 2007 |
| KISS | UGC deemed-category register date 25 August 2017 |

[Utkal Act,p.4](https://utkaluniversity.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/University-Act.pdf) · [Central Act,pp.1,3,17](https://cup.edu.in/sites/default/files/Documents/Gazette.pdf) · [Centurion Act](https://cutm.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/1355.pdf) · [Centurion establishment](https://cutm.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/2160.pdf) · [UGC deemed register](https://deemed.ugc.ac.in/Home/ListOfDeemedToBeUniversity).

These historical Acts establish identity, not a review of all later amendments. Centurion’s 2013 UGC letter approves a compliance report after an expert visit; it is not a blanket present-day programme approval. The Andhra Pradesh Centurion entry is a different UGC identity. Utkal University and Utkal University of Culture also remain distinct. [2013letter,p.1](https://cutm.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/4992496_CenturianUniversity.pdf).

## Read performance through more than one measure

SOA and KIIT have dated national visibility in NIRF’s University category. SOA’s published score moved 62.61→63.14 from 2024 to 2025 while its rank moved 14→15; KIIT’s score moved 62.53→62.87 while its rank moved 15→17. Both rank declines remain visible alongside the score increases. Teaching/resources, research/professional practice, graduation outcomes, inclusion and perception component scores are saved separately. These are ranking measures, not direct learning tests or research-impact estimates.

**Utkal University is in the 101–150 University band in both 2024 and 2025.** Alphabetical order inside the band does not supply an exact rank, and an unchanged band does not establish an unchanged score. [2024band](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2024/UniversityRanking150.html) · [2025band](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2025/UniversityRanking150.html).

### Graduate outcomes: optional evidence view

The following are institutional submissions to NIRF 2025, **four-year undergraduate programmes**, grouped by graduation year. Disciplines may differ between universities and cohorts. Pay is nominal annual median among placed graduates only.

| Institution / graduating year | Graduated in minimum time | Placed | Selected for higher study | Median annual pay of placed graduates |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SOA 2021–22 | 1,978 | 1,595 | 207 | ₹4.50 lakh |
| SOA 2022–23 | 2,453 | 2,205 | 235 | ₹5.75 lakh |
| SOA 2023–24 | 2,471 | 2,218 | 237 | ₹6.00 lakh |
| KIIT 2021–22 | 4,162 | 4,021 | 141 | ₹9.00 lakh |
| KIIT 2022–23 | 3,878 | 3,769 | 109 | ₹9.50 lakh |
| KIIT 2023–24 | 3,611 | 3,513 | 98 | ₹9.70 lakh |

[SOA submission,p.2](https://www.nirfindia.org/nirfpdfcdn/2025/pdf/University/IR-O-U-0363.pdf) · [KIIT submission,p.2](https://www.nirfindia.org/nirfpdfcdn/2025/pdf/University/IR-O-U-0356.pdf). KIIT’s reported placed count falls as the graduating cohort shrinks; the rising pay figure should not conceal that. These are different cohorts, not the same individuals’ pay growth. They are not independent job audits, state employment totals or student return-on-investment estimates. KIIT’s first-year admission figures exceed its stated intake for these cohorts; retain that scope question before deriving utilisation or completion rates.

### Connections and next evidence

[Achyuta Samanta](../people/achyuta-samanta.md) connects to KIIT and KISS institution-building; the KISS deemed-status date must not settle an earlier school-founding dispute. [Buddhist learning](../history/buddhist-learning.md) offers a separate historical reading path without claiming institutional continuity. [The public story](../stories/odisha-university-evidence.md) turns selected evidence into a readable card.

Further profiles should add discipline-specific work and comparable public/central/private graduate cohorts. IIT, NIT, NISER, IISER and AIIMS need their own institutional and campus identities. Current programme approvals, admissions, costs, 2026 rankings and independent employment evidence remain open.

[Related reading](../people/achyuta-samanta.md) — Separates institutional legal milestones from a founder’s biography.

## School, university and institutional outcomes · 2 October 2026 UTC

[Samanta’s expanded record](../people/achyuta-samanta.md) adds original KISS university notification evidence, a KIIT continuation instrument, Parliament service and university-only signed financial statements. The KISS school and university are explicitly distinct. Existing KIIT graduate cohorts remain canonical here and are linked, not duplicated.

## KISS student evidence · 2 October 2026 UTC

The [Samanta/KISS record](../people/achyuta-samanta.md) now links postgraduate stock and tuition support, annual doctoral completions, and AQAR pass/placement fields. School populations stay separate. The higher-study count refers to the previous graduating batch, so it cannot be combined with current placements. The canonical observations are in culture-learning.json under kiss_outcomes_checkpoint; they are not duplicated as statewide education totals.

body:
# Kodingamali and Baphlimali: output, processing and accountability

**Two bauxite mines, two different stories.** OMC’s Kodingamali adds a regulator-recorded output series. Baphlimali connects a mine to the Utkal Alumina refinery and an international certification record. Neither capacity nor certification measures mineral revenue or household prosperity.

## Kodingamali: consistent output, a separate expansion plan

IBM’s September 2024 inspection records **3 million tonnes of ROM bauxite in FY2023–24**, against a 6 million-tonne proposal. It explicitly identifies a 3 MTPA environmental-clearance constraint. This is a historical inspection, not confirmation of today’s permission.

| Financial year | Actual ROM tonnes | Proposed tonnes |
|---|---:|---:|
|2019–20|3,000,000|3,000,000|
|2020–21|2,999,500|6,000,000|
|2021–22|3,000,000|6,000,000|
|2022–23|3,000,000|6,000,000|
|2023–24|3,000,000|6,000,000|

Five observations span four elapsed years: this is a broadly flat series. The register identifies OMC, mine code 07ORI09005 and Koraput. Its non-captive classification does not identify a buyer. Rehabilitation-area observations remain held until their annual/cumulative basis is clear. [IBM, PDF pp.1–5](https://ibm.gov.in/writereaddata/files/172965925667188178a68e6MCDR_Inspection_Report_202324_KBM.pdf).

## Baphlimali: a documented mine-to-refinery link

The ASI audit describes bauxite travelling by covered conveyor to Utkal Alumina’s refinery. Its overview reports approximately 1,017 people, including 82 women, and 8.5 MTPA capacity. These are audit-period site figures; local residence and comparable workforce categories remain unverified. The annual-return follow-up below supplies a separate FY2024–25 output measure. The overview describes a lease spanning Rayagada and Kalahandi, so the registered district alone must not become a whole-mine geographic boundary. [Audit, PDF p.4](https://aluminium-stewardship.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ASI-Audit-Report-Utkal-Alumina-International-Limited-Certificate-557-PS.pdf).

**Certificate 557 was issued 19 May 2026**, with an expiry date 18 May 2029 subject to continuing conformance. Its scope covers bauxite mining and related processing/transport; the refinery is expressly excluded. [Certificate and audit, PDF pp.1–4](https://aluminium-stewardship.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ASI-Audit-Report-Utkal-Alumina-International-Limited-Certificate-557-PS.pdf). The issuer’s announcement records **nine minor non-conformances** requiring corrective action. [ASI announcement](https://aluminium-stewardship.org/asi-certifies-baphlimali-bauxite-mines-of-utkal-international-limited-against-performance-standard-v3-1).

Retain the findings alongside the milestone. For example, the audit’s forced-labour criterion finding concerns inadequate statement coverage; the auditors report finding no forced labour. A living-wage assessment was missing, and documented overtime guidance was incomplete. Corrective-action closure is not yet verified. [Audit, PDF pp.17–18](https://aluminium-stewardship.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ASI-Audit-Report-Utkal-Alumina-International-Limited-Certificate-557-PS.pdf).

## Evidence that needs reconciliation

Hindalco’s undated page contains 8.5 MTPA in its header and 7.0 MTPA in its body. Its 18.5 km conveyor description also differs from the audit’s 18 km. Preserve the respective records rather than manufacturing a single precise current value. [Company profile](https://www.hindalco.com/about-us/operations/baphlimali-bauxite-mines).

A compliance-index link retrieved under Baphlimali led to a report whose cover names **Bimarla in Jharkhand**. It is excluded from Odisha observations. The annual return and the actual Baphlimali compliance report have now been read as text; retrieval limits are recorded below.

[Detailed observations, conflicts and next source routes](../references/data/mining-programme.json) · [Koraput](../statistics/districts/koraput.md) · [Rayagada](../statistics/districts/rayagada.md) · [Kalahandi](../statistics/districts/kalahandi.md).

[Mining overview](mining.md): Connects mine identities and reported output to separate work, permissions and community questions.

[Existing NALCO chain](bauxite-to-aluminium.md) supplies a separate processing case; do not combine company or mine totals without boundaries.

## Annual-return follow-up · 2 October 2026 UTC

**Baphlimali reports 7.657 million tonnes of ROM bauxite in FY2024–25.** Its annual return records 7,657,426 tonnes produced and 7,657,000 tonnes dispatched for captive consumption by Utkal Alumina. Opening stock plus production minus dispatch equals closing stock; the 426-tonne difference is preserved.

The mine reports **₹64.22 crore paid to DMF** for that financial year, converted from ₹642,173,879. This is a company payment disclosure, not proof of completed local projects or money received by households. [FormG-1, PDF pp.6,12–13](https://www.hindalco.com/Upload/PDF/baphlimali-form-g1-annual-return-2024-25.pdf).

The work table separates 9,763 direct and 193,300 contract **person-days**. Its 556.3 average daily persons employed cannot be compared as growth against the later ASI approximate 1,017 people. Complex table fields await visual review; local residence remains unknown. [FormG-1, PDF p.4](https://www.hindalco.com/Upload/PDF/baphlimali-form-g1-annual-return-2024-25.pdf).

The compliance report distinguishes **8.5 MTPA EC capacity from 8.0 MTPA operating consent**, citing an order valid through 31 March 2027. Its scanned consent annexure was not readable, so this remains the company’s September 2025 account. [Compliance report, PDF pp.2,11](https://www.hindalco.com/Upload/PDF/baphlimali-half-yearly-ec-compliance-report-april-2205-sept-2025.pdf).

Backfilled, afforested and reclaimed-rehabilitated areas also have different labels and dates. District-area headings do not reconcile to one lease total. Both comparisons are held. Direct PDF downloads failed; readable publisher text supports this checkpoint, with no visual or human review claimed.

body:
# From Koraput’s bauxite to Angul’s aluminium

**Odisha’s mineral story includes the factories that turn ore into metal.** NALCO’s reported chain joins Panchpatmali in Koraput to the Damanjodi refinery and Angul smelter, with surplus alumina moving to Visakhapatnam for export. [Operating description](https://nalcoindia.com/business/operation/alumina-refinery/).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 P[Panchpatmali bauxite mines · Koraput] --> D[Damanjodi alumina refinery · Koraput]
 D --> A[Angul aluminium smelter]
 D --> V[Visakhapatnam export facility · Andhra Pradesh]
 T[Pottangi · development project] -. Planned supply .-> D
```

The diagram shows reported supply relationships, not mineral conversion ratios, equal quantities or an independently checked logistics map.

## A measurable processing story

NALCO reports **471,701 tonnes of aluminium in 2025–26**, up **2.5%** on 460,137 tonnes in 2024–25. Alumina hydrate output rose from 2,075,500 to 2,300,000 tonnes, **10.8%**. These are company figures; successive material stages must not be added into one production total. Five annual observations from 2021–22 to 2025–26 span four elapsed years.

Markets moved differently. Aluminium domestic sales increased from 323,809 to 461,081 tonnes across those endpoints, while aluminium export sales fell from 133,085 to 13,238 tonnes. Total company export-sales value also fell from ₹5,516.97 crore in 2024–25 to ₹4,701.54 crore in 2025–26. Quantities and rupee values answer different questions. [Annual report, p.296](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

## What can we say about work?

The company reports 1,715 permanent employees, 3,149 permanent workers and 16,722 other-than-permanent workers at 31 March 2026. The first two categories reconcile to its 4,864 on-roll workforce. These totals include its wider operations and cannot be presented as Odisha-resident jobs created.

A more local connection is the **83% share of wage costs** reported for its semi-urban category in 2025–26, compared with 81% the year before. Its footnote identifies Nalco Nagar Anugola and Damanjodi. This is a wage-cost share, not an employee share or household-income change. [Annual report, pp.14,59,93](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

## Existing mines and expansion have different timelines

The report identifies Panchpatmali’s Central/North and South blocks separately, with company-reported lease validity to 16 November 2032 and 19 July 2029. Original current permits still need checking.

For **Pottangi**, NALCO reports an MDO appointment on 9 December 2025 and expects production in Q4 FY2026–27, or January–March 2027. Dilip Buildcon names itself as MDO and DBL Pottangi Bauxite Mines Private Limited as the agreement SPV. Its undated project page retains a mid-2026 target. Neither target proves production has started. [Annual report, pp.12–14](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf); [developer record](https://dilipbuildcon.com/project/pottangi-bauxite-mine/).

## Community outcomes remain a separate question

Pottangi’s reported conveyor and water-facility components list 415 and 48 affected families separately, with the rehabilitation package awaiting finalisation in that report. Do not add the counts without checking overlap. The report also describes honey and ginger-processing livelihood projects; beneficiary descriptions establish reported programme reach, not increased income.

Safety remains part of the story: the company reports zero worker fatalities in 2025–26 after two at its smelter in 2024–25, and one recordable worker incident each at the smelter and captive power plant in 2025–26. These are own-operation disclosures; the report’s external value-chain partner totals use a different boundary. [Annual report, pp.74,93,97,102](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

[Detailed evidence and open fields](../references/data/mining-programme.json) · [Mining overview](mining.md) · [Industrial production](../statistics/industrial-production.md) · [Koraput](../statistics/districts/koraput.md) · [Angul](../statistics/districts/angul.md) · [Honey and forest livelihoods](forest-products.md).

[Mining overview](mining.md) — Connects named mineral-processing relationships to separate public revenue, work and community questions.

## Local suppliers: a new reading of the saved report

NALCO reports **₹652.19 crore** of goods/services purchases from Odisha-based MSEs in 2025–26, within₹1,447.94 crore of all-location MSE procurement. This is about45.04% of that MSE total, not a share of all company purchasing. Purchases do not measure supplier profit or employment. [Saved annual report, printed p.56 / PDF p.76, section 19(a)](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

This extends the inspected scope of the same original report; it is not independent corroboration. [A readable supplier story](../stories/minerals-and-local-suppliers.md).

## Apprenticeship is another route into industrial skills

NALCO reports **925 apprentice trainees engaged during 2025–26**, up to 31 March 2026. This is a company-wide annual engagement figure, not the number appointed to permanent jobs, a placement result, or an Odisha-only count. The report does not allocate it between Damanjodi, Angul and other locations. [Same saved annual report, printed p.49 / PDF p.69, section9.2](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

This reading extends the existing source; it does not add independent corroboration. The report’s 9,284 employee-training figure also must not replace the 4,864 on-roll workforce: annual training participation and payroll headcount measure different things. Current unit-level payroll and contractor counts remain open.

## Work volume gives a plant view, not a headcount

NALCO’s FY2024–25 injury-statistics table reports these working-day volumes:

| Unit | Employee man-days | Contractor labour man-days |
|---|---:|---:|
| Alumina refinery, Damanjodi | 376,561 | 1,854,408 |
| Aluminium smelter, Angul | 489,800 | 1,308,875 |

Employee rows include executives and non-executives. Do not divide by an assumed working year to invent a count of people. [Report, printed p.79](../sources/mining-nalco-sd2025.md).

The existing **16,722** company-wide non-permanent-worker observation is reused. The annual report’s BRSR calls its table year-end details, while printed p.49 describes the same number as contractor workers engaged during March 2026. Neither passage supplies a plant split or unique-person method. Current unit payroll and local-resident shares remain missing.

body:
# Indian Metals and Ferro Alloys (IMFA)

IMFA dates its establishment to **1961** and places its beginnings at Therubali, described using historical Koraput geography. Its history credits [Bansidhar Panda](../people/bansidhar-panda.md) alongside Ila Panda; it lists [Subhrakant Panda](../people/subhrakant-panda.md) as managing director. Establishment, plant commissioning, production and installed capacity remain distinct measures.

[Entrepreneur collection](../people/entrepreneurs-and-business-leaders.md).

## From captive ore to ferrochrome · FY2025–26

IMFA identifies captive chromite mines at Sukinda and Mahagiri supplying its smelting operations. Its annual report describes three manufacturing facilities in Odisha, including the acquired Kalinganagar unit alongside Therubali and Choudwar. The company states that its extracted chrome ore is used captively. This establishes a company supply chain, not a mine-to-furnace shipment allocation. [Report pp.4,14–15,40,51](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/IMFAAnnualReportFY2526.pdf/IMFA_Annual_Report_FY_2526_10bbee90f9.pdf).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 M[Sukinda and Mahagiri chromite mines] -->|Company captive supply; allocation unknown| F[IMFA Odisha ferrochrome facilities]
 F --> D[Domestic industrial customers]
 F --> E[International industrial customers]
```

| Measure | FY2024–25 | FY2025–26 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Ferrochrome produced, tonnes | 260,190 | 267,301 |
| Domestic sales, tonnes | 34,066 | 48,769 |
| International sales, tonnes | 225,801 | 221,355 |
| Sukinda ore, tonnes | 285,851 | 273,802 — held for reconciliation |
| Mahagiri ore, tonnes | 416,012 | 536,810 |

Production rose 2.73%; domestic sales rose 43.16%, while international sales fell 1.97%. The earlier Sukinda growth comparison is now held because a mine submission gives a different FY2025–26 value. Mahagiri’s annual-report series rose 29.04%; the later template distinguishes a lower ROM field without explaining the scope. Ore, alloy and sales are different stages and cannot be summed. The acquired plant changes the company perimeter, so output growth is not a like-for-like measure. [Table, p.40 / PDF22](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/IMFAAnnualReportFY2526.pdf/IMFA_Annual_Report_FY_2526_10bbee90f9.pdf).

### Acquisition and expansion have different dates

The MD reports completion of the acquired 100,000-tpa Kalinganagar unit transaction in February 2026 and production starting within two weeks. The separate greenfield unit and further furnace construction were still forward-looking in this report. The current-capacity and post-expansion figures belong to different stages; a July publication cannot establish October commissioning. No new investment total is added to the existing tracker. [pp.4,14–15](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/IMFAAnnualReportFY2526.pdf/IMFA_Annual_Report_FY_2526_10bbee90f9.pdf).

### People and suppliers: retain the boundary

At 31 March 2026 the standalone BRSR lists 860 permanent employees, 1,327 permanent workers and 5,206 other-than-permanent workers. These are national entity categories, not plant-level Odisha jobs or jobs created during the year. Direct sourcing from MSMEs/small producers represented 15.32% of total input value, up from 7.40%; suppliers within India represented 72.29%, up from 67.29%. The overlapping categories do not disclose an Odisha supplier share. [pp.57–59,97](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/IMFAAnnualReportFY2526.pdf/IMFA_Annual_Report_FY_2526_10bbee90f9.pdf).

Plant-specific output, payroll, contractor definitions, named local suppliers and mine despatch allocations remain open. [Trade story](../stories/odisha-ferrochrome-markets.md) · [Mining context](mining.md).

## What the plant and mine records add · 2 October 2026

The ministry’s **4 September 2026 clearance-transfer letter** identifies the acquired Kalinganagar facility as four implemented 16.5-MVA furnaces. Its annexure lists the proposed 33-MVA furnace and 67.5-MW captive power plant as **not implemented**. The transfer covers the implemented furnaces only. This concerns KNR2, not the separate KNR1 greenfield project; it does not establish October operating status. [Letter pp.2–4](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/IA_OR_IND1_04092026.pdf/IA_OR_IND_1_04092026_a1432f31b5.pdf).

Choudwar’s Unit-II statement provides furnace-specific input ratios rather than annual production: chrome ore per tonne of HCFC rose from 2.200 to 2.36634 at CCP-2 and from 2.263 to 2.4052 at CCP-3 between FY2024–25 and FY2025–26. Ore grade and operating conditions are not controlled here, so these ratios alone cannot explain efficiency or emissions. [Statement p.3](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/EnvironmentalStatementUnitII202526.pdf/Environmental_Statement_Unit_II_202526_4e5b4b9277.pdf).

Mine manpower tables are captured but held for clarification. The template defines local as from the State; it does not split direct and contract employment. Mahagiri’s local categories total 495 against a stated local total of 477. Sukinda’s category denominators total 799 against an overall 1,170. These are company submissions, not independently verified employment counts or awarded star ratings. [Sukinda p.31](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/SukindaMinesStarRating202526.pdf/Sukinda_Mines_Star_Rating202526_907f7142d9.pdf) · [Mahagiri p.28](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/MahagiriMinesStarRating202526.pdf/Mahagiri_Mines_Star_Rating202526_e5c85f9972.pdf).

Sukinda’s submitted ROM is 269,075 tonnes against 273,802 in the annual report. Both are retained, and the earlier growth calculation is quarantined. Mahagiri’s general field rounds to the annual-report value but differs from its underground ROM field. [Detailed captures and holds](../references/data/mining-programme.json).

Integration review: the annual report’s combined ore figure is also held for reconciliation because it includes the disputed Sukinda component. The reported value remains preserved; no revised total is inferred by mixing the annual report with the mine templates.

Odisha State Finances Audit Report 2024–25 — Chapter 1
Odisha Directorate of Mines and Geology: mineral revenue collected

body:
# From mineral revenues to working community services

A mine can generate revenue, a fund can pay a contractor, and a village can still be waiting for a working service. This research follows the steps between those events. It is a draft evidence account, with dated findings and government replies, not a present-day verdict on a district.

## Follow each rupee without skipping a stage

State mining receipts and DMF contributions are separate financial routes. Within the DMF route, follow sanctioned projects, released funds, expenditure, completed assets, operating services and community outcomes as distinct stages. OMC dividends, mine-level payment returns and DMF interest also need separate labels.

## Actual receipts and estimates

The original CAG State Finances Audit Report 2024–25, Table 1.7 (printed p. 15), gives these rounded figures in ₹ crore:

| Accounting head |2023–24 actual|2024–25 budget estimate|2024–25 revised estimate|2024–25 actual|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries|45,046|48,600|46,600|41,052|
|Coal and lignite|1,351|832|2,560|1,015|

The sum of these two actual-receipt heads is 46,397 in 2023–24 and 42,067 in 2024–25. These are our sums of rounded source rows, not newly reported statewide totals. The Directorate’s 2023–24 mining collection series reports 46,396.27. The original comparison differs by 0.73 crore. A higher-precision Finance Accounts check below separates the rounding effect from a remaining 0.20 crore difference; the accounting-head bridge is still unverified. Dividends are excluded. Do not interpret the government’s non-ferrous accounting label as a list of non-ferrous commodities only.

The original [Finance Accounts 2023–24, Volume I](../sources/mining-fa2023-24-vol1.md), Statement 3 (printed p. 10 / PDF p. 28), reports **45,045.55** for non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries and **1,350.52** for coal/lignite. Their sum is **46,396.07 crore**. Each head rounds to the SFAR figure above. Summing the whole-crore heads adds 0.93 crore relative to this two-decimal sum; the Directorate's 46,396.27 is 0.20 crore above it. That residual requires an accounting reconciliation or scope explanation. It is not evidence of missing funds. Preserve each source edition rather than replacing the rounded historical observations.

The legacy [F05](../evidence/f05.md) figure of 53,000 crore is a 2026–27 **budget estimate**. It remains intact and cannot establish actual collections or a realised increase over 2024–25.

## Six district funds, one explicit audit period

CAG Report 7 of 2026 covers 2015–16 to 2023–24, with later field checks and January 2026 replies. Table 5.1 reports collections **including interest** in this six-DMF sample; do not compare them directly with the existing all 30 DMF leaseholder-contribution total. Amounts below reproduce Table 5.1 in cumulative ₹ crore. **The Dhenkanal/Jajpur expenditure and sample release/expenditure figures conflict with Table 4.1; retain them as source-specific values pending clarification.**

|DMF|Collection incl. interest|Sanctioned|Released|Utilised|Completed / sanctioned projects|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Dhenkanal|100.28|61.62|56.39|44.14|350 / 623|
|Jajpur|2,395.21|2,848.77|1,514.89|1,164.42|2,994 / 6,414|
|Keonjhar|12,227.12|9,733.37|5,701.34|4,410.10|1,023 / 3,269|
|Mayurbhanj|125.22|109.17|98.64|85.99|208 / 652|
|Nabarangpur|2.47|1.17|1.17|1.17|7 / 7|
|Sundargarh|7,717.87|8,193.42|5,788.32|4,386.71|5,108 / 6,470|

In Table 5.1, collections including interest for these six DMFs were 22,568.17 crore, sanctions 20,947.52 crore, releases 13,160.75 crore and expenditure 10,092.53 crore. Interest included in collections was 1,772.66 crore. These stages must not be summed.

Using Table 5.1 amounts, expenditure is 48.18% of sanctions and 76.69% of releases. These ratios inherit the unresolved cross-table conflict below. The original §5.1 prose says 79.69%, while Table 5.1 says 76.69%; the raw amounts support the latter. This discrepancy is preserved in the structured record. Table 5.2 also carries a rupee heading over project-count columns: use the column labels and accompanying narrative, not that heading, for units.

The sample reports 9,690 completed projects from 17,435 sanctioned (55.58%); 6,551 were ongoing and 1,194 not started/dropped. Completion says nothing by itself about staffing, utilities, sustained use or residents’ welfare. These six districts were audit-selected; neither their spending ratio nor these selected failures estimates all Odisha DMFs.

## The report contains conflicting totals

Original Table 4.1 (printed p. 24 / PDF p. 58), inspected visually, gives different amounts for the same district funds and audit period. We have not established a reason for the differences.

|Measure, ₹ crore|Table 4.1|Table 5.1|
|---|---:|---:|
|Six-DMF funds released|13,160.84|13,160.75|
|Six-DMF funds utilised|10,104.28|10,092.53|
|Dhenkanal released|56.48|56.39|
|Dhenkanal utilised|55.89|44.14|
|Jajpur utilised|1,164.43|1,164.42|

Dhenkanal accounts for the ₹11.75 crore difference between printed expenditure totals. Table 4.1's district expenditure rows sum to ₹10,104.29 crore, ₹0.01 crore above its printed total; rounding or a source error is possible but unconfirmed. Table 5.4 repeats Table 5.1 amounts within the same report and is not independent corroboration. Six affected observations retain their original values and now carry a publication hold; this includes the ratio derived from the disputed expenditure. These differences do not themselves establish missing money.

## A second district series needs its own definitions

The original [Lok Sabha answer of 11 December 2024](../sources/mining-dmf-ls2607-2024.md) supplies annual district collection, **allocation** and expenditure, plus a March 2024 balance table. It does not explain interest coverage or reconcile its figures to CAG. Allocation must not be renamed release, and a balance must not be reconstructed from unrelated totals.

|District expenditure, ₹ crore|FY2021–22|FY2022–23|FY2023–24|Three-year sum|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Dhenkanal|10.28|4.81|6.10|21.19|
|Sundargarh (source: Sundergarh)|1,449.14|1,989.52|1,052.56|4,491.22|

Dhenkanal's three-year subtotal lacks the earlier years needed to assess either cumulative CAG figure. Sundargarh's subtotal already exceeds CAG's longer FY2015–16 to FY2023–24 figure of 4,386.71 by 104.51 crore. That is a warning against combining unreconciled definitions or vintages, not a finding of cash loss. The original answer's FY2024–25 column ends in October 2024 and must not be compared as a full year. Six selected district extracts and their source labels are retained in the structured programme, separately from the CAG sample.

A bounded official-domain search recovered no matching corrigendum for the CAG table conflict; this does not prove that none exists. The six existing conflict holds remain.

## How the audit selected its sample

Section 1.5 describes risk-stratified random district selection using collections, expenditure and tribal population, with Mayurbhanj additionally selected following media reports of fraud. Block selection combines the highest project counts with random selection; Gram Panchayats were randomly selected. This corrects the earlier structured checkpoint's blanket description as “purposively selected.” The four problem-case bundles below still cannot estimate the prevalence of failure across all projects.

## Four cases: completion, use and the reply

Each case below can include more than one facility. Combined costs must not be repeated as per-facility costs. All four are audit-selected problem cases; they are not a balanced evaluation of the programme.

### Dedicated NICU/PICU at District Headquarters Hospital, Keonjhar

Equipment procured January–February 2022 and installed March 2022 according to CDM&PHO records cited by Audit. Equipment approved and paid during December 2021–June 2022: ₹2.18 crore.

Joint physical verification on 29 April 2025 found units not operational and equipment unused; staff/doctors had not been deployed.

**Government reply:** January 2026: government said the assets strengthened crisis healthcare infrastructure. **Audit response:** CAG said the reply did not address non-use for the purchased purpose, continuing through January 2026.

**Next evidence:** Dated commissioning and duty-roster records, de-identified admission/service aggregates and independent patient/community accounts. Current operation in October 2026 is unverified. Locator: §6.6.3, printed p. 60 / PDF p. 98.

### Boys and girls hostels, Deogan village, Sukinda block

Completion certificate dated 16 July 2022 from R&B Division, Panikoili. Combined construction cost; do not assign the full amount to each hostel: ₹4.34 crore.

Not handed over to Education Department; joint verification 10 December 2024 found non-functional buildings, with water and electricity pending.

**Government reply:** January 2026: handover to BDO Sukinda would occur once critical utilities were in place. **Audit response:** CAG maintained the hostels had remained non-functional since completion.

**Next evidence:** Utility connections, handover/occupation certificates, staffing and anonymised occupancy by term. Current operation in October 2026 is unverified. Locator: §6.6.6, printed p. 62 / PDF p. 100.

### Digital medical records in DHH Sundargarh, SDH Bonai and Government Hospital Rourkela

Installed September 2019 at Bonai and November 2019 at the other two hospitals. Combined payment for system/equipment at three hospitals; sanction 1.52 crore and release 1.33 crore are separate stages: ₹1.32 crore.

Initially operated; audit records end dates 25 February 2020 at Sundargarh/Rourkela and 28 December 2020 at Bonai. Verification 4 March 2025 at Sundargarh found non-functioning system and 24 of 40 tablets stored unused.

**Government reply:** January 2026: acknowledged non-functioning since March 2020 and unsuccessful vendor engagement on compatibility with OeHMIS. **Audit response:** CAG attributed the failure to unresolved compatibility and ineffective use of warranty support; ₹1.32 crore termed infructuous. The general government reply date does not erase the hospital-specific dates.

**Next evidence:** System migration/asset redeployment records and dated evidence of records successfully used in care; do not infer all healthcare at these hospitals stopped. Current operation in October 2026 is unverified. Locator: §6.6.4, printed pp. 60–61 / PDF pp. 98–99.

### Wholesale market complex and Mission Shakti Café, Vyasanagar/Jajpur Road

Sanctioned in 2021–22/2022–23; audit describes completion and handovers in February/November 2023. Combined completed cost of two facilities; not separate per-facility amounts: ₹6.39 crore.

Joint verification November 2024 found intended beneficiary allotments absent and facilities not in use.

**Government reply:** January 2026: construction completed and facility handed to KNDA on 25 November 2023 for operation/management. **Audit response:** CAG retained its finding of defunct facilities; the handover reply does not establish operation.

**Next evidence:** Allotment and opening records, dated activity, tenant/SHG revenue and beneficiary testimony, with costs split by facility. Current operation in October 2026 is unverified. Locator: §6.6.9, printed p. 66 / PDF p. 104.

## Follow-up search: what remains unverified

A bounded public-record search on 2 October 2026 did not recover a later, facility-matched operating record for any of the four bundles. This means current status is unknown; it does not mean the facilities are still closed.

|Case|What the follow-up established|Evidence still needed|
|---|---|---|
|Keonjhar NICU/PICU|An official medical-college bed-listing lead appeared in search, but its page could not be retrieved and the units were not matched to the DMF equipment. Bed counts alone would not establish care delivered.|Commissioning, staff deployment and de-identified service counts tied to those units.|
|Deogan hostels|No matched later utility, handover or occupancy record recovered. Same-named villages and older hostel stories cannot safely be substituted.|Utility connections, handover and anonymised term occupancy for the Sukinda buildings.|
|Sundargarh digital records|An old annual-report lead and a general PMU tender do not establish restoration or migration of the three-hospital system.|Dated migration/redeployment record and evidence of routine use in care.|
|Vyasanagar market/café|The original [27 March 2023 Parliament reply](../sources/mining-npcc-rs2970-2023.md) lists **scheduled** completion of the market on 27 April 2023 and café on 25 November 2023. These are not opening dates.|Facility identifiers, allotments, trading activity and beneficiary evidence after the audit.|

The parliamentary list supports a candidate match by name, locality and client; a shared project identifier remains unverified. The café's scheduled date happens to match the later government handover date, but those are different claims. The market's schedule must not overwrite the audit's earlier handover account. Direct district-portal retrievals also failed; search snippets and recent crawl dates were not promoted to current facts. The structured follow-up preserves these retrieval limits.

### Next records, rather than another identical search

Further attempts to retrieve the Jajpur 2023–24 accounts, its 2022–23 annual report and the Keonjhar infrastructure page failed. A general hospital-service description and an old OeHMIS navigation link do not verify the audited equipment or digital system. None of the four case bundles has newly established current operation or beneficiary outcomes.

The structured programme now has six **unsent** record questions: the receipt-head reconciliation; the conflicting DMF tables and Parliament accounting basis; and one request for each facility bundle. They identify the relevant record holders and the exact documents needed—asset/project identifiers, actual commissioning/handover dates, staff and utilities, and de-identified service or occupancy counts. No outreach or application has been sent. Revisit a case when one of these records, a dated operating update or a restored source endpoint becomes available; repeated search failure is not new evidence of closure.

## An operating asset can still raise a different question

In §6.5.1 (printed p. 46 / PDF p. 84), CAG records Birsa Munda International Hockey Stadium as functional during January 2025 verification, while separately questioning DMF funding eligibility and benefit to mining-affected residents. Government's January 2026 reply cited larger public interest and Sports and Youth Services permission; CAG said that department could not authorize this use of DMF funds.

This is useful context, not a control group: **operation, funding eligibility, beneficiary access and community impact are separate questions.** A service can operate while its funding is disputed; a completed building can have eligible funding while still awaiting staff or utilities.

## What would establish benefit?

A completed hostel needs functioning water/electricity, staff and evidence of occupation. An ICU needs staff and evidence of care delivered. A market needs occupied stalls and trading activity. A digital system needs evidence of use in care. These are proposed verification fields, not findings that the evidence already supplies.

For each case retain: stable identity and geography; funding source; sanction/release/expenditure dates; completion and handover records; operation dates; maintenance/staffing; de-identified service counts; intended and actual beneficiary scope; and attributed community accounts. An outcome claim needs an appropriate baseline/comparison and cannot be inferred solely from use. Never collect identifiable patient or student records for this research.

Chapter VII records weak public disclosure and absent asset registers in the audited sample. January 2026 replies describe training and progressive asset-register compilation; these are reported responses, not independently verified remediation. The cumulative reading now covers §1.5 and Chapters III–VIII (collection, planning, fund management, implementation, monitoring, conclusions and recommendations). Appendices have not been exhaustively reviewed; this is source reading, not an independent re-audit.

## Sources and connected knowledge

- [CAG DMF audit](../sources/mining-cag-dmf2026.md): §1.5 and Chapters III–VIII; Tables 4.1 and 5.1–5.2 retain their discrepancies.
- [Parliament construction schedule](../sources/mining-npcc-rs2970-2023.md): Annexure IV, rows 193/213; planned dates only.
- [CAG State Finances](../sources/macro-cag-fy2025.md): original PDF Table 1.7.
- [Directorate revenue table](../sources/mining-directorate-revenue.md): collection-series scope.
- [Finance Accounts 2023–24](../sources/mining-fa2023-24-vol1.md): higher-precision receipt heads.
- [Lok Sabha DMF reply](../sources/mining-dmf-ls2607-2024.md): annual district figures and dated balances.
- [Mining research](mining.md) · [Minerals and mining statistics](../statistics/minerals-and-mining.md) · [Public finance audit](../statistics/public-finance-audit.md).
- [Structured cases, amounts and follow-ups](../references/data/mining-programme.json) · [Observation atlas](../references/data/statistics-atlas.json).

Research checkpoint only. No independent human review, local testimony, full accounting reconciliation or website story publication is claimed.

body:
# Forest products: household use, markets and livelihoods

**The central question is how forest knowledge and produce support everyday life and paid work.** Keep foods connected to the wider non-timber forest-products economy without calling every product food.

| Research group | What to document |
| --- | --- |
| Fruits, kernels, flowers and honey | Identity, use, season, preservation, supply origin and food-processing evidence |
| Leaves and leaf products | Sal-leaf collection, plate-making, labour, local buyers and processing; examine other leaf identities separately |
| Oilseeds, gums, resins and lac | Product and grade, actual end uses, processing yields and prices |
| Bamboo, cane, fibres and brooms | Material, maker, end product and commercial channel |
| Kendu leaves | A non-food commodity used as bidi wrappers; separate leaf trade from any fruit entry |

These groups define research coverage. Inclusion does not establish present procurement, sustainable supply, exports or proven medicinal effects. The TDCCOL product page is currently a partially captured discovery lead, not a verified current buying list.

## Follow value through each transaction

A proposed reporting chain is **collection → household use or local sale → aggregation → processing → retail or export**. Verify actual buyers before claiming a product follows that chain. Record procurement separately from sales, and collector receipts separately from turnover and net earnings. Prices require date, place, grade, moisture and unit. Published support prices do not prove procurement at that price.

[The first market checkpoint](../statistics/forest-products.md) saves a kendu series and one honey-processing capacity observation. It is not an estimate of Odisha's entire forest-food market. [Forest foods](../food/forest-foods.md) retains household and culinary context; [history](../history/forest-livelihoods.md) provides dated evidence rather than invented ancient origins.

## Next evidence to obtain

Product-level TDCCOL/Van Dhan procurement and realised sales; collector payments and costs; women-led groups and named community enterprises; seasonal haat prices; storage loss and processing yields; state-origin export quantities. Export promotion, an online listing or an overseas buyer mention alone does not establish measured shipments. For land, collection rights and ecological effects, use current primary decisions and location-specific studies.

[Structured research register](../references/data/forest-products.json).

[Related reading](../food/forest-foods.md) — Connects commodity research to household uses and ingredient identities; forest origin requires its own evidence.

[Related reading](../history/forest-livelihoods.md) — Adds dated institutional and community-study context without dating the origin of traditions.

[Related reading](../statistics/forests.md) — Provides land-cover context; forest area does not estimate product yields or household income.

[Related reading](../economy/mining.md) — Connects research on land and livelihoods; no causal effect of a named mine is asserted.

## Named products · 1 October 2026

Start with [kendu patra](kendu-patra.md), [Mohu/honey](../food/mohu-honey.md) and [mahua/mohula](../food/mahua-mohula.md). The structured register now separates flowers, seeds and leaf products rather than treating one tree as one market commodity.

Vasundhara's own livelihood account names sal leaves, siali leaves, sal seeds, char seeds, mahua and honey among products sold through the collectives it supports. It describes women-member producer groups and business unions. The page is undated; we use it to identify products and research routes, not a current count of enterprises or an independent income-impact claim. [Organisation account](https://vasundharaodisha.org/Welcome/page/Livelihood).

Tamarind, harida, bahada, karanja seed, kusum seed, lac and hill brooms are additional leads from the previously saved, indexed TDCCOL list. Each needs direct product-level verification; inclusion is not evidence of current buying, a market size or exports. Bamboo, cane, gums and other materials remain in the broader research groups.


[Related reading](../economy/kendu-patra.md) — Connects the leaf commodity to the saved market series; leaf sales do not describe edible fruit.

[Related reading](../food/mohu-honey.md) — Connects honey processing and collector questions while preserving forest-collected versus managed-hive origin.

[Related reading](../food/mahua-mohula.md) — Connects separate flower and seed uses with botanical identity and attributed cultural research.

[Siali: leaves and fibre](siali-products.md) — separates a climber’s identity and community-attributed fibre uses from sal and mahua. Its named product records inherit no statewide market totals.

[Mahua preparation and processing](../food/mahua-mohula.md) now connects local historical food practice, qualitative market constraints and a university-developed processing unit. A plant design or batch rating does not establish enterprise sales or collector earnings.

## Leaves are a material economy too

[Sal](sal-products.md) and [siali](siali-products.md) now distinguish tree and climber, leaf and seed/fibre, maker processes and local seasonal accounts. Collection, stitching, pressing and selling need separate measures. Current market totals and exports remain open; the historical craft evidence does not fill those gaps.

## Fruit and kernel value chains

[Tentuli](../food/tentuli-tamarind.md) distinguishes pulp, seeds and sale grades. [Chara/chironji](../food/chara-chironji.md) distinguishes fruit, hard nut and kernel. Historical community-market accounts are saved; processing yields, current prices, realised procurement and exports remain open.

## From sale proceeds to worker support

[The payment evidence](../statistics/forest-products.md) adds dated kendu welfare statements and a separately labelled compassionate-grant table. These belong to the non-food forest economy. TDCCOL product procurement and actual collector payments still need accessible original statements; tenders, targets and indexed tables are not realised purchases.

## Mine-to-processing checkpoint · 1 October 2026

[Mining and livelihood links](bauxite-to-aluminium.md) preserves NALCO’s reported honey/ginger project descriptions. Beneficiary counts do not measure collector earnings or market sales.

## Named enterprise leads and reported sales · 2 October 2026 UTC

[The Van Dhan story](../stories/van-dhan-enterprises.md) now has a dated parliamentary sales comparison. To connect it to people and products, the [ministry's 2021 account](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1715921) supplies these leads:

| Named cluster or group | Place stated | Activity described in the historical plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Luguburu, Maa Dharithri and Bhimakund | Mayurbhanj | Collectively: sal-leaf plates/cups, kusum oil and processed wild honey |
| Anchalika Khandadhar | Keonjhar | Mango preparations, turmeric powder and mustard oil |
| Ban Durga | Not specified in the cited paragraph | Tamarind processing, sal shampoo and packed char seeds |

Do not distribute the collective product list to each Mayurbhanj cluster. Current operation, women ownership, product sales and collector payments are unknown. These five named leads are a research list, not a census. Programme aggregate sales cannot be assigned to them.

The next evidence sought is a dated procurement ledger, completed-sale statement and actual collector-payment record for the same product, grade and period. Recent departmental PDFs and TDCC pages failed retrieval; index snippets and auction notices remain leads. Retry on 8 October, retaining the accessible historical evidence.

title: Odisha’s GDP story: scale, momentum and meaning
description: Odisha’s GDP story: scale, momentum and meaning — research and reuse notes.
body:
# Odisha’s GDP story: scale, momentum and meaning

The most useful economic narrative connects the size of the economy to visible sectors and places. Lead with a clear, dated number and then show what it represents.

## Opening evidence

The preserved survey records give **₹9.88 lakh crore nominal GSDP** and **7.9% real GSDP growth** for FY2025–26, both advance estimates. These are two different measures: [economic size](../evidence/e02.md) and [inflation-adjusted annual growth](../evidence/e01.md). They can sit side by side if labelled properly.

## Suggested message

“Odisha’s next chapter is taking shape.” Follow it with the economic-size number, its estimate label, and a sequence covering ports, production, food, services and people. Treat the phrase as campaign language rather than a statistical finding.

## A richer proof sequence

Use [construction’s five-year real growth](construction.md), [fisheries production](comparison-01-fisheries.md) and [Paradip cargo](comparison-05-port-logistics.md) as distinct stories. Their measures must stay separate: economic value added, physical output and port throughput. They cannot be added into a single “growth” total.

The [industry growth collection](index.md) retains complete six-year sector series so the campaign can use both the positive endpoint comparison and a truthful chart. A changing trajectory is more informative than an invented uninterrupted boom.

## Publication controls

Use a common vintage and price basis for any India comparison. The state survey’s national comparator and later national estimates are not automatically comparable: see [survey comparator](../evidence/e04.md) and [later national estimate](../evidence/e05.md). Do not call nominal expansion real growth. Do not turn per-capita income into a claim about every household. Announced investments and jobs remain announcements until completion is established.

The nominal ten-year tripling angle from earlier work needs its historical starting value added as an independently locatable record before it becomes a website headline.

## Fresh series expansion

The [economic-size and income atlas](../statistics/economic-size-and-income.md) records the current-price 2018–19 to 2025–26 series with revision/advance-estimate labels and explicit lakh-to-crore conversion. It supports the saved five-year nominal comparison, not a real-growth or ten-year claim.
