body:
# Agriculture

The saved Economic Survey summary reports rice production of 118.6 lakh metric tonnes and pulses production of 16.6 lakh metric tonnes in 2024–25. These provide a starting point for the farming story; named food varieties, farm incomes and local diets require their own evidence.[^nature-survey-summary]

## What these measures explain

What is grown, how much is produced and what is procured? Cultivated area, output, procurement and procurement targets belong to different stages of the farm economy.

## Selected facts to explore

- **Ragi procurement: 4.5 lakh quintals** — KMS 2023-24, Odisha.[^nature-agri]
- **FPO procurement agencies empanelled: 130 FPOs** — 2024-25, Odisha.[^nature-agri]
- **Ragi procurement target stated during year: 8 lakh quintals** — KMS 2024-25 target in activity report, Odisha.[^nature-agri]

## Read this in context

Subject: [Food and farming](../subjects/food.md). Also part of [Economy, livelihoods and infrastructure](../subjects/economy.md), [Nature and environment](../subjects/nature.md).

- [Koraput Kalajeera Rice](../food/koraput-kalajeera-rice.md) — Explore a named rice tradition; statewide production is not that variety’s output.
- [Water Irrigation](water-irrigation.md) — Read irrigation scope before explaining production change.

These are editorial reading connections, not assertions of causation, proximity or a verified supply chain.

## Evidence view

| Measure | Value and unit | Period / geography | Evidence and readiness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ragi procurement | 4.5 lakh quintals | KMS 2023-24; Odisha | indexed-primary-extract; needs_source_table_review[^nature-agri] |
| FPO procurement agencies empanelled | 130 FPOs | 2024-25; Odisha | indexed-primary-extract; needs_source_table_review[^nature-agri] |
| Ragi procurement target stated during year | 8 lakh quintals | KMS 2024-25 target in activity report; Odisha | announced-target-indexed-primary; needs_source_table_review[^nature-agri] |
| Rice production | 110 lakh metric tonnes | 2020-21; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Rice production | 118.6 lakh metric tonnes | 2024-25; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Pulses production | 10.4 lakh metric tonnes | 2020-21; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Pulses production | 16.6 lakh metric tonnes | 2024-25; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Vegetable production | 97.8 lakh metric tonnes | 2020-21; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Vegetable production | 111.02 lakh metric tonnes | 2024-25; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Millet cultivation area | 2.7 lakh hectares | 2024-25; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Reported increase in millet cultivation area | 62.7 percent | 2020-21 to 2024-25; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |
| Cropping intensity | 165 percent | 2024-25; Odisha | primary-source-reported; source_checked_editorial_review_pending[^nature-survey-summary] |

## Interpretation limits

- Earlier 2.99-lakh figure was an incomplete season snapshot.
- Empanelment does not establish each agency procurement volume.
- Historical target; later survey reports a different achieved value. Never present target as outcome.
- Rounded survey series; no causal programme-effect estimate established.
- Rounded prose value; summary chart gives 2.71 lakh hectares.
- Use reported percentage; do not recompute from rounded 2.7-lakh endpoint.
- Multiple cropping can make this exceed 100%; not share of land under crops.

The [structured atlas](../references/data/statistics-atlas.json) retains indicator IDs, exact source locators and definitions. [Coverage and gaps](coverage.md) · [Atlas home](index.md).


[^nature-agri]: [Activity Report 2024-25](https://agri.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-03/Activity%20Report%202024-25%20%28English%29.pdf)

[^nature-survey-summary]: [Odisha Economic Survey 2025-26: Highlights and Executive Summary](https://pc.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2026-02/ES-Highlights%20and%20Executive%20Summary%202026%20Web%20Upload.pdf)

## Science connections · 1 October 2026

[Science and documented contributions](../people/science-and-contributions.md) connects rice seed systems and public-health research with named contributors and credited teams. A contribution record, a patient sample and statewide economic or health outcomes have different scopes.

[Rice economics](../economy/rice-economy.md) adds a 2023–24 production baseline and KMS procurement/price evidence with rice and paddy kept separate. Exact observations are in the atlas; current variety-level prices and profit remain unknown.

[Rice’s comparable historical trend](../stories/rice-productivity.md) now retains consecutive annual observations and adverse years. [Rice economics](../economy/rice-economy.md) separates those crop measures from experimental returns and unresolved procurement payments.

## Regional cost evidence · 2 October 2026 UTC

[The paddy cost case](../stories/rice-income-after-costs.md) adds eight source-located observations. Survey/valuation year remains unspecified, so these do not enter time-series comparisons or statewide farmer-income totals. The source reports costs including family labour and land; source definition conflicts remain visible in the rice register.

## Procurement payment scope · 2 October 2026 UTC

The [rice payment story](../stories/rice-procurement-payments.md) adds the later department report with eleven scoped observations. Its 2023–24 MSP amount agrees with the saved volume at common MSP after rounding. The 2024–25 payment includes assistance; do not calculate like-for-like growth against MSP alone. Seasonal seller counts remain separate, and financial-year physical totals are not marketing-year revisions.

body:
# Odisha coal: growth with the full timeline

**Odisha produced 269.363 million tonnes of raw coal in 2024–25—25.71% of India’s total.** Output rose **88.3% over five years**, from 143.016 million tonnes in 2019–20. These Coal Directory figures cover the state, not just Mahanadi Coalfields.

The path was uneven: output fell **0.90% in 2019–20**, while national share slipped from **24.52% to 23.99% in 2023–24** even as output rose. [Ministry of Coal, Table 3.9, pp.59–60](https://coal.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-03/28-11-2025a-stc.pdf).

## Read the series

Ten annual observations run from 2015–16 to 2024–25; their endpoints span nine years. The five-year comparison uses 2019–20 as its base. Detailed observations and calculation inputs are retained in the [mining register](../references/data/mining-programme.json).

| Financial year | Raw coal, million tonnes | Share of India |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 2015–16 | 138.461 | 21.66% |
| 2016–17 | 139.359 | 21.18% |
| 2017–18 | 143.328 | 21.22% |
| 2018–19 | 144.312 | 19.80% |
| 2019–20 | 143.016 | 19.57% |
| 2020–21 | 154.151 | 21.53% |
| 2021–22 | 185.069 | 23.78% |
| 2022–23 | 218.981 | 24.52% |
| 2023–24 | 239.402 | 23.99% |
| 2024–25 | 269.363 | 25.71% |

## Resources, output and local value

The same directory records geological coal resources at **1 April 2025**, separately for Ib-River and Talcher and for proved, indicated and inferred classes. These are not automatically mineable reserves or annual output.

Six selected block records retain company labels and dated production. Dulanga was flat across the three recorded years; Jamkhani declined in the last year. Blank earlier cells remain unknown.

OCPL locates Manoharpur in Hemgir, Sundargarh. Its [rehabilitation page](https://ocpl.org.in/RandR.asp) includes October 2019 status tables and an objective to double displaced families’ incomes within five years. That objective is not evidence that incomes doubled. Its land figures also differ between narrative and table; reconciliation remains open.

[Mining: minerals, industry and people](../economy/mining.md) — Connects dated coal output to separate processing, fiscal, livelihood and environment questions.

## Ore reconciliation checkpoint · 1 October2026

The recovered state table confirms121.102 million tonnes for2014–15 and269.363 for2024–25. Several intervening years differ from CCO, including237.131 versus239.402 in2023–24. The CCO timeline above remains unchanged; do not splice the two. [Reconciliation](ore-production.md).

body:
# Statistical coverage, conflicts and next research

## Coverage means recorded evidence, not completeness

This edition combines state, district, institutional and national-comparator observations. It spans people, livelihoods, tourism, infrastructure, nature, finance and enterprise. The 30-district banking layer is complete for the selected table, but district health, education, jobs, agriculture and service quality still require expansion.

## Research gaps and source conflicts

- **economy:** SLBC June 2025 statewide CD ratio is 75.05 on printed page 1 but 75.16 in district-table total; retain district cells and do not derive a statewide change from the inconsistent total.
- **economy:** SLBC minority advance differs between headline and later section; excluded pending reconciliation.
- **economy:** District banking covers all 30 districts; other district indicators still require their own evidence.
- **economy:** DES catalogue includes private-sector Gross Fixed Capital Formation 2011–12 to 2015–16 provisional series; retrieve and inspect before claiming full statewide realised investment.
- **economy:** Current-price GDP series was read from official indexed table; full report exceeds browser PDF size limit.
- **economy:** CAG GSDP vintage differs from latest survey; preserve both rather than replacing frozen records.
- **people:** Reconcile NFHS-6 restatements with original NFHS-5 estimates before joining editions: vaccination 90.7 versus 90.5; menstrual hygiene and violence columns also differ. Maintain vintage/version fields.
- **people:** Do not use the absence of anaemia and mortality indicators in the NFHS-6 factsheet as proof that outcomes disappeared; consult specialised surveys and final technical reports.
- **people:** Add current SRS maternal/infant mortality with confidence intervals and multi-year reference windows; older positive endpoints are not sufficient for a current trend.
- **people:** Retrieve PLFS 2024 annual/calendar-year releases and survey-redesign documentation before replacing July–June annual series; later releases may use changed survey designs or periods.
- **people:** Add district-level NFHS-6 and UDISE outcomes, tribal/rural/urban inequality, learning results and skill-placement retention; statewide averages conceal substantial variation.
- **people:** Census counts remain 2011 historical baselines here; establish authoritative projection vintage and boundaries for any contemporary population denominator.
- **people:** Administrative water/internet availability is not a measured daily service-quality assessment. Tourism accessibility and public-service experience need their own evidence.
- **nature:** CDA ecology page literally reports 15 dolphins for 2025; this looks suspect and conflicts with expected survey scale. No dolphin population adopted. Next: Find signed 2025 and 2026 dolphin census releases and methodology; do not silently replace 15 with an assumed missing digit.
- **nature:** CDA avifauna paragraph says 62 orders and 20 families, apparently transposed; no order/family totals adopted. Seagrass narrative lists an extra species beyond its stated count. Next: Read original 2020 avifauna and botanical papers before detailed taxonomic use.
- **nature:** ISFR 2023 change is against revised raster 2021 assessment; naive subtraction from older printed 2021 value produces a different change. Next: Archive exact ISFR comparison definitions and district table before publishing historical chart.
- **nature:** Irrigation potential, revived ayacut and actual irrigation are different measures; project cross-programme overlap unresolved. Next: Build annual district potential/utilisation series and stable project IDs; do not sum programme areas.
- **nature:** ISFR, water and agriculture full PDFs were not successfully fetched; values are fresh indexed primary extracts. Next: Capture and inspect source table images before headline publication of these extract-only values.
- **nature:** Crop pairs span four annual intervals, not a full five-year growth interval. Fisheries longer series already in KB still needs primary appendix recheck. Next: Use explicit endpoints; extract complete annual crop/fisheries series from appendices.
- **nature:** Current wildlife counts, mangrove time series, district water quality, air quality and wetlands condition require their own methods and current releases. Next: Add Odisha Wildlife Census, ISFR mangrove table, CPCB/OSPCB and Ramsar condition records; do not infer cleanliness from forest cover.
- **connectivity:** State bulletin reports 53,392 foreign visits in 2024; central February 2026 Annexure II reports 87,854 for the same calendar year. Central 2025* row is 59,683, with asterisk to resolve in full PDF. Next: Obtain full 2025–26 state tourism annual report, bulletin revision history and Ministry footnotes; determine definition/revision/data-entry difference before choosing headline series.
- **connectivity:** Department index lists Odisha Tourism Annual Report 2025–26 (7 August 2026); direct PDF failed to open. Next: Retrieve latest report and complete 2025 calendar/2025–26 fiscal series, preserving separate periods. Index: https://dot.odisha.gov.in/en/publications/tourism-download
- **connectivity:** March 2025 Internet figures contain carried-forward operator data; March 2026 state Table 1.41 has now been extracted in the weekly update. Next: Reconcile operator reporting and denominator revisions before current-growth marketing; March 2026 levels are saved separately.
- **connectivity:** Two commissioned solar projects do not constitute a state capacity or generation total. Next: Reconcile CEA installed physical capacity, Odisha allocated/contracted capacity, GRIDCO procurement and generation before statewide energy claims.
- **connectivity:** No fresh statewide road-length or rail-route-length series established in this tranche. Rail release has ambiguous average-period phrasing. Next: Use MoRTH Basic Road Statistics and Railway statistical statements with route km vs track km, project scope, and completion dates.
- **connectivity:** 2019–20 census is historical; Odisha department At a Glance page appears to retain much older Five-Year Plan material. Next: Obtain recent handloom/handicraft annual reports, census definition reconciliation, district worker/loom counts and sales outcomes.
- **services:** PIB release 2238852 has displaced state rows: its Odisha row shows implausible small-state numbers, while Odisha-scale numbers appear under Puducherry. Next: Do not import that table. Use narrative in Parliament question 2625, which explicitly names Odisha and date; no silent row repairs.
- **services:** JJM connection coverage does not establish regularity, potability or amount supplied. Next: Retrieve Odisha-specific Functionality Assessment 2024 sampling results and WQMIS denominators.
- **services:** City annual PM10 observations currently stop at FY2023-24. Direct parliamentary PDF timed out; station completeness unavailable. Next: Get signed CPCB/OSPCB 2024-25 and 2025-26 annual series, station coverage and common-site comparisons. Do not use isolated daily AQI to claim cleanliness.
- **services:** Newest H&UD reports 2024-25 and 2025-26 are listed, but direct downloads failed. Historical 2023-24 inventory has no exact cutoff and cannot be presented as current. Next: Obtain newest PDF and municipal operating data; record actual throughput, generation, collection, processing and compliance separately.
- **services:** Fresh primary indexed survey section 7.4.8 lists Capital Region passengers 8.15 crore and Rourkela 1.47 crore, but retrieved table lacks period heading. Not imported as a dated observation. Next: Inspect Table 7.3 heading and CRUT annual report; retain passenger journeys versus unique people distinction, and current fleet versus annual stock.
- **services:** H&UD 2023-24 report prose includes a suspected helpline-number-as-count issue (14,420), inconsistent sanitation-worker infographic and an implausible metro completion sentence. None imported. Next: Resolve against original programme documents before using those statements.
- **enterprise:** Central DPIIT and state Startup Odisha registries measure different recognition populations; cumulative recognition is not active enterprises. Next: Capture current registry export and closed/dissolved status before live total or survival-rate claims; do not merge counts.
- **enterprise:** Ordinary patent filing rose from 350 to 1,656; institution and grant/commercialisation breakdown not extracted. Next: Identify applicants and grant outcomes; retain application label and avoid equating filing surge with realised innovations.
- **enterprise:** ASI 2023–24 notes factory-definition modifications including Odisha; raw selected-sample count is not state factory total. Next: Extract weighted registered/operating factory estimates and document coverage break before five-year comparisons.
- **enterprise:** Historic event scope established, current attendance, tourism spending, annual facility usage and public access not established. Next: Check final tournament match archive and venue annual reports; no economic impact inference.
- **enterprise:** NALCO company capex is not geographically allocated in headline source. Next: Reconcile segment/project disclosures and state location before using any amount in statewide investment totals.

## Next collection priorities

District Statistical Handbooks; full annual time series; current mortality and learning outcomes; pollution concentrations and station coverage; water and sanitation service quality; disability/accessibility; housing costs and affordability; migration; language/cultural participation; verified creator and craft incomes; sports participation; project-level realised investment. Add missing statistics as unknown, never zero.

[Atlas home](index.md).


## Weekly monitoring · 27 September 2026

Added 2025–26 fisheries production and seafood exports. Production components differ from the reported total by 0.01 lakh tonnes at displayed precision. The [NFHS release notice](../sources/weekly-nfhs-district-release.md) identifies district factsheets for the next retrieval pass; it does not verify Odisha district values. Browser failures on earlier PDFs remain recorded as unavailable in the run report, not evidence of unchanged values.

## Homestay evidence gaps

The [homestay collection](../statistics/homestays.md) distinguishes scheme targets, financial rules, registry stock, marketplace listings and event inventory. The 2025 Gazette conflicts on 1,800 rooms versus beds. Retrieve April/July amendments and the full Cycle-1 primary target table; confirm district/GP changes before map publication. Active properties, bookings, disbursements and net host income remain unestablished. The [monitoring register](../references/data/homestay-research.json) records missing measures and failed source fetches. No registered-property count is silently replaced by listings or app downloads.


## Regional and everyday-life coverage · 30 September 2026

The [connected collections](../collections/index.md) add regional context, making and everyday services. Four Census 2011 observations for Bargarh and Sambalpur were checked on district government pages. Koraput demographic pages timed out; no new population claim was imported. District literacy labels need denominator review. Comparable district health, education, job-quality and maker-income evidence remains incomplete. The progress cards retain unknown operating and outcome fields rather than turning targets or installed capacity into results.

## Recovery checkpoint · 30 September 2026

RES-003 completed its bounded-attempt deliverable, without recovering report contents. Exact Finance alternative and DES workbook links, retrieval failures and an 8 October retry are saved in the [recovery register](../references/data/source-recovery.json). RES-004 documented the remaining tourism conflict using an accessible December 2025 Ministry release; the [tourism page](tourism.md) preserves both values and keeps affected headlines on hold. Discovery-year labels are not dates for every table cell. No district or GDP values were added in this pass.

People-and-creations research added five observations for broad textile/apparel/handicraft exports (FY2020–21 to FY2024–25). Garment-type and sweet-specific exports remain unresolved; see [new topic](textile-and-apparel-exports.md).

[Mining: minerals, industry and people](../economy/mining.md) — twelve angles, existing-data reuse and five bounded follow-ups (RES-051–055).

[Forest foods, products and livelihoods](../economy/forest-products.md) — household uses, market evidence and dated history; RES-056–058 deepen existing records.

# Digital Connectivity

## What these measures explain

How is connectivity measured? Subscriptions, school internet facilities and people’s reported internet use have different denominators and should appear as complementary views.

## Later snapshot: March 2026

TRAI reports **30.56 million internet subscriptions** in Odisha at 31 March 2026: 18.74 million rural and 11.81 million urban. Reported densities are 64.79 per 100 people overall, 49.30 rural and 129.15 urban. These are subscriptions, not unique residents.[^weekly-trai-mar2026]

# District Banking

## What these measures explain

Where are deposits and advances recorded across Odisha’s districts? Banking location is a useful lens on finance, but it does not measure district wealth or district GDP.

All 30 districts have deposit and utilised-credit balances at June 2026, plus reported June 2025 and June 2026 credit-deposit ratios. This is one domain of district coverage, not complete district profiles. Banking location is not a measure of household wealth.

# Economic Size And Income

## What these measures explain

How large is the economy, and how does output per person change? Read nominal size, inflation-adjusted growth and per-capita averages separately; an average does not describe the distribution of income.

## Selected facts to explore

body:
# Ecotourism: income, visitors and community livelihoods

**Reported programme income rose about 26% to ₹19.12 crore in FY 2024–25**, from ₹15.17 crore in FY 2023–24. The Wildlife Organisation’s 2025 publication supplies the two full-year figures; this is a comparison of reported monetary income, without an established inflation adjustment. It does not measure household earnings.

Visitor footfall increased from 151,517 to 170,365, about 12.4%. The same table records fewer non-Indian visitors: 104 to 76, a fall of 26.9%. These categories describe recorded visitor activity; unique people, nights stayed and occupancy are not established.

## Where local communities fit

The report describes **more than 700 community members managing 53 ecotourism destinations** in its 2025 snapshot. It names work such as cooking, housekeeping, reception and guiding. This is programme participation, not 700 verified permanent jobs or a current 2026 headcount.

Its income-sharing mechanism assigns 35% to community wages/salary, 25% to recurring costs, 10% to infrastructure, 10% to village development through EDCs and 20% to a corpus for hospitality experts, promotion and major maintenance. These are allocation rules. Multiplying the income total by 35% would not prove that amount reached workers; no payroll or payment ledger was obtained.

## A longer view

Reported income increased from ₹6.58 crore in FY 2019–20 to ₹19.12 crore in FY 2024–25, about 190.5% over five years. The programme’s changing destination mix is not controlled here. Keep this as aggregate programme growth rather than growth at the same properties.

The latest row in this publication is **partial FY 2025–26, through 6 September 2025**: ₹5.16 crore and 45,028 recorded visitors. It cannot be compared with a full year to claim a decline or extrapolated into a final result.

<details>
<summary>Annual evidence: reported income and visitor footfall</summary>

| Financial year | Income, ₹crore | Indian | Non-Indian | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2016-17 | 1.5612 | 11,463 | 36 | 11,499 |
| 2017-18 | 3.4014 | 17,108 | 40 | 17,148 |
| 2018-19 | 5.5674 | 24,666 | 106 | 24,772 |
| 2019-20 | 6.5816 | 30,685 | 99 | 30,784 |
| 2020-21 | 8.3227 | 56,951 | 11 | 56,962 |
| 2021-22 | 10.5143 | 70,205 | 11 | 70,216 |
| 2022-23 | 13.7912 | 131,969 | 84 | 132,053 |
| 2023-24 | 15.1705 | 151,413 | 104 | 151,517 |
| 2024-25 | 19.1189 | 170,289 | 76 | 170,365 |
| 2025-26 through 6 Sep 2025 | 5.1553 | 45,005 | 23 | 45,028 |

</details>

Source: [Wildlife Odisha 2025, printed p. 135](https://s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/wildlife.odisha.gov.in/uploads/901bab61-9987-4131-b23e-2fdf2ee5c6db.pdf). Programme context is on printed p. 122; the colophon dates publication to 9 October 2025. Retrieved 1 October 2026. [Structured evidence and calculations](../references/data/ecotourism-livelihoods.json).

## Read this alongside

- [Debrigarh and Hirakud](../places/debrigarh-hirakud.md) — A site-level livelihood case needs its own worker and income evidence; statewide totals do not verify it.
- [Homestays](homestays.md) — Nature-camp programme outcomes and the state homestay scheme use different populations and stages.
- [Tourism](tourism.md) — State tourist-visit totals use a broader scope and cannot be added to this programme series.

These are editorial connections, not claims of causation or a common statistical denominator. Subject entrances: [Economy](../subjects/economy.md), [Nature](../subjects/nature.md) and [People](../subjects/people.md). Source checked; human editorial review remains pending.

## Debrigarh evidence extension · 1 October 2026

The [Debrigarh record](../places/debrigarh-hirakud.md) now links a historical JICA revenue baseline and an official account recognising women’s conservation work. Neither supplies a modern wage ledger. Recent ₹5.01/₹5.11 crore reporting needs a scope bridge before a site growth comparison.

body:
# Forest products: what the market numbers measure

**OFDC's kendu-leaf realised sales were ₹533.58 crore in FY2023–24**, down **6.39%** from ₹570 crore in FY2022–23. The 2025 forestry report's series is:

| Financial year | Realised sales, ₹crore |
| --- | ---: |
| 2019–20 | 399.09* |
| 2020–21 | 460.84 |
| 2021–22 | 591.77 |
| 2022–23 | 570.00 |
| 2023–24 | 533.58 |

Quantities sold include arrear stock. These nominal sales are neither collectors' net income nor the total forest-food market. **Kendu leaves are a non-food product.** Source: [Odisha Forestry Sector2025, printed p.159](https://odishaforest.in/admin/data/documents/publication_file_1151142053.pdf).

*The undated [OFDC webpage](https://www.odishafdc.com/kenduleaf.php) reports ₹399.14 crore and2.621 lakh quintals for2019–20, against ₹399.09 crore and2.625 lakh quintals in the2025 report. Both competing observations are held for reconciliation; no endpoint growth calculation uses them. The report's separate crop-year series is also not interchangeable with this fiscal-year table.

The same report describes **15 tonnes/year installed honey-processing capacity at Jashipur, Mayurbhanj** (printed p.161). This is capacity, not verified production, utilisation or wild-honey procurement.

[Canonical observations](../references/data/statistics-atlas.json) preserve these boundaries. [Market research](../economy/forest-products.md) explains what remains missing. No statewide forest-food market-size estimate is currently supported here.

## Food-processing research capability

OUAT reports a developed mahua candy/nectar unit rated10 kg per batch in its2020–21 report (printed p.23). [Source](https://ouat.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/annual_report_2020-21_3.pdf). This is a research-unit specification, not an operating-factory census, annual output or commercial success. The observation is saved separately from OFDC honey capacity.

## Worker welfare: preserve the payment year and scope

The 2025 report records **₹250.75 crore distributed during 2023 for crop year 2022**, to more than eight lakh beneficiaries. It separately records **₹108.60 crore of bonuses and incentives during 2024 for crop year 2023**, to about nine lakh beneficiaries. The descriptions cover different benefit scopes; do not calculate a like-for-like decline or average worker earnings from them. [Printed p.150](https://odishaforest.in/admin/data/documents/publication_file_1151142053.pdf).

The [live welfare portal](https://kenduleaves.odisha.gov.in/welfare-measures), updated 9 September 2026, now displays ₹250.39 crore for year 2022, ₹116.07 crore for 2023 and ₹100.69 crore for 2024. Its year basis is unspecified. The older search-indexed snapshot contains different values again. These are held as a scope/vintage conflict, not silently substituted into the older report.

## A separately labelled grant table

| Financial year | Reported grant records | Total amount, ₹crore |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 2023–24 | 587 | 11.235 |
| 2024–25 | 1,216 | 24.060 |
| 2025–26 | 1,235 | 24.635 |
| 2026–27, partial; cutoff unstated | 257 | 5.130 |

Source: [Compassionate Grant table](https://kenduleaves.odisha.gov.in/welfare-measures), read 1 October 2026. Amounts above convert the original rupees by dividing by 10,000,000. These death/permanent-disability welfare records must not be presented as distinct people, all worker benefits or household income. A higher grant total is not inherently a better wellbeing outcome. Partial 2026–27 must not be compared with complete years.

## An additional original vintage for the sales discrepancy

OFDC's 2020–21 annual report gives **262,581 quintals** in the FY2019–20 comparative sales column (printed p.17), equivalent to 2.62581 lakh quintals. The page was visually checked. This supports an additional precise historical observation but does not reconcile the existing 2.625/2.621 lakh totals or ₹399.09/₹399.14 crore sales values. Keep the original conflict open. [Annual report](https://www.odishafdc.com/annual_report/Annual_Report_2021.pdf).

## Van Dhan: a dated national comparison · 2 October 2026 UTC

The [11 December 2023 parliamentary reply](https://sansad.in/getFile/loksabhaquestions/annex/1714/AU1179.pdf?source=pqals) reports **₹10.7201 crore** in cumulative Odisha Van Dhan sales, **170 sanctioned centres** and **50,094 beneficiaries**. Odisha's reported sales are the highest of the annexure's 28 state/UT rows and about **26.1%** of its ₹41.0295 crore total. These are programme figures, including MFP and non-MFP activities; they are neither annual sales nor the whole forest economy. The exact common reporting cutoff is unstated.

The annexure was visually checked. A newer departmental report was located but could not be retrieved; its indexed figures have not been substituted. No growth calculation connects incompatible reporting snapshots. [Readable story](../stories/van-dhan-enterprises.md).

## Kendu accounts: where the sale proceeds are allocated

OFDC's FY2020–21 accounts report **₹460.8417021 crore** realised sales in Note26(b), covering receipts from 2016–2020 crops. The allocation reconciles exactly in original rupees:

| Accounting component | ₹crore, rounded | Payment status |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Working-fund advance to Forest Department | 270.03 | Released to department |
| Selling commission | 41.20 | Commission allocation |
| Additional financing commission | 3.20 | Commission allocation |
| Royalty/KLDF | 146.41 | Payable to department |
| Forest development tax | 0.00 | Payable category |

[Annual report, printed p.83 / PDF p.84](https://www.odishafdc.com/annual_report/Annual_Report_2021.pdf), visually checked. Exact values are retained in the structured register. A payable balance is not proof of cash payment; working funds are not a verified sum received by collectors. Do not add these components to welfare grants. The FY2019–20 conflict remains unresolved.

# Forests

ISFR 2023 reports 52,433.56 square kilometres of forest cover and 6,163.45 square kilometres of tree cover in Odisha. Their combined area is 58,597.01 square kilometres. Read the assessment date and mapping definitions alongside the totals.[^nature-forest-pib]

## What these measures explain

What land cover was measured in the assessment? Forest cover, tree cover and forest condition differ, and revised map baselines affect comparisons over time.

## Selected facts to explore

- **Forest cover: 52,433.56 square kilometres** — ISFR 2023 assessment, Odisha.[^nature-forest-pib]
- **Tree cover: 6,163.45 square kilometres** — ISFR 2023 assessment, Odisha.[^nature-forest-pib]

## Read this in context

- [Air Quality](air-quality.md) — Forest extent does not establish city air quality.

These are editorial reading connections, not assertions of causation, proximity or a verified supply chain.

## Interpretation limits

# Health

NFHS-6 records 82.7% of Odisha households with at least one usual member covered by health insurance or a financing scheme, compared with 47.9% in its NFHS-5 comparison column. The Odisha fieldwork was July–November 2024; this is not a 2026 coverage survey. It does not establish coverage of every household member.[^people-nfhs6]

## What these measures explain

How do households access financial protection and maternal and child services? Coverage and utilisation can be described without treating them as proof of care quality or protection from every expense.

## Selected facts to explore

- **Households with health insurance/financing coverage: 47.9 percent of households** — NFHS-5 (2019–21), as reproduced in NFHS-6 release, Odisha.[^people-nfhs6]
- **Households with health insurance/financing coverage: 82.7 percent of households** — NFHS-6 (2023–24); Odisha fieldwork 18 July–28 November 2024, Odisha.[^people-nfhs6]

body:
# Odisha’s homestay opportunity

Odisha is building a public support system for family-hosted stays. The strongest evidence today concerns the scheme, its funding envelope and planned expansion. A historical marketplace report also suggests more properties were being advertised, while actual demand, host income and operating-unit growth remain unmeasured in this collection.

## Three figures to understand

| Figure | Meaning | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **₹50 crore** | Multi-year budget earmark, FY2025–26 to FY2028–29; not expenditure | 2025 Gazette, clause 3.3[^homestay-scheme2025] |
| **450 new homestays** | Overall scheme target; not completed units | 2025 Gazette, section 6[^homestay-scheme2025] |
| **380 homestays** | Reported Cycle-1 target in May 2026; primary allocation PDF still needed | Departmental figures reported by TOI[^homestay-cycle1-may2026] |

The first-cycle report describes 61 Gram Panchayats across 19 districts and 19 clusters, including targets of 60 in Koraput and 50 in Kandhamal. These are selected examples, not a complete district allocation list. They must not be added to the statewide programme target.[^homestay-cycle1-may2026]

## Is popularity increasing?

A January 2025 newspaper report describes roughly 50 properties advertised as homestays in 2017 and over 350 by its publication date. It also counted 270 Airbnb listings, including apartments, villas and other property types. This is a sign of a broader marketed offering, with unclear de-duplication and consistent definitions; it is not a measured statewide booking-growth series.[^homestay-market-jan2025]

The same report describes approximately 100 properties with 250 rooms identified around Bhubaneswar for Pravasi Bharatiya Diwas. That event inventory is separate from permanent registered supply.[^homestay-market-jan2025]

A parliamentary reply of 11 August 2025 lists **14 Odisha rural homestays on NIDHI**, a voluntary national registry. That narrow count neither disproves the marketplace figures nor measures all homestays. The reply expressly says NIDHI does not record tourism or occupancy days.[^homestay-nidhi2025]

## What would demonstrate sustained growth?

Follow the same defined group through applications, approval, construction, commercial operation and annual compliance. Then measure rooms available, room-nights sold, occupancy and host earnings. Keep closures and cancellations. Our [monitoring record](../references/data/homestay-research.json) leaves unavailable outcomes unknown rather than zero.

A useful story now is **“Odisha is investing in family-hosted tourism.”** Claims of an occupancy boom, rising household incomes or a successful 450-property rollout need further evidence.

## Read this in context

Subject: [Economy, livelihoods and infrastructure](../subjects/economy.md). Also part of [Places](../subjects/places.md), [People](../subjects/people.md) and [Governance](../subjects/governance.md).

- [Government support and policy history](../economy/homestay-support.md) — Separate the scheme’s incentives and later amendments from outcomes.
- [Accommodation](accommodation.md) — Hotel inventories and homestay registers describe different accommodation categories.
- [Debrigarh and Hirakud](../places/debrigarh-hirakud.md) — Compare a local community-work case without treating nature camps as registered homestays.

## Evidence and unresolved points

The original scheme uses **1,800 rooms** in section 6(a) and **1,800 beds** in section 7.2(a). Both records are held as a conflict; neither becomes our capacity headline. Later amendment text and the full Cycle-1 allocation remain retrieval priorities. No current application window or property availability is established here.

| Rooms identified for PBD accommodation | 250 rooms | Before PBD January 2025; report 4 January; Bhubaneswar and surrounding area | event_inventory; Final paragraph quoting Tourism director[^homestay-market-jan2025] |

</details>

Definitions, evidence status and publication-readiness fields remain in the [statistical atlas](../references/data/statistics-atlas.json). Policy thresholds are not achieved results. No human editorial review is claimed.

[^homestay-scheme2025]: [Odisha Homestay Establishment Scheme 2025 — Gazette 5549](https://dot.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2026-01/5549%20TOURISM%20%20Deptt_0.pdf).

[^homestay-cycle1-may2026]: [From Deomali to Daringbadi, homestays get a push](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/bhubaneswar/from-deomali-to-daringbadi-homestays-get-a-push/articleshow/131184349.cms).

[^homestay-market-jan2025]: [Homestay count grows manifold in Odisha but local experience missing](https://www.newindianexpress.com/states/odisha/2025/Jan/04/homestay-count-grows-manifold-in-odisha-but-local-experience-missing).

[^homestay-nidhi2025]: [One India, One Registration Initiative under NIDHI Portal](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2155162&lang=2&reg=48).

## Portal geography: a new dated snapshot · 1 October 2026

**61 Gram Panchayats, grouped into 19 clusters across 16 districts**, appear in the public Go Homestay area list captured today. These are calculated counts of distinct publisher IDs in a place list, not homestays built or open. The [saved table](../references/data/homestay-portal-areas-20261001.json) also preserves destination and block relationships.

The earlier May report above says 19 districts. Keep it as a historical secondary claim: the current portal has multiple clusters within some districts. Without the original allocation and amendment texts, this difference cannot establish a reduction, a reporting correction or definitive legal coverage.

Rayagada’s portal rows include both Kulusing and Puttasing, despite the reported replacement amendment. The [policy record](../economy/homestay-support.md) holds this discrepancy. Current eligibility and booking recommendations remain unverified.

[Official public area data](https://gohomestay.odisha.gov.in/api/allowAll/get-notified-gp-list). This is a geography story with a dated scope, not evidence of occupancy, revenue or host-income growth.

## Operating evidence checkpoint · 1 October 2026

World Tourism Day coverage supplies a new lead but conflicting quantities: [Odisha Connect](https://odishaconnect.com/odisha-celebrates-world-tourism-day-2026-with-digital-innovation-and-community-led-tourism/) reports 176 provisional-registration beneficiaries in an indexed passage; [OdishaBytes](https://odishabytes.com/odisha-signs-pacts-to-promote-homestay-heritage-adventure-tourism/amp/) says 17 in its directly read closing paragraph. The event is 27 September 2026. Both counts are held pending an original departmental release/register, outside the headline statistics. The reports may draw on the same event announcement.

OdishaBytes also reports an SBI financing MoU. Its signed terms, loan approvals and disbursements were not obtained. An agreement is not realised lending. No active-property census, completed compliance returns, occupancy or host-income data was recovered in this bounded search. Unknown remains unknown.

[Community ecotourism evidence](../statistics/ecotourism.md) now supplies a separately scoped programme income/visitor series; it does not fill homestay operating gaps.

body:
# Mining: national contribution and local development

**Odisha accounted for 43.7% of India’s mineral-production value in IBM’s 2024–25 highlights, excluding fuel, atomic and minor minerals.** The same vintage reports Odisha’s shares of iron-ore and bauxite output as **55%** and **72.7%**. These are different measures; they must not be added or described as a share of all mining including coal.

IBM reports **3.026 million tonnes of chromite**, all from Odisha, with output **down 3.9%** from the preceding year. Preserve that decline alongside the national contribution. These March 2025-vintage figures remain subject to revision. [IBM, printed pp. viii–ix](https://www.ibm.gov.in/writereaddata/files/1748864652683d8e8cdc8f1MSMP_MARCH25FINAL.pdf).

**Mining-area funds need an outcomes story.** CAG records **₹26,602.66 crore in leaseholder contributions** across Odisha’s 30 DMFs during 2015–16 to 2023–24. In its six sampled DMFs, **₹10,092.53 crore** had been spent against **₹20,947.52 crore sanctioned** by March 2024—**48.18%** of sanctions. The sample is Dhenkanal, Jajpur, Keonjhar, Mayurbhanj, Nabarangpur and Sundargarh. These sampled expenditure figures are not statewide utilisation rates or measures of working services. **Unresolved source conflict:** Table 4.1 reports ₹10,104.28 crore expenditure instead of Table 5.1’s ₹10,092.53 crore. The retained expenditure and derived 48.18% observations are held pending clarification; see the [cross-table comparison](../economy/dmf-community-outcomes.md#the-report-contains-conflicting-totals). [CAG Report 7 of 2026, executive summary pp. ix–x](https://cag.gov.in/webroot/uploads/download_audit_report/2026/Report-No.-7-of-the-year-2026_PMKKKY-06aba7c29ed78b2.53467972.pdf).

## Evidence boundaries

The IBM value comparison uses nominal reported production values, not real GSVA or government revenue. Resource stocks, production, dispatch, processing, sales and tax receipts need separate series. The CAG report was listed on 28 September 2026 but covers an earlier audit period; it is not a September 2026 balance.

[Canonical observations](../references/data/statistics-atlas.json) own the numeric records. [Mining coverage](../economy/mining.md) explains the next questions. New data will retain revision history and resolve older imported comparisons rather than silently replace them.

## Coal series checkpoint · 1 October 2026

[Coal production and resources](coal-production.md) adds fuel-mineral evidence alongside the IBM non-fuel figures. These coverage scopes must remain separate.

## Ore reconciliation checkpoint · 1 October2026

[Ore production](ore-production.md) adds eleven-year state observation coverage and three-year IBM comparison for four ores, including retained source differences.

## Baphlimali returns · 2 October2026 UTC

[Baphlimali’s mine-level return](../economy/bauxite-mine-identities.md) adds FY2024–25 output and DMF payment evidence. A mine’s payment is not district spending or a statewide total.

## Mining and community services · 2026-10-02

[Receipts, six DMFs and four case bundles](../economy/dmf-community-outcomes.md) adds actual/BE/RE scope, Tables5.1–5.2 and selected implementation findings. The existing48.18% uses sanctions;76.69% uses releases. Neither is a statewide benefit measure. All30DMF contributions and six-DMF collections including interest have different scopes.

body:
# Ore production: trends, places and source differences

**Odisha’s bauxite output nearly doubled over ten years in the state Directorate series:** 9.192 million tonnes in 2014–15 became 17.934 million tonnes in 2024–25, a calculated **95.1% increase**. This is ore production, not aluminium output. [State table](https://www.odishaminerals.gov.in/StatisticsReport/DespatchProductionReport).

The evidence now keeps production and despatch separately for five minerals across eleven annual observations. It also retains declines: chromite falls from 3.930 million tonnes in 2019–20 to 3.187 million tonnes in 2024–25 in that state capture, while manganese slips from 0.659 to 0.618 million tonnes in its final year. These attributed series do not settle differences with IBM.

## Where the sources disagree

| 2023–24 production, million tonnes | State Directorate | IBM Yearbook 2024, provisional |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Iron ore | 169.034 | 148.959 |
| Bauxite | 17.539 | 17.591967 |
| Chromite | 3.160 | 3.147954 |
| Manganese ore | 0.659 | 0.650856 |

The cause is unverified. Do not combine one agency’s Odisha numerator with another’s India denominator. Disputed observations are held for reconciliation. Even the two state website routes differ for 2019–20 iron ore: 146.016 versus 142.159; the existing five-year comparison remains a historical imported claim requiring review.

## Put mineral evidence back in its place

IBM’s 2023–24 bauxite producer table links NALCO and OMC to Koraput, and Utkal Alumina to Rayagada. These are mine-location districts, not office addresses or exact lease identities. Its chromite tables preserve Jajpur and Kendujhar quantities and mark Dhenkanal as labour-only reporting; no output is inferred from a reporting-mine count.

Resource tables are dated **1 April 2020** and separate reserves from remaining resources. For bauxite, 409.740 million tonnes are classified as reserves within 2,057.024 million tonnes total resources; for haematite iron ore the corresponding quantities are 2,798.749 and 9,409.331 million tonnes. Historical inventory does not become current mineable supply. [IBM Yearbook 2024](https://www.ibm.gov.in/writereaddata/files/177426215469c1178a48453IMYB_2024_EBookFinal.pdf).

[Structured mining evidence](../references/data/mining-programme.json) — all series, units, original values, source locators and held comparisons.

[Mining: minerals, industry and people](../economy/mining.md) — Connects ore quantities and district evidence to separate processing, revenue and livelihood research.

# Odisha’s textile and apparel export story

**₹757.33 crore in 2024–25**, up **6.9%** from ₹708.13 crore in 2023–24. This Ministry of Textiles series includes handicrafts alongside textiles and apparel.

![Five annual export values; fall in 2022–23 and recovery thereafter](../references/charts/textile-exports-2020-2025.svg)

Across these five annual observations, export value rose from ₹211.67 crore in 2020–21. The endpoints are four years apart; the first is the pandemic fiscal year. Growth was uneven, with a decline from ₹641.05 crore in 2021–22 to ₹528.39 crore in 2022–23. These are nominal rupees, not inflation-adjusted output.

## Evidence view

| Full financial year | INR crore |
|---|---:|
| 2020–21 | 211.6730 |
| 2021–22 | 641.0501 |
| 2022–23 | 528.3892 |
| 2023–24 | 708.1322 |
| 2024–25 | 757.3289 |

Source: Ministry of Textiles, 24 March 2026, DGCI&S table, Odisha row. Original values are INR lakh; divide by 100 for crore. This dated release is not claimed to be the latest available. It does not tell us which garment, named weave, factory or destination generated the sales. The Economic Survey’s narrower textile grouping must remain separate until definitions are reconciled.

## Interpretation limits

- Visits, not unique people; calendar year.
- Visits, not unique people; calendar year. State bulletin foreign count conflicts with Ministry of Tourism February 2026 table (87,854); do not silently replace or blend series.
- Conflicts with state Statistical Bulletin 2024 value 53,392. Hold foreign-growth headline until reconciliation.

## Reconciliation checkpoint · 30 September 2026

The Ministry's [8 December 2025 release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2200323&lang=1&reg=6), Annexure I, reports **87,854 foreign tourist visits in 2024** and **45,173 in 2023** for Odisha. The higher 2024 count therefore appears in an earlier central release as well as the saved February 2026 table. This is corroboration within government reporting, not an independent enumeration.

The state bulletin's saved **53,392** remains unresolved. No correction or definition bridge was found. Keep foreign-growth and affected total-visit headlines on hold. The ministry explicitly separates state visits from international arrivals; neither is a count of unique travellers to Odisha. Follow the annexure's 2020–2024 columns despite a wider period mentioned in surrounding prose.

[Reconciliation evidence](../references/data/tourism-series-reconciliation.json) preserves the checks and failures. [Tourism comparison](../economy/comparison-09-tourism.md) shows why a conflicting component also affects the total; [source recovery](../methods/source-reliability.md) records the remaining document work.

## Community-managed programme evidence

[Ecotourism](ecotourism.md) now has a dated primary income/visitor series. Its narrower programme scope must not be added to statewide tourist-visit totals.

# Editorial journey: Odisha’s Buddhist circuit

Build a focused cultural chapter around [Ratnagiri](../places/ratnagiri.md), [Udayagiri](../places/udayagiri-buddhist.md) and [Lalitgiri](../places/lalitgiri.md). The three records share an official circuit source, but each site should retain a distinct identity.

**Proposed opening:** “Let the stone tell the story.”

Commission an archaeologist or qualified guide to explain one object, structure or discovery at each site. A visual sequence can move from a close detail to the wider site and then its historical context. Religious significance should be explained with care and attribution.

Before publishing a trip, verify the current museum and site arrangements, transport, guiding availability and interpretation. Do not conflate Jajpur’s Buddhist Udayagiri with the Jain caves near Bhubaneswar. Relic identifications require attributed language rather than certainty added for dramatic effect.

Potential audiences include heritage travellers, students and visitors interested in Buddhist history. Market demand has not yet been measured.

## Source-backed opening: a name preserved in clay

**An excavated seal can bring a monastery’s name back into view.** At Udayagiri-2, the published readings identify Simhaprastha Mahavihara. A story can start with that small object, widen to the monastery, and then introduce Xuanzang’s account of learning in the wider region. [ASI,pp.123,141](https://asi.nic.in/admin/publications/ePublicationReportsDetails/download/47).

This is an editorial sequence grounded in different sources, not a claim that Xuanzang described this particular excavated monastery. Use a credited, permission-cleared image before producing a poster. [Related reading](../history/buddhist-learning.md) — Provides the chronology and separates excavation from literary testimony. The account’s 10,000-plus monks must not become an invented Pushpagiri student roll.

# Forest work: understanding the support behind the trade

**₹24.635 crore in compassionate grants is recorded for FY2025–26** on Odisha's Kendu Leaf Organisation welfare page. The accompanying total is **1,235 grant records** across pluckers/binders and seasonal staff. [Official table](https://kenduleaves.odisha.gov.in/welfare-measures).

This is one specific form of support associated with death or permanent disability. It is not the whole welfare budget, the trade's sales value or the earnings of a typical collector. The page was read on 1 October 2026 and displays a 9 September update; individual payments have not been independently audited here.

| Follow the money | What the measure tells us |
| --- | --- |
| Sale proceeds | Value of marketed leaves |
| Wages and collection payments | Payment for work or leaf supply |
| Bonuses and incentives | Separate programme benefits |
| Compassionate grants | Support under a specific welfare category |

These rows are categories to distinguish, not an additive flow diagram. A larger compassionate-grant amount does not by itself show improved wellbeing. The [evidence view](../statistics/forest-products.md) retains prior years, the incomplete current year and unresolved totals elsewhere. An effective story should credit the people and explain the programme without confusing assistance with prosperity.

[Related reading](../statistics/forest-products.md) — Explains how payment categories differ; does not infer typical earnings or improved wellbeing from a grant total.

[The sale-proceeds allocation](../statistics/forest-products.md) now shows why advances, commissions and payable balances must remain separate from verified worker receipts. # Seventy years, from loom to market

**70 years** — Boyanika’s reported institutional milestone in May 2026.

A textile carries more than a pattern: it needs a path from the loom to the person who wears it. Boyanika’s anniversary account offers one dated chapter in that market story. [Original account, 14 May 2026](https://boyanika.com/boyanika-wear-your-heritage/).

**Suggested visual:** a simple line from 1956 to 2026, then three labelled textile details: [Sambalpuri](../handlooms/sambalpuri-bandha.md), [Bomkai](../handlooms/bomkai.md), [Khandua](../handlooms/khandua.md). Photographs and maker permissions are still needed; no media rights assumed.

[Evidence and comparison](../handlooms/garments-and-markets.md). This is an editorial draft based on an institutional account, with no measured livelihood impact or export-growth claim. No human review or publication is claimed.

## A second visual idea: where the pattern enters

Label these as examples from attributed technique descriptions. Commission or obtain permission for process photographs; no existing image rights or maker participation is assumed.

## Story candidate: words woven into cloth

A future visual feature can invite readers to notice the lettering, then meet the named creator through sourced context.

Do not turn them into claims about average artisans’ earnings or current order lead times.

# Institution building, measured one stage at a time

**₹25.20 crore in reported university expenses, FY 2024–25.** KISS Deemed to be University’s signed statement gives a concrete financial scale for one part of Odisha’s education landscape.

The prior-year column is ₹24.02 crore: about 4.94% nominal growth. Expenses include depreciation; the figures are neither cash spending nor measured social impact. They cover the university, not the KISS school, Foundation or KIIT. [Statement, p.2](https://university.kiss.ac.in/docs/Accounts/Balance_Sheets/KISSDU_FY_2024-25.pdf).

The original university notification explicitly distinguishes the school. Keep that boundary visible when connecting institutions, money and students. [Notification, p.2](https://university.kiss.ac.in/docs/IIQA/KISS-DU-NOTIFICATION-DT-25.08.2017.pdf).

[Explore Achyuta Samanta’s journey](../people/achyuta-samanta.md) for parliamentary service, legal milestones and the unanswered outcome questions. Suggested visual: two labelled expense bars with the entity, financial years and nominal basis visible. Editorial draft; no human review or website publication claimed.

[Related reading](../people/achyuta-samanta.md) — Links a scoped institutional financial statement to founder history without equating spending with social impact.

## A second lens: access to postgraduate study

**948 postgraduate students with institution-funded full tuition reimbursement** are reported in KISS’s 2025 NIRF SDG submission. This covers two-year PG programmes across study years, with no explicit census day on the row. It is institution-reported tuition support, not proof of independently measured learning or employment impact. [Submission, p.1](https://university.kiss.ac.in/docs/NIRF/SDG_Institutions.pdf).

Use this as a separate access card alongside the financial story; do not divide expenses by this PG count to invent per-student costs. [Detailed outcomes and limitations](../people/achyuta-samanta.md).

## Preserve the accounts’ vintages

The FY2023–24 original and later comparative statement agree on the ₹24.02crore total but differ in the grants/other-income split. The total-based comparison above is unchanged; component-level growth stays on hold. The original file’s notes mix society/Delhi references and2021 balances with university headings, so further scope reconciliation is needed. [Original accounts, pp.2,11–12](https://university.kiss.ac.in/docs/Accounts/Balance_Sheets/KISSDU_FY_2023-24.pdf). [Exact comparison and founding-stage limits](../people/achyuta-samanta.md).

# Beyond the metal: Odisha’s small suppliers

**₹652.19 crore in purchases from Odisha-based micro and small enterprises.** That is what NALCO reports for 2025–26, giving the mineral economy a concrete connection to smaller businesses.

The company reports ₹1,447.94 crore in total purchases from MSEs across locations. Odisha-based suppliers therefore account for **about 45% of this MSE total**. This is procurement of goods and services, not supplier profit, jobs created or a share of all company purchasing. [NALCO annual report, printed p.56, section 19(a)](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

A simple proposed visual: one bar split into 45% Odisha-based MSE purchases and 55% other MSE purchases. Label the denominator and year directly. Pair it with a credited supplier’s story only after finding a named enterprise and evidence for its actual work; no interview or participant endorsement is claimed.

[The bauxite-to-aluminium chain](../economy/bauxite-to-aluminium.md) explains the industrial context. [Rourkela’s steel case](../economy/rourkela-steel-chain.md) asks the same questions of another industry, without assigning NALCO’s supplier results to it.

[Mining research](../economy/mining.md) — Connects plant and supplier evidence to the broader mining programme without equating company results with household benefits.

## What can be compared

NALCO’s FY2024–25 report records ₹570.46 crore from Odisha-based MSEs within ₹898.76 crore from all MSEs. Preserve these alongside the following year’s figures, with report editions and denominators visible. Supplier location does not prove where goods were manufactured. [Earlier-year source](../sources/mining-nalco-sd2025.md).

Rourkela’s ₹133.46 crore disclosure measures purchase orders placed on Odisha-based LSSIs. It is a separate measure, so we do not combine it with NALCO’s purchases into an Odisha total. [RSP source](../sources/mining-rsp-subplac2026.md).

For a named supplier story, the next evidence needs are an actual award or order, the enterprise’s location and classification at that date, and a paid-invoice or completion record. A tender invitation or vendor registration alone cannot establish business received. No supplier interview or endorsement is claimed.

title: Odisha’s Best-Kept Secret — The Art of Cooking with Fire — campaign draft

body:
# Odisha’s Best-Kept Secret — The Art of Cooking with Fire — campaign draft

## Campaign direction

**Odisha’s Best-Kept Secret**

*The Art of Cooking with Fire*

The user selected this campaign tag and subtitle on 1 October 2026. “Best-kept secret” is evocative editorial language, not a measured claim about awareness. Introduce poda within the story and explain the different cooking methods. Campaign wording approval does not establish factual review, media rights or website publication approval.

## Reader-facing story draft

Start with a vegetable, and follow the heat. Baigana poda turns roasted eggplant into a mustard-scented mash; tomato poda brings another roasted accompaniment to the table. Move to the parcels: mushrooms and fish seasoned and folded into leaves, or prawns charred inside sal leaves. Each wrapper makes the opening part of the meal. [Vegetable account](../food/baigana-poda.md), [tomato account](../food/tomato-poda.md), [mushroom and fish](../sources/food-patrapoda-lopa2024.md), [prawns](../food/chingudi-patrapoda.md).

Then widen the story. A historical Odisha Tourism menu describes leaf-cooked chicken; published reporting connects Odisha’s baunsa poda mansa with meat cooked inside bamboo. These are invitations to meet and credit the cooks behind each preparation, with local details still to document. [Chicken evidence](../food/kukuda-patrapoda.md), [bamboo evidence](../food/baunsa-poda-mansa.md).

The finish can be sweet. Poda pitha brings rice and festival memories; chhena poda brings fresh cheese and a browned surface. Roasted, wrapped or baked, the connection runs across ingredients and courses. **Discover the many ways Odisha cooks.** [Pitha](../food/poda-pitha.md), [cheese sweet](../food/chhena-poda.md).

## Short video script · draft

Estimated 35–45 seconds; not recorded or timed with the user’s clone.

“In Odisha, follow one word: poda. Start with roasted eggplant. Add tomato, sharp with mustard oil. Open a leaf parcel: mushrooms, fish or prawns. Follow the story to chicken in leaves and meat cooked inside bamboo. Then stay for dessert: poda pitha and chhena poda. Roasting, leaf cooking, slow baking—different methods, a delicious connection. Odisha’s best-kept secret: the art of cooking with fire.”

Visual sequence proposal: vegetable roasting → opening a leaf parcel → a credited bamboo-cooking demonstration → slicing pitha and chhena poda. Use consented, correctly labelled footage of the actual method. An oven-baked example must not be presented as a filmed ember preparation. Media and music rights remain unestablished; no video has been generated.

## Poster copy · draft

ODISHA’S BEST-KEPT SECRET

The Art of Cooking with Fire

From roasted vegetables and leaf-wrapped delicacies to caramelised sweets—discover Odisha’s poda traditions.

## Editorial evidence controls

The [nine-entry evidence collection](../food/poda-and-fire-cooking.md) distinguishes source types, methods and unresolved fields. The linked draft is a proposed tasting narrative, not a traditional fixed menu or an available tour. Do not claim “everything is barbecued”, oldest/largest/best in India, uniquely Odishan leaf cooking, or a common origin for all these foods. Enduri’s steaming and modern enclosed/oven adaptations stay distinct. No recipe testing, human factual review, measured audience response or publication approval is claimed.

## Website adaptation · 1 October 2026

“Odisha cooks with fire” is the proposed website collection title, drawing on this campaign direction. The earlier selected campaign wording remains above. The first candidate uses three real, licensed photographs and links three preparation stories to a saved food-reading journey. No video or bookable tasting tour is implied. See the [collection data](../food/fire-cooking-stories.json).

# What remains after growing the rice?

**About ₹14,142 per hectare remained after the study’s C2 costs.** This is a historical regional case published in 2023, with the paddy survey year unresolved—not a current Odisha average.

| The case, per hectare | Reported amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Paddy and by-product value | ₹79,050 |
| C2 cost, including valued family labour and land | ₹64,908.43 |
| Reported net income above C2 | ₹14,141.58 |

[Original study, Tables 6–7](https://ndpublisher.in/countpdfdownload.php?id=5788&pdf=EAv68n1p.pdf). The one-paisa difference from subtracting the displayed rounded costs is retained in the evidence record. Values are nominal; valuation year is unknown.

The editorial lesson is straightforward: a bigger harvest or a higher sale value does not tell us what a farmer keeps. Future rice stories should connect output with actual receipts, paid costs, family labour and land.

[Related reading](../economy/rice-economy.md) — Connects the regional cost case with procurement, seed enterprises and unresolved payment scope.

# Rice kept for taste, seed saved for tomorrow

**A rice story can begin with the meal people want to keep making.** Farmers in a study published in 2026 linked Kalahans with kanika and pakhala, and Sapuri with popped rice at weddings. These are local participant accounts, with their study scope retained. [Food-use evidence](../food/rice-varieties.md).

# The money moving through Odisha’s paddy procurement

**₹28,718 crore in MSP and input assistance** was reported paid to paddy farmers for **KMS 2024–25**. That is the Food Supplies & Consumer Welfare Department’s combined payment figure. It is not farmer profit. [Annual report, printed p.29](https://foododisha.in/Download/annual-activity-glance-25-26.pdf).

The same report separates **7,345,707 tonnes in kharif** and **1,918,528 tonnes in rabi** in its detailed table: about **92.64 lakh tonnes across the marketing year**. Seasonal quantities can be added; seasonal farmer counts cannot be treated as unique annual people without removing overlap.

The combined payment is close to, but does not exactly equal, the detailed quantity multiplied by the common-paddy rate plus assistance. Settlement details remain unverified. The earlier year’s figure covers MSP alone, so a payment-growth percentage would mix categories.

[Related reading](../economy/rice-economy.md) — Explains the payment reconciliation and the difference between marketing and financial years.

# More rice from each hectare: Odisha’s changing harvest

**Rice yield was about 55% higher in 2023–24 than ten years earlier.** The same official historical table shows output up 51.6%, while rice crop area was 2.2% smaller. This is a description of recorded changes; it does not isolate their causes.

![Odisha rice output with every annual observation from 2012–13 to 2023–24](../references/figures/rice-output-trend.png)

The five-year comparison also shows higher output (+49.2%). But 2023–24 production fell 3.3% from 2022–23, and the chart retains the earlier setbacks. Starting-year conditions affect any endpoint comparison. [Source: Odisha Agriculture Statistics 2023–24, printed p.90](https://agri.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-05/OAS%20A4.pdf).

[Rice economics](../economy/rice-economy.md) connects the trend to procurement and the evidence needed to assess farmer returns. This is an editorial draft; source checking is not public-release approval.

[Related economics](../economy/rice-economy.md) — Connects statewide crop trends with economic definitions; higher yield alone does not establish higher farmer profit.

# From milk to market: the work behind a sweet

**A sweet connects more than a shop and a customer.** A published Pahala case study traces chhena from Niali to sweet makers and markets elsewhere in Odisha and West Bengal. It makes dairy supply, preparation and distribution part of the same story. [Study, December 2023, pp.2306–2308](https://ndpublisher.in/admin/issues/EAv68n5z11.pdf).

A useful illustration is a simple chain: **chhena producer → trader → sweet maker and shop → customer**. Show credited people and places once source material and image rights are established.

The research also identifies perishability and packaging as business questions. This is an opportunity to investigate how traditional food reaches wider markets; it is not a measured forecast of growth. The study’s revenue extrapolation is withheld because its quantities and arithmetic conflict.

[Read the evidence and open questions](../economy/rasagola-and-sweets.md) — Connects the story to scoped economic research, preserving sample limits and unresolved market totals.

Editorial draft only. No human review, maker interview, media rights or public release established.

## A rice-based companion story

Korakhai broadens the collection beyond dairy sweets. Its [1999 town-directory entry](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/44136/download/47792/DH_21_2001_KHO.pdf) connects Bhubaneswar’s sweet making with outward trade; [the food entry](../food/korakhai.md) connects it with named confectioners. A possible visual pairs the existing dairy supply chain with this historical rice-based trade record. This is editorial context, not a measured comparison between industries or proof of current export sales.

## People keep the craft moving

The collection now follows a reported Magji family practice in Sadangi and a dated Rasabali market appearance in Bhubaneswar. These suggest portraits of skill and the journey from local preparation to wider selling places. [Magji account](https://interviewtimes.net/dhenkanal-magji-gets-gi-tag/); [Rasabali event reporting](https://www.newindianexpress.com/cities/bhubaneswar/2026/Jan/16/stalls-selling-gi-tagged-products-major-crowd-puller-at-sisir-saras). Use attributed testimony and dated scenes; no sales-growth headline or current maker availability is established.

# Taste Odisha: a collection of kitchens

**Campaign line:** “One state. So many ways to welcome you.”

Open with the act of serving. Move between [pakhala](../food/pakhala.md), [dalma](../food/dalma.md), the [pitha collection](../food/pitha.md) and a [chhena poda](../food/chhena-poda.md) slice. Let each contributor explain what the food means in their own home or business. These selected examples introduce a collection; they do not stand in for every community’s cuisine.

## Proposed formats

- Poster: one dish, its name, place or contributor, and one sensory line grounded in the photographed preparation.
- Short feature: one maker, one attributed preparation, one variation and one occasion.
- Video: serving close-up, maker’s voice, process detail, finished plate and place name.

For a national audience, test “your next food journey.” For international audiences, retain the local name and add a plain-language ingredient or technique description. Gather audience response before choosing a universal message.

## Production needs

Recipe confirmation, contributor consent, original imagery, correct names, ingredient-specific allergy information and current visitor details where a business is featured. The user’s AI clone can provide a connecting introduction once the chosen service and asset are available; the KB does not contain a rendered clone video.

body:
# Utkal: a trading culture, building its next global chapter

## Positioning

**Utkal · Odisha**

**A trading culture. A new global chapter.**

The commercial proposition is that Odisha already has modern trade activity worth showing, and a distinctive way to introduce it. Heritage supplies the opening; present evidence supplies the business case.

## Story sequence

Open with [Boita Bandana](../culture/boita-bandana.md), then show the [Paradip institutional connection](../trade/paradip-bridge.md). Move to the port’s measured activity and the state’s merchandise-export comparison. End with a named maker or business, researched separately, and a useful next action.

The question “If we could do it then, why can’t we do it now?” becomes: **“We are trading today. What can we build next?”** This invites ambition without pretending that an ancient achievement forecasts modern performance.

## Three campaign directions

- **Trade has a place in our culture.** A ritual-led film connected to an actual institution and its work.
- **Odisha is already connected.** A contemporary trade feature with destinations, products and counterparties as the evidence grows.
- **The next voyage begins with what we make.** A maker or exporter portrait leading to an attributable purchase or business enquiry.

## Copy ready for development

“Every voyage begins with the courage to look beyond the shore. In Odisha, the memory of the maritime trader is still celebrated. Today, a new chapter is being written by the people who make, move and trade. Meet the Odisha building its place in the world.”

This is campaign copy. Support accompanying factual captions through the [headline bank](../trade/headline-bank.md). The line does not assert that every modern enterprise descends from ancient traders.

## Creative treatment

Use the project’s deep red, ivory and ochre palette. Pair miniature boats with contemporary activity through an editorial transition, not a simulated historical reconstruction presented as documentary footage. Mark illustrative animation as illustration. Include local voices and credited work.

## Claim discipline

Choose strong facts and clear comparisons. Do not knowingly create a false impression by dropping the unit, hiding a crucial denominator, converting an interpretation into certainty, or making a proposed project look operational. That preserves the campaign’s ability to stand up to scrutiny.

# Forest products, local enterprise: a documented Odisha strength

**₹10.72 crore in reported Van Dhan sales placed Odisha highest in a December 2023 parliamentary table.** The underlying figure is ₹1,072.01 lakh, covering cumulative programme reporting rather than one year's turnover. [Reply, annexure p.3](https://sansad.in/getFile/loksabhaquestions/annex/1714/AU1179.pdf?source=pqals).

Odisha accounted for about **26.1%** of the published all-India programme total. This includes both forest and non-forest products; it is not a measure of the entire forest economy, exports or collector income.

One way to tell the human story is to follow the work: a leaf becomes a plate, honey is processed, and tamarind is deseeded. A [2021 ministry account](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1715921) names community clusters pursuing these activities. Their individual sales and current operations remain research questions.

Suggested campaign direction: **“The value of a forest also lives in the work of its people.”** This is editorial wording, not a measured income-impact claim. Keep the December 2023 date visible in any card or poster; this evidence does not support a present-day ranking.

[Related reading](../statistics/forest-products.md) — Explains the programme denominator and separates turnover from collector receipts.

# Woven in Odisha: meet the making

**Campaign line:** “Know the hands. Know the cloth.”

Begin with a single piece rather than a sweeping claim. A [Kotpad](../handlooms/kotpad.md) textile, a [Khandua](../handlooms/khandua.md) piece or a [Habaspuri](../handlooms/habaspuri.md) example can each lead to a distinct portrait. Ask the maker to explain the decisions visible in the finished cloth.

## Proposed feature structure

Show the whole piece, then a detail. Name the maker and making place. Explain the technique only after it has been verified for that piece. Include material, care and a transparent purchase route where one is established. Record the source of all sustainability claims separately.

For fashion audiences, style a credited object in contemporary use. For design audiences, document process and material choices. Do not describe every Odisha textile as Sambalpuri or every patterned textile as ikat.

## Commercial research

Interview participating makers about commissions, capacity, payment terms and how they want to be represented. Check a seller’s product provenance and current fulfilment. A story should help readers understand value without inventing income, labour-time or market-demand statistics.

Examine how Odisha produces, works, finances enterprise and connects with markets. Separate output from income, credit balances from investment, and approvals from operating capacity. Transport and digital networks belong here as infrastructure and also connect to daily life.

## Homestays and local enterprise

**Internet subscriptions: 30.56 million subscriptions** — 2026-03-31; Odisha.[^weekly-trai-mar2026]

All Odisha state-based internet subscriptions, broadband plus narrowband, wired plus wireless; density uses projected population. Subscriptions are not unique users; density may exceed 100. **Total fish production: 12.7 lakh tonnes** — 2025-26; Odisha.[^weekly-fisheries-jul2026]
